## Qualitying The Life Out of Games
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v62Tj9byHlA

I first played Minecraft back in the days of the beta, and all these years later, the experience of my initial play session has always stayed fresh in my brain. It's one I've talked about before, and certainly will talk about again, because I really can't think of many games that have been able to pull me into the core loop as seamlessly and impactfully as Minecraft did. When I spawned into the vast world, I spent a bunch of time marveling at just how much world there seemed to be, and the level at which I could interact with it. And then, I got to work. Before getting in the game, I had watched part of a video to see if it was something I wanted to buy, and through that, learned a bit about crafting. So I collected and made a few things, but not long after, the sun began to set, and the growls of monsters and hiss of some weird-looking green thing started to close in around me. And the threat of losing everything I had spent all that time gathering became painfully clear. Night was not something to ignore. It had to be planned around. And so my plan became to make a little hole in the wall so nothing would kill me. Not wanting to just stand around forever, though, I did the only thing I really could do, and dug. And then dug some more, and then broke into a cave, and without the game explicitly telling me to, I had fallen into the basic starting loop of exploring outside during the day and in the mines at night. A loop that certainly became less rigid over time, but did still consistently push me to engage with different aspects of the game. That made me plan what to do at night, whether that was fortifying a base above ground or delving beneath it. This simple cycle, the transition between relative calm and true threat, forced me to understand and respect the world. It was the exact kind of thing I always hoped a game could make me feel. A few months later, Mojang updated the game, adding beds that let you skip through the night. The materials needed to craft one were all things you could pretty easily get immediately. Now, I understand that this is a mechanic that isn't necessary to use. And typically when I play the game on my own, I don't use it. That isn't as much of an option when playing with others, though. As it turns out, being the lone holdout that stops everyone else from sleeping while making the argument that skipping the night ruins the sanctity of the game is a tough look. Beyond that, even if one chooses not to use it, it is easier said than done to truly ignore that it's part of the game. It is the simple solution to a complex problem, and pretending like it's not there has a cost, too. Because despite me personally not loving the mechanic, I would actually say that adding beds to Minecraft was the right call. Aside from the game's clear aim at being approachable to a vast audience, there also comes a point in Minecraft where dealing with night and figuring out how to be efficient at any given time becomes less of a point of meaningful tension. Later in the game, it stops being the drive for exploration and progression. Not to mention, the endgame goal of finding the Ender Dragon requires a fair bit of traversing the map in a way that isn't super feasible in the dark, so most players would wait it out anyway. Also, by that point, players have already faced tougher challenges between the Nether and deep cave networks, and will be kitted out accordingly, making the night just a slight inconvenience. When that deep along the progression path, it no longer serves the same purpose of pushing the core loop. Frankly, my real issue is with how easy and early it can be crafted. It is obviously hard to balance a game like Minecraft, as it is so non-linear, but I think the pacing of the game would make more sense if this wasn't something one could get until going through the core loop a whole bunch of times. Maybe have it require something from deep in a mine or even the Nether. Because as it stands, it undercuts one of the aspects of Minecraft that made the game so appealing in the first place. These types of upgrades have always been interesting to me, as they essentially allow players to stop engaging with the previously established core gameplay loop. It is the recognition that the thing that drew players in at the start may push them away by the end, and so some shift needs to happen. Whether it be getting the Lordvessel in Dark Souls that allows players to teleport between bonfires, or Revali's Gale in Breath of the Wild which vastly simplifies traversal, games often have a point where their more frictional aspects have an off-ramp. Sometimes it is a big shift like the ones I mentioned, and sometimes it is a more gradual one like incremental upgrades. Either way, it serves to eliminate or shift the friction that defines the early hours. I've always lumped upgrades like these as being part of the wide umbrella of quality of life. I know we tend to conceptualize quality of life as added-on features, whether that be through patches or re-releases or general design trends across the industry, but I think it fits this as well, as all these things have the same purpose. To take away friction that players or playtesters seem especially annoyed by at one point or another. Now, I know I've already pointed to one quality of life update in a game that I was not a huge fan of, and fairly, some of you might think I'm on the verge of talking about how back in my day we had to walk to school 10 miles uphill both ways and were better for it. So I do want to make it clear that I think mechanics that are often pinned as quality of life features are not inherently bad or good. They are tools that developers can deploy to shape how their game is experienced, and sometimes those tools are needed. The reality is, there are lots of interesting gameplay loops that center around a level of friction that isn't sustainable and will feel burdensome over a long enough period of time, and so it makes sense to add mechanics that ease the amount any player has to engage with them. However, I do worry sometimes about the ways they are implemented, and also the ways we talk about them. There are some quality of life features that I think generally always make sense to include. More often than not, these are ones you will find within menus, whether that be remapping controls or wider accessibility options. Things that players opt into to tailor the experience to their specific needs. Where it gets a bit trickier, though, is with stuff implemented into the core gameplay loop. By and large, I think when the focus is just on reducing friction and providing something that players have grown comfortable with, instead of examining how the reduced friction can be used to elevate a game in other ways, it risks watering down the experience. In relation to upgrades within a game that ease friction from the early hours, it often can turn into a band-aid solution that doesn't properly address the bigger problems. Take The Blood of Dawnwalker. Its core combat is built around a directional system where you can increase your chances of getting a hit by attacking from various angles. And if you press the deflect button along with the direction the enemy is attacking from, you can get a perfect parry and have the opportunity to do all sorts of additional damage. If you do the wrong input, though, you take a hit. This makes it so there is a ton of intentionality with every fight. You can't just mash attack and dodge every once in a while. You have to pay attention and wait for openings. And for better or worse, this gives weight to every single encounter. It asks for a type of involvement that puts a lot on the player. Now, this system, while fun to learn, does get a bit tiring. While it is not a turn-based game, it does have a my turn, your turn feel to the combat, and the enemy variety is not wide enough to keep that interesting for the game's runtime. Even between the various enemies, attack patterns feel too similar. And aside from a couple bosses, the fights never get more interesting than they are in the first few hours. It didn't take long for things to feel rote and restrictive. And instead of upgrades expanding on the core combat system, pretty much every one you get lets you opt out of the directional combat more and more. For instance, you unlock special moves that are able to interrupt an enemy's action so you can get a big hit in or do damage over time. You get various stat buffs that improve the efficiency of your blocks and directional attacks, helping you kill enemies in fewer hits. And you even can spec into an ability that makes it so if you miss the directional input on a parry, instead of taking the hit, it just treats it as a standard block. Of course, it is a big skill tree and you don't need to opt into all of these things, but no matter what you do opt into, it will lead to needing to do directional attacking and blocking less often. Had these upgrades not simplified combat, I think it would have got tiring even quicker, but nothing is really done with this shift to keep things interesting. It's just trying to hold things at bay as fights turn into spamming abilities as much as you can. By contrast, a solid example of a game that capitalizes on simplifying a central mechanic can be seen with Pragmata. The game is based around a hacking mechanic where you have to navigate various sized grids and reach a specific node that then overloads the enemy and exposes their weak spots. What makes this interesting is that it is all done while also shooting enemies and avoiding attacks. It splits your brain in a way that makes both of these relatively simple actions feel so much more complicated than they have any business feeling, setting it apart from really every other third person shooter. That said, it does also require doing this minigame a lot. And like Dawnwalker, it asks for

of things to do and people to see. Also, due to it being easier to find NPCs, they can be on the move far more often, creating a sense that they have lives beyond just waiting around for you all the time. And while they have some patterns, there is loads of variance in terms of where they go and what they do, leading to an overwhelming amount of unique interactions that all help create this illusion that all the other characters are engaging with the town and each other as much as you are. An illusion that the place is alive. Yes, it makes stuff easier, but they find new ways to make things meaningful. Most importantly, it utilizes the lesson friction in a way that Stardew Valley wouldn't have really been able to had Concerned8 patched these things in later, as the core of the game has a different focus. While these two games do a lot of very similar things, and look the same, and sometimes sound the same, they do end up evoking very different emotions in the player. Ultimately, I think it's important for developers and players to always consider what any quality of life mechanic impacts, what it allows for, and what it diminishes. A refrain I hear all too often is something along the lines of it's 2026 and every game should have X, whether that be autosaves or fast travel or minimaps or whatever the convenience feature might be, and that sort of stance focuses on the comfort and not on what the feature can accomplish in any given game. It asks the wrong thing. It also insinuates that the aspects we have quality of life out of most games don't have value, which is very much not the case. I recently finished a title that came out earlier this year called Banquet for Fools. It is an isometric CRPG with a peculiar yet compelling combat system, and in it you explore this massive island to solve the mystery of what happened to one of the outposts. And the devs made a lot of design decisions that I think many would say are unacceptable in a game made in current year. The main one being that there is no automatic quest log or map markers. Instead, tracking these things are at the discretion of the player. You can take quick notes while in conversations, make more detailed ones to track hints and quests and anything else you might want to remember, and place markers on local maps as well as the wider map of the island. Some NPCs may repeat a few key points, but many will not. So you actually have to pay attention to what is said. It typically is pretty obvious what pieces of information will be relevant, so you won't be transcribing every conversation, but it does require players to lock in in a way most games do not. Just clicking through is not an option. I wasn't fully sold on any of this before trying it, but it ended up giving me one of the most engaging gaming experiences I've had in a long time. It asked me to care about and respect its world and story, and I was rewarded with a world and story worth respecting, worth putting the effort in for. It also made every quest feel more like a mystery than a checklist. One of the cooler things the game does is whenever you finish a quest, it jumps to this little victory screen where your characters pose and you're told what rewards you get, the best of course being when your aura is increased. What makes this so cool is that you don't always know you're even technically on a quest, or that what you're doing is what you are supposed to do. So every time it cut to this, I felt such a rush to see some proof of progress. All of this combined also makes things more memorable. I got busy in the middle of my playthrough and took a few weeks off, and then I was worried that I'd go back and be completely lost, so I took another few weeks off, and then two months had passed before I decided to give it a shot again. Between looking through my notes as well as having memories triggered from just being back in the game, I remembered pretty much everything that mattered within two minutes of playing. Comparatively, I've taken far shorter breaks with games that remind you of stuff all the time and not been able to remember anything. I've seen posts from people who gave up on the game saying they wish it had quality of life features like a quest log, that it'd be better with one. And while I agree that more people probably would have played it if that were the case, I also think far fewer people would adore it in the way they do. Now, I will admit, as much as I loved Banquet for Fools and found the experience of playing it to be so refreshing, the truth is, I'm not interested in playing another game that asks that much of me for probably another year. And so the point is not that this should be the norm. It is that we should question why things are the norm and what they actually add. We should question why we think we need certain mechanics in everything, and what we might be missing from refusing to engage with any game that doesn't have them. It's that we should ask more from quality of life. Of all the games I've ever played that have pushed me out of my comfort zone, that have asked me to engage with them in ways that go beyond what most titles would dare to ask, none of them have resonated with me quite as much as Rain World. And so when Lost in Cult, this video's sponsor, announced their latest design works book that is all about Rain World, I was beyond thrilled. For years now, Lost in Cult has been producing some of the best gaming-centric books out there. Whether it's collections of essays like this one from a few years back about mansions in games, which I actually wrote a piece for, or their design work series that examines the creative process of some of the best indie games ever made, like Outer Wilds and now Rain World, they consistently put out wonderfully crafted books that are worth having for both the writing and art within them. This book on Rain World, which will be out next year as a celebration of the game's 10th anniversary, includes detailed insights on its production from its primary developers, an examination of its reception and the community that has been built around it, especially in regards to modding, and a collection of the bits of lore hidden throughout the game's world and the fan theories that have sprouted around them. Along with the book, they are also offering a deluxe edition that comes with all sorts of extras, like a field guide on the flora and fauna of Rain World, a deck of cards with daily pearls of wisdom, a reversible poster, hologram stickers, a postcard set, and the most perfect bookmark to ever exist. The deluxe edition will be available until November 30th, 2026, so if any of that sounds interesting to you, don't wait too long. ## How We Play Games
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=knXjtvIoBpg

Gaming doesn't feel the same anymore. This is a sentiment I've seen more and more every passing year. Countless videos with this exact thesis have come across my feed on YouTube, always paired with a wistful thumbnail that makes the nostalgia centers of my brain explode with longing. They tend to be emotional explorations as to how gaming has changed, how it used to hit different, how it used to be better. Honestly, I'd be surprised if this isn't something you felt to some degree. I know I have. I definitely still love games, and every year I play plenty of titles that surprise and move me, but playing games now does feel different than it did 10 years ago. 20 years ago. Dare I say it, 30 years ago. With a lot of these examinations, and especially the conversations they spur, the blame often gets placed on games themselves. Typically boiling down to modern games bad, classic games good. Now while I do relate to feeling some amount of dissatisfaction with modern gaming, I actually think by and large games today are as good if not better than they've ever been. The best stuff isn't always coming from the types of studios they used to come from, but incredible games are still coming out all the time. Just looking at the past 2-3 years, I can easily point to multiple titles that rank amongst my favorites of all time, as well as many, many others that aren't all that far off. In this era, we are getting more games than ever, which of course does mean there are also more mediocre and bad games than ever as well, but the number of quality titles at our fingertips is staggering. Truly, this year alone has been more than I can keep up with. But despite all of that, the sense of missing something that used to be there does still linger. I don't always feel it while playing stuff, but when I do, it's hard to push away. It'd be nice if there was a single, clear source of this feeling, as it'd make it easier to address, but ultimately, it seems to be a lot of things working together, and depending on whom you are, certain aspects will hold more weight, whether that be the ways one's taste and personality changes as they get older, or how the gaming industry is at the complete mercy of corporate interests and stockholder happiness, or the feeling that tech is advancing at a less noticeable rate than it once did, leading to games not looking all that different than they did a decade ago, or the countless other things that create a layer of distance between people and the things they play. There is one piece of it that I find myself thinking about more than the rest, though, a piece that weighs heaviest on me, and it's that the ways we play games have changed. Or at least, the ways I play games have changed. And I don't think there's any way to really go back. To a degree, this aspect relates to pieces of all the other aspects I already mentioned. For instance, on the point of growing up, lots of people like to say that gaming not feeling the same anymore is part of maturing, that games are something you eventually move past as you find better ways to spend your free time. I think this specific read is largely bullshit. At the end of the day, hobbies are all meant to entertain, and I don't think there's a lot of use in rating how valuable they are. And if we were to rate that, given that the place you'll see these kinds of thoughts most often are on Instagram posts and YouTube comments, implying that the people saying these things like to spend their time on those platforms, I do not believe they are using their free time any better. They have not reached some sort of enlightenment. With all of that said, getting older has undeniably shifted things for me. But it is less about maturing past games, and more about how maturing has created barriers to playing games. Obviously, as an adult, I have responsibilities I did not have in the past. A job, housework, and most notably, kids. Admittedly, as my job is to make videos about games, I am able to dedicate way more time to playing them than the average person my age, but even for me, there are still limitations to any given play session that can add a sort of pressure to it all. A feeling that I need to accomplish a certain level of enjoyment within whatever window I've got. Additionally, by virtue of being alive for as long as I have been, I've played a ton of games, and that has shaped my tastes in a way where I value stuff that feels fresh and unique. As such, there are plenty of times where I play something I recognize as being good, but it treads too much of the same ground I've already seen in a dozen games before, making the experience fall a bit flat to no real fault of the game. While these aspects do create some friction, I believe they can largely be worked around through intentionality with one's time and what they choose to play. The part of growing up that has impacted how I play games more than anything else, though, isn't as easy to work around. And that's how my living situation and social life have changed over the years. When I think back to playing games as a kid, the golden years of gaming, someone else was almost always there with me. My brother, my neighbor, my friends, sometimes even my parents. Whether it was single player or multiplayer, it was rare for any gaming session to not be witnessed by someone else, at least for some amount of time. Pretty much whenever I invited a friend over, the pretext was that we would play video games. Sometimes it would be the main focus, and other times it would be the thing we do with our hands as we talk about whatever seemed to be the most important thing in the world at that moment. Games were a shared experience. My friends were familiar with all the same titles as I was because we were watching each other play almost everything. Of course, I did still play stuff on my own and found that to be a meaningful way to play as well. However, it was not the norm. Things shifted a bit when I went off to college, but gaming still felt like a social thing. When I'd play stuff, I'd leave the door to my room open and my roommates would pop in and out, seeing what I was trying and if they'd have any interest in it too. One of my roommates and I would play a round of Peggle every night as a part of our respective evening rituals. Eventually though, I didn't live in a place with so many people passing through. Hangouts with friends weren't as frequent as we all were busy with jobs and other aspects of life. All of us lived in different cities, different states, and getting together became more about catching up than anything else. Around this same time, I also shifted away from playing games on console, opting to build a PC, and gaming became something I largely did on my own, instead of it being the center of my social life, it became me alone in a room with headphones on, completely locked in. To be very clear, there is nothing inherently wrong with experiencing games in this way. There are plenty of times where it is my preferred approach, as it can make it easier to completely focus on the thing in front of me with no external distractions. It lowers the barriers that can get in the way of fully diving into worlds and mechanics, but there is undeniably a distancing feel to it. In a lot of ways, immersion, by design, is meant to be distancing. What actually was the problem, or kind of is the problem, is that this used to just be one way I play games. But for a good while now, it has pretty much been the only way. There are certainly occasional disruptions to it, like whenever my wife and I do something for gaming for a non-gamer, but that is still a far cry from when gaming was one of the pillars of my social life. Obviously, I can't know for sure, but I suspect that this is the thing a lot of people who are struggling to enjoy games in the way they once did are missing the most. The environment in which they used to play games. Because that environment is so much harder to recreate when the barriers of adult life all suddenly spring up around you. Now, it should be noted that playing games with friends is easier today than it has ever been. Online gaming has found a strong foothold, and there has been a huge surge of titles centered around goofing off with friends. I love having this option. It has given me the chance to form friendships that I otherwise never would have formed, and play stuff every week with old friends who live in different states than me. It is amazing and something I am grateful for, but also, if it took as little effort to play games with friends in person as it does to play with them online, I would choose to play in person 99% of the time without question. Like obviously, I would be shocked if most people don't feel that way. Playing online is the compromise I'm willing to make to be able to play games with friends at all. I do value it, but in most cases, it is a lesser experience than being in the same space as them. What's especially frustrating is that this compromise has largely become the standard. Local multiplayer, while not non-existent, is mostly a thing of the past. Like I do get it, most people will be able to utilize online multiplayer, while only a small portion of players will get much out of local, and on top of that, split-screen essentially requires running multiple instances of the game, which takes a lot of computing power and probably will impact visual fidelity and performance. So it makes more sense for devs to not allocate their already limited resources to getting all that to work. However, I fear that this compromise becoming the norm will mean that the current generation of young people who do live in an environment primed for playing games together in person won't,

I skipped being a part of something cool because of the paranoia of a maybe. Admittedly, experiences like this one are few and far between. However, the specter of will this be a video does impact how I feel about the stuff I play, which in turn impacts the way I communicate about the stuff I play. And given that my job relies on communicating in a way that connects with those of you who watch, I fear sometimes that the way I play games for videos will make those videos not resonate in the way I hope they do. ## The Best Mechanics From "Bad" Games
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MNPDDH8Ap9Y

The 2009 reboot of Bionic Commando is the kind of game you think of when imagining an average game from 2009. You know, the ones you played when waiting for stuff like Arkham Asylum or Uncharted 2 to come out. The ones you more than likely only ever saw at a friend's house. The ones that can best be described as 360-ass games. Its story is incomprehensible, its gunplay, encounter design, and general combat feel clumsy and repetitive, and its aesthetic is so derivative of literally everything else that came out during that time that it's almost painful. Upon release, it received middling reviews, barely sold any copies, and quickly garnered a reputation, especially among fans of the original Bionic Commando, as being one of the worst reboots ever. But also, in it you can do this. Nathan Spencer's Bionic Arm is one of my favorite grappling hooks, honestly, ever. The swing has such a satisfying sense of momentum to it, and that momentum feels earned. From figuring out the timing of when to release a swing to picking the right spot to aim the next shot, there is constantly something to be thinking about. Nothing here is automatic, creating a good bit of room for skill expression. The arm also has the ability to quickly pull Spencer in, a move not only useful for scaling tall buildings, but also for kicking enemies in the face. Together, this creates a movement kit with tons of versatility and potential, and all of this is further enhanced by stellar animations. Spencer always seems to know exactly when to do a flip to achieve maximum coolness, and swings flow so well into each other. Additionally, the Bionic Arm also has a whole throwing mechanic where Spencer can grab cars, broken bits of armor, even the various grunts and toss them at oncoming enemies or into the abyss. In one fight, I swung behind this big dude with a laser cannon, grappled onto his back to kick him, grabbed the laser cannon that he dropped, and slammed it into him. And moments like this are when the full potential of what Bionic Commando could have been can be seen in full force. The issue, of course, is that while the various mechanics tied to the Bionic Arm are intriguing and provide flashes of brilliance, as I stated at the top, the wider game built around them doesn't properly support their potential. For instance, while the swinging creates this grand sense of freedom, that freedom is often disrupted by hard-to-distinguish radiation zones that will quickly kill you for going a little too high up or the tiniest bit off the beaten path. The game really isn't about discovery or adventure. You mostly move linearly from one of these beacons to the next with the objective of killing the bad guys around them in order to unlock the path forward. Unsurprisingly, this becomes repetitive quickly, an issue that's further exacerbated by the lack of enemy variety as well as the fact that the core mechanics never really evolve. The majority of fights don't take much thought and it becomes far too easy to spam certain attacks. Not to mention, the ability to throw stuff, which is what makes combat fun at all, doesn't get introduced until the second half of the game. They seemingly wanted to have some sense of character progression, and I can see why they thought doing it this way was a good idea, but the throw should have been a starting ability that gets built upon as the game goes on, like by adding a spin move or being able to send an electric charge through the grapple to cause an explosion or something. It's too cool to have ended with its introduction. Most aspects aside from the swinging feel underbaked, and given that the developers' grin not only released a game two months before Bionic Commando, but also one literally on the same day, stretching what even their sizable team could handle, it isn't a huge surprise that the game didn't feel properly built around the central mechanic. And that's a shame. Bionic Commando's grappling hook certainly shares some DNA with the Spider-Mans and Just Causes of the world, but it offered something different than either of those, and I at least haven't seen anything quite like it since. And so even though Bionic Commando leaves so much to be desired, even though throughout most of my time with it I oscillated between feeling bored and disappointed, those few moments, those perfect encapsulations of the mechanic at its best, have stuck with me. A while back, Jacob Geller released a video titled Perfect Moments in Bad Movies. In it, he examines two scenes, one from Spider-Man 3 and another from The Matrix Revolutions, that stand out as something special amidst the messiness of the rest of those films, and ever since watching it, I've regularly thought about video game analogs for this. Obviously, the cleanest parallel would be centered around levels or sections of games, but every time I found myself thinking about bad games that interest me, it's always had less to do with any given stretch of a title and more to do with the mechanics. Ones like the Bionic Arm. Those cool ideas that got bogged down by other aspects of a title and failed to be implemented to their fullest. The ideas undercut by rushed development and budget constraints. The ideas that could have been something. That could still be something. I find it hard not to be drawn in by games with mechanics like these. There's a joy in tragedy to them in that something so intriguing can be found in something so flawed. Bionic Commando is not exactly a rare example of a title that delivers a uniquely great mechanic while falling apart in most other ways. Frankly, there are plenty of examples from that same exact era that do the same thing. With the runaway success of Gears of War, the space became flooded with third-person military shooters all trying to capitalize on what it had established while also aiming to stand out in one way or another. One of the more compelling mechanics to emerge from this can be seen with Fracture, a game that asks the question, what if you could create your own cover in a cover shooter? Through the use of a terraforming gun, you can raise and lower the ground based on where you shoot it. Not only allowing you to control sightlines, but also to launch yourself or enemies into the air. Having so much control over the terrain is wildly satisfying and there are moments where the full potential shines through. I'd cut a bunch of enemies off by raising the ground so that I could focus on one guy without taking crossfire. And once he was down, I'd lower a different bit to try to get the drop on those running around the obstacle I had made. It creates a remarkable sense of battlefield control, and as enemies hit pretty hard, using the mechanic well truly feels like it matters. Most encounters aren't like this though. Battles tend to be too chaotic to get a great handle on anything that's happening. There are constant explosions that shake the screen, making it a nightmare to aim and generally get your bearings. And as enemies hit so hard, if you find yourself out of position for even a second, chances are you will be dead before you can do anything to react. Also, in some sections, the focus moves away from terrain manipulation and more on the gunplay, which is not the game's strong suit as it feels sluggish and limp. Shots against you hit like a truck, but the ones you land hardly feel satisfying at all. Furthermore, a significant chunk of Fracture's short runtime is spent in what may be the worst driving sections I've experienced in a game, as well as fighting the same boss type four different times. Something that isn't a problem in a game with dozens of bosses, but does feel underwhelming when it is the only one the game has. Regardless, its core idea is still incredible due to the way it can quickly shift the appearance and functionality of a battle, giving an additional layer of control and consideration to every fight. The mechanic also has a decent amount of potential for puzzles. The ones in the game end up being underwhelming, largely consisting of rolling a ball down a hill or lifting a fallen object, but the mechanic itself provides plenty of space for more complex implementations, even if those can't be found here. Both Fracture and Bionic Commando ultimately failed to balance the ideas that made them stand out with the ideas that were popular at the time, leading to messy experiences that blended in with the field they were trying to stand out from. In a similar vein as titles that fall short trying to implement something that sets them apart from everything else, there is also something fascinating about games that miss the mark when attempting to address a common critique of the genre they are in. For instance, in the 90s, turn-based RPGs were one of the most popular types of games out there, and especially when things shifted into 3D, there was a growing desire to see what a more interconnected experience would feel like. One that didn't have separate perspectives or character models for combat, primary locations, and the overworld. And Nintendo's attempt to address that can be seen with Quest 64, developed by Imagineer. To preface, Quest 64 is the first game I remember not liking. During my early years of gaming, I found the mere act that I could play video games at all to be exciting enough to get me through any experience, but Quest 64 ended that. In it, very little is done to explain how things work, it is filled with a ludicrous amount of empty space that is annoyingly easy to get turned around in, the camera is awful, the characters have nothing to them, and the sound of Brian's walk chips away at your sanity bit by bit until nothing is left. And yes, they named the protagonist of their fantasy video game Brian. FF7 has Cloud, Legend of Dragoon has Dart, and Quest 64 has Brian. Anyway, when comparing this to other titles on the N64, the gulf in quality is unignorable.

with hazards across the map. When possessed, the ghosts can influence the human's movement and where they look, and the humans try to counteract this by pressing the opposite direction on the joystick to stop the movement, all while mashing A or trying to shoot an anti-ghost cloud up their feet to become dispossessed. This all allows for plenty of mind games and the exact type of discord you're looking for when playing games in the same room as your friends. Admittedly, the mode isn't as fleshed out as it could be. It would have gone a long way if instead of both teams just trying to kill each other, the humans would have had some alternative objective that the ghosts were trying to stop them from doing. Also, as you might expect from a first-person shooter on the Nintendo GameCube, the movement and gunplay do not feel that good, all leading to an experience better remembered than played. But still, the existence of this mode revealed the wider potential the core mechanic had. It bums me out that this sort of thing is so much less common today. Multiplayer titles obviously are still thriving. Frankly, the last few years have seen a pretty huge resurgence of them. However, these experimental multiplayer modes that pull from the assets and mechanics of a game's core single-player mode are far more rare. It used to be that the vast majority of titles would include some sort of separate mode for local multiplayer, and that eventually shifted into most of them having some sort of separate mode for online multiplayer, and now it's either nothing or co-op. The latter of which I am certainly happy to see, but these modes rarely are reworking the mechanics into a new form. It's just adding another player. Unfortunately, with game development being as time-consuming and as expensive as it is now, it feels less and less likely that studios will take the risk of diverting resources to see the weirder ways their game could work. It is promising to see some bigger studios dip their toes into modes like Valhalla and God of War, but this isn't exactly reasonable for the average dev team. While understandable, it's a shame to see the experimentation of that era be left behind, as I think it will leave the potential of a lot of mechanics unrealized, both ones from back then that are unlikely to be revitalized in the current landscape, as well as ones from modern day that would be better suited in a different mode. Now, even though that era has passed, at least the games and mechanics from it are theoretically playable, something that can't be said for all modern titles. On January 12th, 2026, the servers for BioWare's Anthem shut down, leaving the game completely unplayable. If I'm being honest, I had kind of forgotten that Anthem even came out. I remember seeing trailers for it and being impressed, but after its release was largely met with negative reviews, critiquing it for being filled with the kind of bloated game design I had grown all too tired of by that point, I entirely forgot about it, as nothing seemed to be there for me. One thing you'll find in most reviews of the game, though, as well as in many of the recent re-evaluations due to the shutdown, is praise of the flying mechanic, the feel of weightiness to it, the movement tech needed to keep the engines cool, the quick transition from air to ground and ground to air. A big reason there was so much hype behind the game to begin with was because of how cool the flying looked, and that at least they nailed, and a part of me regrets never giving it a shot. To be clear, I still don't think I would have liked Anthem, and I definitely wouldn't have wanted to spend the money on it, but now with this mechanic locked away due to the game being online only, I can't help but wish I had tried it at least once, to know what this flying in particular felt like, to have considered how it worked and how it could have fit within the game better, to not have had to rely on a friend of a friend to get footage for it. There are countless reasons to support game preservation and chastise companies like EA for not having an end-of-life plan for their online-only titles, the simplest being that if you buy a game, you should be able to keep playing it. Another major one for me, though, is that losing these titles eliminates the chance for future devs to study them and use the aspects that worked as a jumping-off point for something new. With how many games are out there, it can be hard to even remember the ones that are considered good, and so it tends to be even harder to remember those that are considered bad, and it's all too common to dismiss them entirely. But I want these games to be remembered, and to be playable. If it wasn't clear already, I have a lot of affection for the titles I've talked about. To go back to Jacob's video, my favorite point he makes in it is that when it comes to art, the opposite of good is uninteresting, and while all of these titles failed to present stable and cohesive experiences, the mechanics they champion are anything but uninteresting. Not to mention, as mechanics are so central to a title's moment-to-moment feel, there is this weird thing with all of these games where despite the underwhelming design that surrounds their stellar mechanics, they still can be fun. And if you play them just for small bursts and only focus on those little bits, you can walk away feeling pretty good about them. Also, as most of these mechanics haven't been explored all that thoroughly, these titles are still the best way to experience them. In some ways, I think this means time may be kind to these games. With something like Bionic Commando, the further removed we become from 2009, the easier it will become to ignore the ways in which it fell short by 2009 standards. On one hand, I like the idea that these games will age well because they do stuff that nothing else really does. On the other though, I think it would be a waste if these mechanics ended with them. When it comes to conversations around game design from folks like myself, things understandably tend to center around successes. Like, it stands to reason that when talking about good game design, the focus should be on games that people broadly like, ones with few shortcomings that are fairly easy to look past. And this also holds true for design trends in the industry. Dark Souls came out and everything started to take ideas from Dark Souls. Breath of the Wild came out and everything started to take ideas from Breath of the Wild. Ballotrow came out and everything started to take ideas from Ballotrow. And again, it makes sense. These games are all good and filled with good mechanics to build off of. They should be a point of conversation and inspiration. However, I do think this instinct can cause the gaming landscape to feel homogenous. A lot of these ideas that started out as great have become stale more quickly than they maybe should have due to the market being flooded by so many things that feel the same. If I had to see the Breath of the Wild pen one more time, I may lose it. This amount of oversaturation can be detrimental to the reach of any game that pulls from something popular, as sticking too close to everything else not only makes it harder to stand out, but also makes it less likely to get out from the shadow of the original inspiration. Where genre classification like roguelike has become relatively disconnected from the actual game rogue, when it comes to more recent stuff like Dark Souls, like Breath of the Wild, like Ballotrow, that same degree of separation doesn't exist. And so instead of being purely a classification, it is also a comparison, one that doesn't always help newer games. All of this is to say, I love when devs take inspiration from past works that aren't so prevalent in the zeitgeist, especially those that were seen as failures, and I hope more start to do it. There are so many intriguing systems waiting to be revived by the right dev, and while I understand the interest and financial incentive that pushes studios to iterate on the mechanics that are most relevant within the current gaming moment, the untapped potential of failures contains a staggering amount of promise. Now, as there are more games out there than ever, it is possible that these ideas have been iterated on, and I just haven't seen it. I suppose if you've played something with mechanics reminiscent of any of the ones I've talked about, please let me know. I'd love to play them. It is also possible that despite me liking these mechanics, they don't actually have as much potential as I believe they do, that the reason these games struggled to be great was because they were limited by their mechanics. With most of these, I don't think that is the case, but it is hard to know without actually trying to develop them into a new game, which unfortunately is not currently something I have the skills or capacity for. However, I hope someone can prove that notion wrong with all of these, because they're mechanics I want to keep experiencing. Of course, if the only way I can keep experiencing them is by dealing with stupid guards, incessant footsteps, and repetitive fights, I suppose that will have to do.

## The Games That Got Me Through 2025
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Hh4IGoNFEPQ

2025 has been another year, and luckily I was able to play a bunch of video games throughout it. As has become tradition, that means it is time for me again to talk about some of the ways they had an effect on my life. In last year's video, one of the main takeaways was that I didn't play anything that meant all that much to me. I enjoyed a bunch of games, but I didn't connect with any in the way I often do. While I largely assumed this was due to picking the wrong games and also being in a weird headspace as I was navigating life with both a toddler and a newborn making it hard to process much of anything, a small part of me worried that my relationship with games had fundamentally shifted, that this change was a part of me getting older, that I was becoming less capable of finding experiences to resonate with on a deep personal level. And 2025 has proven that this was not the case. I don't know that there's been a single year of my life where I played more titles that left a profound impact on me than I did in this past one. Like, there are multiple games that if I had played them in 2024, they probably would have been the primary focus of that video, but they kind of get lost in the shuffle when put next to the many incredible experiences I had last year. Simply put, it was one of the most enjoyable years of playing games I've ever had, and I want to share some of it with you. So I'm going to start where I always do, with the first game I played last year, which this time was Hypnospace Outlaw. Hypnospace Outlaw is the weird type of game where what would be considered the actual game part largely is just a vehicle to get you to engage with the lore. The player takes the role of a moderator of forums and webpages that feel straight out of the 1990s, and this setup provides all the motivation needed to scour every page for potential infractions. While finding these violations requires a good bit of deduction, making them satisfying to discover, it is the actual contents of these pages that make Hypnospace Outlaw a game I reflect on often and fondly. It presents an alluring representation of the old internet, an era that at least in my experiences didn't truly exist, but has an undeniable appeal all the same. One of community, of shared passion, of making art, all without the algorithmic hand and financial incentive that defines the current internet. Every page is filled with so much personality and explores the stories of various characters in ways that feel shockingly authentic. There is no shortage of media that cops the 90s aesthetic, but a lot of the time it feels like a hollow imitation, one that coasts on the belief that doing stuff like reminding you of the pattern on the side of those disposable cups will be enough to pull you in. But here there is humanity behind everything. There is a sincerity to even the most unhinged pages that makes the forums feel like the kind of digital space people would want to be a part of. The artistry on display is on another level. The writing, images, music, all of it weaves together to make these webpages feel like an artifact of the past, but with all the boring parts shaved away. Even the art that is meant to be quote unquote bad is enjoyably bad, which is not an easy thing to do. They pulled off a nearly impossible feat and it really is something special. As a trademark 90s kid, it's no real surprise that this game tapped into my nostalgia for that era, but that's not really why I enjoyed it. And I don't think you have to have nostalgia for the 90s to enjoy it. Because honestly it did more than just remind me of the past, it elevated it. I had a similar feeling with a couple other titles last year, the first being Burgist. It's a game that feels like it would have been right at home on the PS2, but has design philosophies that are decidedly more modern than anything that actually would have come out on the PS2. To my knowledge, the developer Guerin Studios hasn't specified what games influenced Burgist, instead pointing to things like history, animal behavior, numerical sequences, and oddly shaped rocks. And honestly all of that does show. However, it feels like it takes cues from stuff like Shadow of the Colossus, Drakengard, and even Brutal Legend, leading to something entirely unique and surprisingly singular in vision. It finds ways to meld these ideas that seem like they should never work together and somehow nails it. The other game was Angeline Era. With a chunky PS1 slash N64 aesthetic, it takes what seems like the most simple approach to combat, that being bumping into enemies to attack, and creates all sorts of interesting levels and encounters around it that brings far more depth to the mechanic than it has any business having. Through and through, the design is just so thoughtful. For instance, the majority of levels are made up of locked rooms where you need to clear the encounter to move forward. As the game is pretty tough, especially so if you're on a higher difficulty, there's a good chance you'll die a bunch, sending you back to the start of the level and making you do it all over. It's a runback of sorts, which I know people have opinions on, but what works about it here in terms of avoiding the frustration that can come from this type of setup is that unlocking the door to the next room doesn't require killing every single enemy. Instead, each encounter has a specific clear condition, generally tied to taking out a much smaller fraction of the enemies. So with every attempt, you're not just figuring out how to better position yourself in order to not take damage, but also what the criteria is to unlock the way forward. It adds a new layer of thought to every room and quicker ways to progress, keeping these runbacks from becoming tedious. Not to mention, once you've played enough, you'll start to recognize sort of themes and patterns, making it possible to predict what might clear the door. And when you're able to do this on a first time through a level, it feels incredible. It's an elegant approach to difficulty and failure as it tests both the player's skill as well as their knowledge. This makes it so having to replay sections feels far more palatable as there are multiple ways to improve and the success almost always comes from an increase in the player as opposed to the character. From top to bottom, Angeline Era is filled with playful design like this that rewards players for noticing things. As Giovanni Colantonio put it in his piece on Angeline Era, the result is a rare retro game that actually plays the way I remember old games feeling, even though it's nothing like them at all. In my experience, this felt true with Angeline Era, Burgist, and Hypnospace Outlaw. Each of them harnesses an aesthetic from the past to set players' expectations and then deploys game design ideas that do not draw specifically from a single title from those eras, but instead from many, many titles from all sorts of eras. Where you may be able to see some sources of inspiration, but would struggle to really say it is just like one specific thing. It is not uncommon for indie games to look like retro games or even feel like retro games, but to Colantonio's point, it is rare for them to make you feel the way you did when playing old games or when living in old times. It isn't enough to just be familiar, it also needs to have something fresh, and these three titles have that. And so they remind me of how much I love video games. And not just playing them, but also thinking about them. Seeing creative spins on old ideas that prove that we are really just at the beginning of what games can be. Not to mention, these three titles were made by relatively small teams. And to be clear, I'm not saying that to demonize games with far bigger ones, but to point out that there are many ways to make a game, and that a team with a strong creative vision that learns to master limitations and iterate in unexpected ways can create some of the most compelling art out there. Throughout 2025, I continued the trend I started the year before of getting more into multiplayer games, as playing stuff with other people, as it turns out, is fun. I finally got around to It Takes Two with my wife, which maybe will be a video someday, but at the very least, it was just fun to watch her adjust to the ever-shifting nature of that game. I established a game night with a couple of my friends that I've known since we were kids, and it has been such a welcome routine in my life. I know for a fact that when we were 10 years old playing Melee in my parents' basement, we never would have expected to still be doing some version of that nearly 25 years later. And so it has been a great joy that we have. Now with the widespread of games I played with them, as well as with other friends, there is one title that really defines my multiplayer year. That was Elden Ring Night Reign. Night Reign is a weird kind of good. In a lot of ways, it feels messy, which is understandable as it smashes together a bunch of stuff from older FromSoft titles and then uses the Fortnite storm to tie it all together. It truly is a testament to how fun and varied the combat is in Elden Ring that Night Reign stays as enjoyable for as long as it does. After my first few runs, I figured I'd play it until beating all the bosses once or twice and then would never pick it up again. However, at this point, I got all of the achievements around the 30-hour mark and have put in 70 hours since then. And frankly, I feel like I have a lot of runs still left in me. And of course, a big part of my enjoyment came from the

I was relishing as the two are so often paired together. I basked in getting truly and utterly lost, refusing to use the compass because I wanted to really know my way through Farlum and by the end I did. I found assurance in Hornet's strength of personality, her insistence on imposing her will on the world despite how treacherous and powerful that world may be, and refusing to let it happen the other way around. Really, this last part is the one that surprised me the most. Hollow Knight's narrative primarily exists through lore just below the surface, but Silksong stands in the forefront. Hornet has purpose and she makes that known. Through her and her observations, the game explores the effects of power, whether it be from structures or individuals, and I never thought I'd be so inspired by the confidence of a little bug. I never thought I would need to be so inspired by the confidence of a little bug. But here we are. Over this past year, I've dabbled a bit with doomerism. I'm not proud of it, but it regularly seeps into my thoughts. Never before in my life have I seen more pieces of news where it was hard to think anything other than, it's so over. To be clear, I don't really think that it is, or at least I can't really think it is, because I just can't. However, we are in the midst of an era of great consequence, socially, economically, and technologically, and those who are at the helm, those who have the most power to dictate how the next 20 years will go, are the people I trust the least to act in the collective us's best interest, proven by how they never do. And so maybe it isn't a surprise that the three games I connected to most last year explored what it takes to survive within an ultra-capitalistic hellscape in its latest stage, what we are left with when each passing generation has less of a future than the last, and how the stubborn and careless use of absolute power decays a society from the top down. It's sometimes good to be seen by the things you play. I think a lot about games as a form of escapism, and what has always been the case for me, what it always seems to come back to with the games that get me through the year, is that the ones that bring me the most relief aren't the ones that make me forget everything, they're the ones that help me process it all in a way that doesn't feel as heavy, in a way that doesn't feel as impossible, in a way that doesn't feel like it's so over. Because thinking that it's over is useless. It doesn't help anyone. Despair is easy, and those who wield it as a weapon know this. The goal is to make it all seem like an impossible machine for any individual to do anything about, but it's not about any individual doing everything, it's about many individuals doing something. It is about community, and reminders of this are what get me through each day, whether they come from watching my kids grow up and witnessing the ways they are loved not just by me and my wife, but by family and friends and teachers, all of whom have played a part in shaping who they are now and who they will be one day, or from seeing people rally together like those in Minneapolis who have engaged not just in protest and fundraising, but also in a level of dedicated local mutual aid unlike anything I've seen before in my life, or even from playing as a bug who discovers that despite there being no quick and clean way to undo the rot of corruption, the best path forward is and will always be to help those who need it and be willing to accept help from them too. There are many reasons to want to despair, and so it has been important for me to do everything I can to find even more reasons to not. It doesn't matter where they come from, it just matters that they do. That instead of feeling paralyzed by the inability to fix everything, I have the clarity to focus on the ways I can do something. I needed games in 2025 in a way that I don't think I have in a long time, maybe ever, and what still kind of surprises me is that they met the moment. Frankly, I probably willed them to meet the moment. Playing them and talking about them made me feel human. What's more is that instead of simply distracting me from the pervasive sense of existential dread that is just part of my life now, they helped me refocus. They made tackling everything else feel easier. I get the sense that 2026 will be the same way. Like always, I do not know what this next year will bring. I have my hopes and I have my fears, but neither truly matter that much. What does matter is that it isn't over. It's never over. So here's to the new year and remembering that Hollow Knight Silksong actually came out. So anything is possible. Reflecting on my year in gaming is something I look forward to every January, and I also look forward to hearing other people's thoughts on the stuff they played and what it meant to them. So with that in mind, I thought it'd be fun to have a recorded conversation with two of the people I talk about games with the most, Iron Pineapple and YakoCMN, to discuss our thoughts on gaming in 2025. We talked about our games of the year, our not-so-obvious games of the year, more granular stuff like favorite mechanics and moments, and even our biggest hater takes. ## How Much Failure is Too Much Failure?
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fMbVMO4FfHE

There are many important aspects that make video games feel like video games, but one that I find especially interesting due to our complex relationship with it is failure. Without some sort of setback, or at the very least the potential of a setback, games run the risk of losing meaning. The best way to make success feel good is by earning it, and so space for failure is a key part of almost any game's design. This can take all sorts of forms, both big and small, harsh and forgiving, and everything in between. There are tons of ways to incorporate it, and ultimately it comes down to what a game is aiming to make you feel. What makes failure tricky, though, is that it is a thing we instinctively want to avoid. Like when I come across a new boss in a game, a part of me always hopes that I will be able to clear it on my first attempt. Of course, if this actually always happened, the feeling I would inevitably walk away with is that the game was too easy for me. Doing it only actually feels good when it's rare. Despite our aversion to failure, we need it. The threat of it is what gives games stakes. It's what makes your inputs matter. And for it to really work, the threat can't just be a threat. The consequences have to be carried out, because if you never experience friction, the threat will no longer feel threatening, causing the game to feel more like a ride than a game. On the other hand, though, there is only so much failure most players will be willing to endure, creating this push and pull for developers where they have to consider how to implement failure in a way that will feel meaningful and be in line with the type of experience they're trying to create without driving away their core player base out of frustration. Over the past couple months, there has been a lot of discussion around Hollow Knight's Silksong for this reason. The game is incredibly difficult. The various gauntlets and boss fights will almost certainly have you dying over and over again, and what has been one of the more controversial aspects is that in most cases, instead of respawning in a spot close to whatever fight you were just in, you most likely will be sent far, far away and need to engage in a dreaded runback. Runbacks have long been a part of Metroidvanias and other genres that take heavy inspiration from them, but there has been a somewhat recent push away from the use of them. In regards to the runbacks in Silksong, a comparison I've seen a lot is with how Elden Ring does it, that being always providing some kind of checkpoint right by a boss, allowing players to immediately retry after a loss. The challenge is not the level as a whole, but instead it's the boss, and this format pairs logically with the immense difficulty of some of these fights. They are balanced around the assumption that players will come in at full strength, and therefore they pull very few punches. The friction comes from how difficult they are, not from how much they will punish the player. In Silksong, bosses also seem balanced around the assumption that players will be coming in at full strength, despite them having to travel so far to get to them. In fairness, with Silksong, players are never that far away from being at full strength, as the primary resource they will deplete, silk, can be recovered without any sort of item, unlike in Elden Ring where the player can only restore their primary resource, flasks, by resting or dying. Also, after every death, Hornet leaves behind a cocoon, and breaking it fully restores her silk, creating the opportunity for the player to start every fight with a good amount of health. Even with all that though, there is still far more friction here. Every death has the weight of two failures, and instead of getting to practice the part that caused them to fail, players have to work through a section that calls for a different skill set that they already feel like they overcame. Now, despite what people who hate them will say, it should be noted that there are plenty of folks out there who do like runbacks, and particularly like the ones in Silksong. They like that the challenge comes from mastering an area on a wider scale instead of in tiny segments. They like having space between attempts as it pushes them to approach every fight with consideration instead of casually throwing themselves into a meat grinder. They like finding the optimal path back and perfecting their movement through it. They may even like the temptation it creates to go somewhere else for a little while that they may have missed. Sickos like this do exist. And yes, I am sickos. I like bile water. I refuse to apologize. Admittedly, while I have started to find runbacks to be a bit tiring in many soulslikes I play, I didn't have that same feeling in Silksong, largely due to it being a platformer. Where awkwardly weaving between enemies in Dark Souls kinda goes against what the game wants you to do, speeding through areas in Silksong feels natural and fun. There are a bunch of moves specifically designed to help you smoothly traverse areas and bypass enemies, so instead of it feeling like cheesing the intended design, it feels like the intended design. Now, even as someone who found value in them, it is undeniable that this type of failure is grating for tons of people, and this mostly comes down to how often any given player has to do it. Like obviously, runbacks will feel different to those who only end up doing 2-3 attempts for boss, compared to those who come closer to 30 or 40. Doing more runs not only takes up more time, but also will lead to diminishing returns in terms of your improvement at the actual runback. For many, there is a good chance that after a bunch of attempts, getting back to the part they're stuck on will become near mindless, leaving it feeling less like a part of the challenge and more like a minute or two they'll never get back. Unsurprisingly, the more punishing failure is, the less patience players will have for it. Discourse around Silksong often gets boiled down to it being too hard, but as plenty of other people have started to point out, it has more to do with how punishing it is than how difficult it is. These things are intertwined, but it's not as if the hardest parts of Silksong are so far beyond anything a game has ever done before. It's that failing at them means replaying a different hard part where dying on the way back could mean losing all of your hard-earned money. It is a tension that is hard to hold, and based on the discussion surrounding the game, it seems like for a good amount of people, that tension shifted into frustration. Failure in Silksong can so easily beget more failure, and that kind of spiral downwards is hard to stomach. Honestly, I think a big part of why roguelites have gained so much popularity is because a lot of them do the opposite of this. They are designed around small chunks of gameplay where yes, you most likely will fail time and time again before having anything that comes close to even looking like a successful run, but due to various forms of metaprogression, every failure is a chance to improve your character, whether it be increasing their stats or unlocking new moves or anything else that might give you an edge. Failure in a roguelite is inevitable, but the consolation is that the playable character will be more effective. Even in ones with horizontal progression where it's more about increasing gameplay options instead of stats, having a wider pool of upgrades and abilities to choose from gives players more opportunities to craft powerful builds. The improvement is impossible to avoid, giving players a sort of permission structure in a way other types of games don't. For instance, a pretty common phenomenon with titles like Silksong or Elden Ring is that players will come across a boss, be underpowered in some way, but still bash their head against it until they beat it. Typically, bosses like this aren't designed to be brute forced. They are meant to be barriers that push players to explore elsewhere so that they get more powerful and come back better equipped. You've heard all that before. However, doing that can feel like giving up, which isn't easy for a lot of players to do. Exploring elsewhere is choosing to progress the character's ability over the player's ability, leading to the fight being inherently different when they do come back. If the character gets too powerful, it may not be challenging at all, and so beating the boss won't feel nearly as satisfying because of a choice the player made. In a roguelite, due to the structure, instead of coming back to a boss with a massive increase in the character's power, it will almost certainly be a more gradual one, making it unlikely that the fight will be trivialized due to the increase and also causing it to be harder to determine what deserves more credit in the success, the character or the player. Also, more and more roguelites have started to offer a number of ways to increase the challenge once the player has started to figure things out and substantially upgraded their abilities. The heat and fear systems in the Hades series are solid examples of this. Before each run, players can select modifiers ranging from simple stuff like damage and health increases for enemies to more interesting obstacles like new versions of bosses, time limits, changes that have a significant effect on what a run feels like. It is a challenge players opt into, customize to their liking, and maybe most importantly, can gradually implement. It lets them increase the challenge to make it clear that their own skill is what deserves the credit, while still rarely getting that feeling of running into a brick wall. All of this creates a system that offers a smooth, challenging, and varied experience that regardless of skill, never feels like the player is doing the exact same thing over and over again. To be clear, I'm not trying to say that this

There seems to be a fatigue setting in, and it's not just that a new group of people who never liked more punishing design are joining the conversation. It's that a lot of people who used to be more on board with this kind of design have started to sour on it. There are a lot of things that could explain this shift from the general mental exhaustion of being a human in our current digital and cultural age, to gamers as a whole getting older, thus having less time and patience for punishing forms of failure. As far as things directly related to the industry, though, I think it is important to acknowledge the Dark Souls of it all. Obviously, Dark Souls did not invent being hard, but its approach to difficulty has been massively influential on modern gaming. Not only has FromSoft launched themselves from being a niche studio to one of the most popular ones out there, but countless other developers, whether they be indie, AAA, or anything in between, have taken cues from the Souls series. And it's not even that there are too many Souls-likes now, although I know plenty would argue that there are. Beyond that, though, it's that more and more games in all types of genres have adopted aspects from the Souls series, leading to the average game now being more punishing than the average game was 15 years ago. After an era of pretty streamlined titles, the pendulum has swung the other way. Certainly not anywhere close to where it was in the 80s and early 90s, but games as a whole have moved in that direction. I don't think this is exactly a bad thing, and I'm sure many of you have welcomed games becoming a bit more punishing. But it does feel like we're starting to hit the edges of what a broader audience is interested in engaging with. As the average game seems to have increased in difficulty and harder ones have continuously tried to top themselves to present a new level of challenge, failure in games feels heavier now than it has in a long time. And when mixed with how most things in life feel heavier now than they have in a long time, it is no real surprise that there has started to be more pushback. That general audiences have grown tired of the heaviness they experience within the hobby they turn to in order to escape all the other stuff for a little while. Failure makes games better. In some ways, it is what makes them games at all. But submitting to it is no easy feat, as there is no guarantee that the reward will feel worth it. That your time will be respected. And part of this is because what any given person views as their time being respected will vary greatly depending on countless factors that developers can't realistically control for. Not to mention, at the end of the day, games are not designed expressly with you, or more tragically, with me in mind. They instead are designed for the nebulous us. More specifically for subsections of the nebulous us. And as that us gets bigger and bigger, and those subsections become more varied, more and more people will fall outside of the target. All of this amplifies the frustration that comes with failure, and I don't blame anyone for feeling this way. I do think there is value in submitting to failure. I also think sometimes we are so averse to it that we don't even allow it to be an option, which is a shame. Due to our natural inclination to avoid it, I think it can be hard to identify what amount of failure and what kind of failure we will be okay with dealing with. And sometimes I think we underestimate ourselves. We write something off as not being for us a bit too quickly. With that said, it is quite easy to get pushed too far. This is a big part of what makes failure so hard for developers to balance. They are trying to find a line that is so circumstantial. A line that is frankly hard to hit even in games that offer plenty of ways to augment the difficulty. A line that players are instinctively trying to push against. I expect to see the gaming landscape shift in the other direction as a response to the current state of things. Truthfully, I wouldn't be surprised to see more and more games move towards structures reminiscent of roguelites. And I think this is kind of supported by the fact that tons of major studios have started to experiment with that formula. Whatever may happen and however games shift in the future, I do hope you all continue to fail. But I hope it is just the right amount of failure that leaves you in the perfect spot to feel accomplished.
