## Pointless Mechanics That Make Games Better
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Fpg4U08E9yQ

I've been playing a lot of Hades 2, and given that I was a big fan of Hades, I've unsurprisingly been loving it. It expands on the ideas and mechanics of the first game in so many interesting ways, providing countless intertwined systems that are a joy to engage with. There is so much to uncover and dive into, and nearly everything you do leads to some type of notable progression, creating one of the most satisfying feedback loops I can think of. However, there is one mechanic that I've been thinking about more than all the rest, and it's actually one of the few that isn't part of those intertwined systems. That being, the salute. Death to Kronos. Death to Kronos. When the protagonist, Milenawee, comes across a character or boon associated with one of the two factions she's a part of, she has the option to give a quick salute. It is always just a couple words, typically either a mantra of the Unseen, the band of folks residing in the main area of the crossroads, all of whom aim to unseat Kronos, the god of time, or the Silver Sisters, a group of moon goddesses in service of Nyx, the goddess of night. The salutes do not improve Milenawee's relationships with other characters, yield any reward, or move the story forward, you just get a tiny bit of dialogue, at most variations on the core set of phrases. From a progression standpoint, it has no purpose. Yet even after 40 hours of playtime, I still do it every chance I get. It just feels like the right thing to do, the thing that my Milenawee would do. For such a small action, it somehow holds massive implications, and also unique implications depending on who it is being done to. Like with Hecate, the headmistress of the crossroads, it seemed like the expectation, the call and response of a student and teacher after a lifetime of instruction and training. With Odysseus, it seemed like a way to show respect for the wisdom and aid he brought to the cause. With Artemis, it felt like a way to build camaraderie. With Nemesis, it felt like a challenge to get on the same page, and every time she refused to salute back, it made me want to get to a point of common ground all that much more. With the Shrine of Hades, it felt like a promise to make things right. There are a few other interactions similar to the salute. Milenawee can confide in her pet frog, brood over a family portrait, admire flowers she's planted, assist with incantations, sing alongside Artemis. All of this is in the service of adding flavor, and despite it just being a simple button prompt, that flavor goes so much farther than it has any business going. This starts with the fact that there are so many variations of these inputs, not just with what Milenawee can do, but also in terms of what is actually said, the way it is said, and what the response is. Amid all of its incredible gameplay systems, one of the most impressive things about the Hades series is the sheer scope of unique dialogue the games contain, and the fact that that attention to detail is present even in these tiny interactions is mind-blowing. Obviously, the repetition of the mantras Milenawee regularly repeats is the whole point, but due to the slight variations, it somehow never manages to feel repetitive. It doesn't come off as a video game character saying the same canned line over and over again. It feels like Milenawee saying something important. Beyond that, it also creates a sense of community within the crossroads. This is a group that has long been working together, building resistance against the unruly Titan. While the player is just now being dropped in, Milenawee is not. She has a history here, and more importantly has bought into the ways of the Unseen and the Silver Sisters, of Hecate and the witchcraft she practices. So with something like the incantation, it so easily could have just been a moment that she stands around watching, but instead she has the chance to be a part of it, to demonstrate her awareness of how the crossroads work and play a small part in helping her mentor. It informs who Milenawee is. While the player does not have control over how she responds to any given situation in the way some titles do, they do have control over if she responds to certain things. If she is the type of Milenawee who will take a moment to sing with her friend, to stop and smell the flowers, to pay respects to a father she only knows through stories. I've not watched many people play the game, though I imagine it is a mechanic that falls to the wayside for most, because there is no real reason to do it. It could be removed and nothing else would really be changed. But I have no doubt in my mind that the game would feel lesser without it. There technically does become a mechanical purpose for the salute later on. Once you get a certain incantation, saluting effectively changes the seed of your next run, which is to say, it doesn't really have a purpose for 99% of people. It's sort of just an easy way to help out speedrunners and those who do very specific types of runs. And I'm really glad that this is the extent of its purpose, as had they made it a part of the actual progression, I think it would have cheapened the interactions for me. For a comparison, consider Red Dead Redemption 2. In it, there is a mechanic that has some similarities to this one, where Arthur can greet or antagonize anyone he comes across. However, unlike in Hades 2, this shapes who Arthur is in a much more direct way. It isn't about if he engages, it is how he engages. And along with that, there are wider mechanical implications, as greeting or antagonizing people will raise or lower Arthur's honor, respectively. This has impacts on how he is treated by those he comes across, and how certain things play out. On one hand, it does seem like a clean way to get players to engage with the system. The problem, though, is that as it has a mechanical effect, it becomes more of a resource than a form of expression, a resource that is very easy to farm. This encourages players to spam it every chance they get. It goes from being a way to characterize Arthur and get pulled into the world to being exploitable, incentivizing players to do the action that will move their honor in the direction they want instead of using the mechanic in an organic way. It certainly still is a fun inclusion that I'm glad is there, but I can't help but think it would have been more effective if it weren't tied to any sort of gameplay system, if it were mechanically pointless, or at least closer to it. Throughout the lifetime of this channel, I've often advocated for gameplay systems that motivate players to engage with every mechanic, typically by giving them a notable role within how progression works. However, more recently, I've found something extremely compelling about features like the salute in Hades 2 that are pretty much disconnected from everything else. It isn't just that it's optional, it's that choosing to engage with it doesn't really have any tangible reward. That isn't to say it has no effect. Obviously, it does, otherwise I wouldn't be making this video, but it's something the player engages with for intrinsic reasons. For some, they are the sorts of things that will be dismissed as a waste of time, but for others, they can bring shape to a gaming experience in a significant way. A mechanic like this that I appreciate for entirely different reasons than the salute in Hades 2 can be found in Grand Theft Auto 5. If you hit circle or B, depending on the controller you're using while in the middle of a jump, whoever you're playing as will ragdoll in the air. To my understanding, there really is no reason or benefit to ever do this. It is not a useful mechanic in terms of completing missions or escaping chases or getting the edge in gunfights. It doesn't even make sense in terms of being a movement a character would want to do as no one would ever choose to do a faceplant like this. Truthfully, the only reason I can imagine the developers included it is because it's very funny. Being able to bail mid-jump and crash into the ground or do flips off a house into a pool or bowl into a group of people just trying to enjoy their afternoon provides a kind of mechanical expression that feels really good to mess with. And it just feels so GTA. Despite being well-crafted games with notable stories and missions, a big part of what has made the Grand Theft Auto series so famous has nothing to do with what could be considered the core of each game. I imagine there are many of you who have played dozens and dozens of hours of these titles without even playing a mission and instead have just engaged with the chaotic playgrounds they provide. This small mechanic of being able to ragdoll at will is in service of that side of these games. The side that isn't focused on Michael, Franklin, and Trevor. That doesn't care about the corrupt antics of the FIB. The side that's only goal is to allow players to create as much chaos as they possibly can. This stupid ragdoll dive opens up so many opportunities for self-imposed challenges and general goofing around. I imagine it is something many will never even know is there, but it does add so much for those who do. A less self-destructive version of a mechanic in this vein can be seen in Chia, where if you hold right trigger while in midair, you can then use the right joystick to spin and flip. There isn't any sort of scoring system, it doesn't boost your speed or make terrain easier to clear, it is just cool. There are many different ways to traverse the world, but as running is probably the one you'll be

I think having a reward for everything can feel exhausting, and at its worst, it can condition players to care more about the act of progression than the gameplay the progression unlocks. With how a lot of games are designed now, it is easy for your brain to fall into autopilot. And I don't think that's entirely bad. Sometimes shutting your brain off is exactly what you're looking for and maybe even what you need. However, as more and more things in the world have become designed for us to shut our brains off, I find myself craving intentionality more than I ever have before. And I think that is part of why I've spent so much time thinking about this stupid salute and mechanics like it. No one else's desire is what gets me to engage with them. I am fully in control of making that choice. To be very clear, I don't think games should get rid of progression systems or mechanical motivation. However, I do think it's important for them to include mechanics that are separate, that slow things down, that gives players a way to play that feels like their own. So whether it's raising Chao in Sonic Adventure 2 Battle, dancing on the ship in Lethal Company, looking out at a vista in Hob, yelling Mario when pressing A in Luigi's Mansion, barking in Okami, or saluting in Hades 2, I hope we never stop getting pointless mechanics in games. While this video has largely stripped games down to how they function mechanically, there obviously are so many aspects that make a game a game that have little to do with their gameplay mechanics. Like Hades 2 isn't Hades 2 without its incredible dynamic soundtrack, and something like Okami isn't Okami without its astounding art style. Interestingly, the developers of Okami originally planned to use an art style inspired by the then recent Resident Evil remake, which is jarring to imagine given the final product and how much the art style they went with influences the gameplay. I learned about this from the first part of KingK's new series, Masterful Mimicry, which examines the importance and influences of Okami, among other things. ## My Favorite Game Mechanic (that nobody likes)
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w6kvy6Ci0zU

In the opening hours of Cyberpunk 2077, things go really badly for the main character V. After the heist they're on falls apart, V is forced to implant a biochip in their head that malfunctions and starts eroding their neural network, replacing it with the data on the chip. V is given a prognosis of just a few weeks to live, and the main quest is all about their desperate search for some sort of cure, forcing them to take on countless jobs no matter how risky or seemingly hopeless. Signs of V's neural degradation regularly pop up throughout, and not just in the main story, but also in tons of side missions both big and small. At times, it occurs in places you'd never really expect it to, blurring the line between main content and side content in an effective way, and most importantly further selling the idea that V is dying, that time is running out. Of course, it's not. For most players, the amount of in-game days that will pass from just doing the main story will exceed V's original prognosis by a fair bit. The data that is overwriting V's brain is an engram of Night City legend Johnny Silverhand, and when the chip is first implanted, Johnny is openly hostile towards V, so it could be argued that as the initial estimate came during a time where Johnny was actively trying to accelerate the process, it isn't representative of how long V actually has to live. And as the two start working together after this point, that extends how long V has. While this may be good and true, it ultimately ends up being a weak justification, as V has an infinite amount of time to live in Night City. All they need to do is ignore the problem. And unlike all the times I've tried to do this in real life, there is no consequence. Their spleen won't rupture. My spleen's never ruptured, but it could. V can live forever. While the weight of being in the process of dying may be felt in the story, it isn't felt within the gameplay itself. While I do appreciate their attempts of having V's terminality be addressed in some ways as to not let the player entirely forget what is going on with them, it doesn't solve the disconnect that occurs when engaging with any activity that isn't actively helping V find a cure. Aside from an early mainline quest that requires earning a certain amount of money, there isn't really a good narrative reason for V to engage in boxing matches, races, and all of the other types of gigs out there. Screw it, I'm saying it, it creates ludonarrative dissonance. Please don't leave. What's kind of a shame is that there's a really good and fairly easy solution for this that CD Projekt Red could have implemented, and it would have led to the gameplay and story actually complementing each other instead of conflicting with each other, and that's a time limit. I know that may seem counterintuitive for an open world game where you're meant to get lost within a massive city and follow whatever thread interests you the most, but I think it would have added much needed stakes to everything you do. Also, there are ways to integrate a time limit that actually incentivize exploration and engaging with side activities. Take Unsighted. Every character in the game, not just the protagonist, has a set amount of in-game hours before they become mindless husks of themselves. However, there is a resource called Meteor Dust that can extend the life of any character. This not only allows you to save other people, but it also helps keep your character from expiring. While there certainly is still a push to be efficient in various ways, exploring the world and engaging in side activities is the best way to get more time to complete the game. 2077 could have had something similar. Maybe a resource that you get from doing side missions or an item you can buy if you have enough eddies. It even could have been partly tied to Johnny's disposition towards V, so taking on missions he wants V to do or even just doing missions in ways he might align with could buy even more time. This could create some interesting conflict, as Johnny's way of doing things sometimes can be really not good, so players would be tempted to make choices they normally wouldn't make in order to help V live longer. Regardless of the specifics, the primary way to get it would be by doing things other than the main quest. Not only would the mechanical pressure of the time limit align with the story, but it'd also make it so every activity is in some way contributing toward the primary goal of keeping V alive. This would make it so doing some amount of side content would be mandatory, but it'd be on the player to decide what those things are. All in all, it would push players to engage with the game as an open world and not just as a linear story in a big space. The main missions would still be more important than the side ones, as they'd be focused on finding a permanent fix instead of a temporary one, but this would create a more compelling and realistic reason for V to do random jobs despite only having weeks to live. Like the setting props V up as someone who needs to take on as many gigs as possible to get by, but it isn't all that hard to beat the game by just doing the main path. Between quest rewards and drops from enemies you kill, you can get more than enough money to keep V properly stocked and upgraded. If the reward for side jobs had a mechanical effect that literally kept V alive, the pull to do them would be so much stronger and better fit with the game's themes. When used in the right way, time limits can apply just the right amount of pressure to get players to actually feel the themes a game is trying to explore and push them to engage with the full scope of abilities, items, and mechanics at their disposal in order to be efficient. It is a very powerful tool that can incentivize player behavior in all sorts of interesting ways, and like with Cyberpunk, I often find myself wishing more games turned to them. Like Baldur's Gate 3, which similarly to Cyberpunk kicks off with a bio-tadpole being implanted in the main character's head with the threat that it will turn them into a mind flayer after a certain amount of time has passed. Pretty early on, there is an in-game reason provided as to why you can spend as much time doing whatever you want without turning into one, but it felt like a huge missed opportunity to not have some sort of larger timer. There's a whole short and long rest system that largely doesn't matter. There are a few quests where if you take a long rest during them there may be some consequences, but for the most part the system isn't really utilized. An actual ticking clock probably wouldn't make sense here, but some sort of day limit would have made the rest system so much more engaging, and they also could have done the unsighted thing of adding some resource that gives more time. It could have even been tied to the various tadpoles you find. Like, there could have been two ways to consume them, one that extends your timer and one that lets you access the powers, so it'd be on you to decide what would be more valuable, to have more days or have more abilities to be more efficient. This would create all sorts of interesting choices that entice you to make decisions you might not normally make. I also felt that Dredge could have been improved with a timer. While the day-night cycle does provide some pressure to get stuff done efficiently, the lack of any sort of overarching limits makes it a bit superfluous. Sure, it creates a reason to go back to town and sell your stuff, but the inventory limit already will get players to do that, making the time mechanic a bit redundant. Due to the player having as many days to beat the game as they want, there is never much of a reason for them to push their luck and go out on the water at night. Having a limit on the amount of days that could pass in order to achieve a certain ending could have given a really compelling reason to risk going out and facing the elder horrors. In general, a timer would have made all of them way more scary. Honestly, as the game currently stands, encounters with them are pretty underwhelming. It's only fun when you get away. If the player does get caught by one, it'll either end with their ship being sunk, forcing them to reload from the last checkpoint, or do damage that then needs to be repaired. The thing about taking damage and surviving though, is that in most cases, you're better off just scuttling the ship as then you don't have to pay for repairs or take the slow and tedious trip back to a port after losing your motor, which you almost always will. What should be the game's most tense moments are undercut by having no real consequence, except for having to replay a couple minutes. If there was a day limit, instead of getting a game over when getting shipwrecked, it could have cost the player a few days and a decent bit of money to get a new ship, turning those boring and tedious trips back to a port after taking damage into ones of the utmost importance and intensity because not getting back safely would actually matter. All of this would have made the eldritch horror themes in Dredge be felt instead of just being a flavor. Ghost of Tsushima seemed like it would have benefited from a timer as well. After Act 1, a prompt pops up that says Mongols have taken back locations on the island and that Jin must liberate them, and for a moment I felt really excited about the prospect of having to strategically push back the enemy invasion, but that's not what it is at all. You don't need to save these farmsteads. In fact, doing so really doesn't do anything aside from getting you a bit of experience and a few supplies. Implementing some sort of time mechanic could have gone a long way in making this feel like it actually mattered. For instance, Mong

that feels separate from the rest of the game, and they see it as a thing they need
to get through to get back to enjoying what they actually like.
The takeaway they have is that timers are bad, when the actual issue was that it didn't
match their expectations for the kind of challenge they thought a game would present.
A similar thing could be said when a strict day-night cycle is used in a game that signals
as being cozy, making it so any sort of time pressure clashes with the expected experience.
Also, the fact that game-wide timers in particular have largely been cordoned off to games for
sickos like me, it makes it so even if someone who isn't a fan of time mechanics is willing
to give one a shot, their options will be some of the least forgiving games out there.
For instance, the time limit in something like Pathologic 2 is certainly a stressor,
but there are so many other aspects about the game that make it tense and unsettling.
Honestly, getting rid of the time limit really wouldn't make it that much more approachable
for those who fall outside of its target demographic.
So as people's exposure to the mechanic is often tied to some of the most extreme
uses of it, or in a game that they played in the hopes of getting away from real responsibility,
or as a short inclusion in a title that otherwise isn't about time pressure, it's no wonder
people struggle to connect to it.
Maybe the problem is that there's not a modern, introductory title to this kind of
mechanic.
And I don't know.
I get that everyone has different tastes and interests, that we all live different lives
and that shapes what we find to be fulfilling ways to spend our free time.
But also, I think there are a lot of people, maybe even you, who could like game-wide time
limits.
Who could benefit from the pressure they create.
However, the wider industry doesn't have much of a reason to pursue titles for that
potential audience as it is so unproven.
More casual games aimed at wider audiences are just less likely to take the risk of alienating
players in that way, even though it could be the type of experience that gets them to
change their mind on the mechanic.
Of course, I am almost certainly being overly idealistic, as if more people would like game-wide
time limits if only more titles used them.
If only there was one in your favorite genre.
The reality is, that's not the case.
I can hold out hope that it is just a misunderstood mechanic, but there are plenty of valid reasons
to have issues with them.
It's not just that they are stressful, they have other downsides.
Like if everything is not perfectly balanced and there is one playstyle that is more effective
than the others, players will always default to that for the sake of being able to get
through the game quicker, regardless of whether or not it is actually more fun.
Timers also disincentivize engaging with stuff that may not have any practical benefit, but
does help establish the tone and detail of a world.
Sure, the conversations NPCs have with each other in Cyberpunk 2077 is not a core part
of the game, but it does provide texture to the world that no doubt plays a role in a
feeling so special and alive.
And it would be much harder to appreciate that texture if you were always running by it.
Also, as much as I might like to, I can't dismiss the fact that they are stressful.
I do believe that's the point, and a good thing, but I get that most people won't
be compelled by that.
Because stress is a hard feeling to hold onto for that long.
Even if we had more modern games that were balanced similarly to Pikmin or Dead Rising
where the use of a timer is not there to create a brutal experience, but instead to give structure
and stakes, most people still wouldn't want to have to hold onto that tension for the
duration of a playthrough, regardless of the mechanical motivation it provides.
And part of that is not every player needs mechanical motivation in the way I do.
They don't need the pressure of time to engage with other mechanics.
They don't need to feel the themes of the game through gameplay and instead are able
to connect with them just as much by simply seeing them.
They don't have the same problems with games that I do.
And with those who do, if the stress is felt too heavily, which it often seems to be, that
might only serve to make it harder to connect to it.
To make it harder to turn the game on at all.
It is a solution to many game design issues that by and large people don't want.
And I suspect they never will, no matter how many stellar games come out that incorporate
them.
And I get it.
There are already too many games to play, and making time for one that has a mechanic
that is intentionally designed to make you stressed is a hard sell.
It doesn't matter whether or not it is more interesting if it makes whatever gaming time
you're able to carve out for yourself less enjoyable.
Unfortunately, games that are more fun to talk about in video essays are not always
more fun for the average person to play.
Ghost of Tsushima, Dredge, Baldur's Gate 3, and post-Phantom Liberty Cyberpunk 2077
are all wildly beloved and well-reviewed games.
That doesn't mean they're perfect or couldn't have been better with different systems, but
it isn't as if the problems with them that I think could have been fixed with game-wide
time limits are massive, glaring flaws that ruin the experience.
Most people were able to look past them.
A game-wide timer may have brought the gameplay and narratives of these titles closer together
and incentivized diving into these worlds with more purpose, but having one probably
would have also led to far fewer people playing them.
I'm glad some developers still find the mechanic to be worthy of exploring.
There is a lot that can be done with it, and I really don't think games have even come
close to scratching the surface.
Maybe my idealistic side is right, and if enough great games come out that prove how
effective time limits can be at crafting incredible experiences, people will come around on them.
I know they won't, but one should be allowed a few futile hopes.
Ultimately, time is weird, and being reminded that we only have so much of it, especially
when trying to kick back and relax, when trying to get lost in the vibes of a moment, when
trying to be okay with staying still for a bit, will never appeal the most.
When I started making this video, I hoped to prove that the reason people don't like
time limits is because they haven't given them a proper chance.
I do think there is truth there, but given the current offerings, I don't know if giving
them a chance would even matter.
Furthermore, it is hard to envision a world in which there is a big shift in opinion on
them, as it would require a lot of studios to take a massive risk and a lot of players
to step outside of their comfort zone.
All I can do is hold onto the belief that time limits are good, actually, and be okay
with the idea that there might not be enough time in the world for me to convince you of that.
Whether it be in regards to games with time limits or just weird games in general, it
is reassuring to know that there are creatives out there who just want to see their vision
for what a game can be come to life, regardless of how weird it is.
Developers who aren't afraid to take big risks even in an industry that often disincentivizes it.

## Playing Games in Unfun Ways
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DmsS1jF9_EE

Last month I replayed Dark Souls 3 for the first time since it came out. Up until now it was one of the few FromSoft titles I had only beaten once, and it's a shame it took me so long to get back to it as Dark Souls 3 is very good. I can't think of many better examples of a studio firing on all cylinders to create stellar levels, music, characters, and of course bosses that add up to be so much more than the sum of their parts. After finishing the base game and finally getting the chance to play the DLC, I couldn't help but be swept away by its brilliance. And in the joy and excitement of revisiting this masterpiece, I was struck by a terrible idea. I should get all of the achievements. For those of you who also made the mistake of 100%ing Dark Souls 3, this staircase will be irritatingly familiar to you. It is the most reliable way to collect the covenant item for the Blades of the Darkmoon called Proof of Concord Kept. You can exchange 30 of them for a ring and miracle that is needed for two of the achievements. These two silver knights have a very low chance of dropping one. I've seen contrasting information across wikis and reddit posts, but broadly speaking, based on the gear I was using, the drop rate for the item was somewhere between 3.5 and 4%. On a perfect run, I could do a loop in about 35 seconds, and on a not so perfect run, well the time definitely could add up. Even when estimating at the higher end of the drop rate and a fairly generous run average of 45 seconds per loop, the pace would roughly be one Proof of Concord Kept every 12 runs, or about 9 minutes per proof. Extrapolating it out even further, and that's around 4.5 hours of grinding to get the necessary amount. There are 5 other covenants with items like this. In fairness, none of the other grinds are as bad as this one. Most have more efficient farming spots, and a couple can be done through summoning a friend. But regardless, all of it put together will take most people around 15 hours. When I started, I knew this would not be time well spent. I'd be doing the exact same motions over and over again, not in service of learning something new or getting more skill, but rather in service of RNG. I have no issue putting a ton of time into figuring out how to do something challenging, but this was not that. The challenge was purely in mustering the patience to kill the same two enemies hundreds of times. Throughout it all, I found myself constantly asking, why? Why am I doing something that isn't fun, that isn't rewarding, that isn't enriching? There are hundreds of games in my backlog I could be playing instead, all of which have the promise of being a way better use of my time. Like man, Ultra Kill looks so rad, and I've been saying I should play Citizen Sleeper 2 for months now, and maybe it's finally time to give the Kingdom Come Deliverance series a shot. But then I didn't. I came back to the staircase anyway. I suppose I felt a sense of obligation to 100% the game. FromSoft has been my favorite developer for a good while now. I've gotten all of the achievements in Dark Souls 1 and 2, for Bloodborne, for Elden Ring and Night Reign. It seemed a shame to not complete the Dark Souls trilogy just because of some grinding. This is a weird impulse I get with certain titles. With those that really click with me in a specific way at just the right time, I feel this desire to honor them. Like I owe them something for providing me with a monumental experience. There's something about having that 100% next to a game that feels like it accomplishes that. It shows that it was worth it to do everything. The thing is, it very rarely is worth it. I've talked about this idea in the past, but most games don't really have great achievements. So often, like this grind on the staircase, they call for you to engage with the game in a way that is fundamentally different from what makes the game good. The stuff that made me want to get all of the achievements in the first place. With Dark Souls 3 specifically, the desire to 100% it came after the high of defeating Medir and Slave Knight Gale, arguably the best fights in the entire game. Ironically though, fights that aren't tied to any achievement. Despite that, I knew what the achievements would entail. I knew it wouldn't just be the fun stuff. But once I made up my mind that I wanted to do it, it was hard to want to abandon that. And once I collected one proof of concord kept, and then a couple more, and then a couple more, it seemed like I should just stick with it. It was as if just by starting the grind, I had sullied my ability to have my playthrough end by experiencing one of the best bosses FromSoft has ever made for the first time. So if I couldn't end on peak, I might as well see this stupid thing through to the end. I wish I wasn't this susceptible to sunk cost fallacy, but it happens more often than I'd like it to. I reach the point where I'm not having fun, and you know, not in a good way that will eventually have a real experiential payoff, but I stick with it anyway. A very similar thing happened to me earlier this year with Clair Obscura Expedition 33. I adored the game so much that when I hit credits, I didn't want to leave the world behind. I wanted to stay in it and honor the game by experiencing everything I could. And luckily, or I guess unluckily for me, Clair Obscura has tons of optional content to engage with. Now some of it is pretty incredible, but a lot of the optional stuff is just re-skinned versions of older enemies. And as it is pretty easy to create incredibly powerful builds, most of it becomes trivial. Like I didn't even use the Stenhall build that could one-shot bosses, but I was still beating most things I fought before they could even get a turn. And that includes the actual cool unique bosses. What had mostly felt like a well-paced and decently balanced experience throughout the core of my playthrough turned into an exercise of just watching lights and colors for 15 hours as I collected every journal, gathered every record, and killed every boss. Without the gripping narrative to propel me forward or the challenging combat to keep me engaged, continuing to play it felt empty. Regardless, I kept with it long after I had grown tired of it. When I had rolled credits, I probably would have put it in my top 5 games of all time. When I got the last achievement though, I just thought it was really, really good. There is of course something to be said about loving a game so much that you end up overexposing yourself to it and enjoying it less. What better way to honor a game than be willing to experience the worst parts of it? This is a silly impulse. I imagine most developers would probably prefer players to not follow through on it. But it is an impulse I feel all the same. I hope that in 5 years or something, I forget about how I felt by the end of my time with Clair Obscure and only remember the best bits. It could be argued that remembering the experience of me kind of ruining the game for myself might help me avoid doing it again in the future. But I kind of doubt that's the case because only 3 months passed between me grinding the endgame of Clair Obscure and me grinding this stupid staircase in Dark Souls 3. And the disappointment of that experience didn't deter me in the slightest. Now this grind is not the intended way to gather the proof of Concord Kept. The way you're supposed to get them, as well as all the other Covenant items, is through PvP. I imagine getting these was more reliable at release when tons of people were still playing, but now it is pretty hit or miss. Not only is it exceedingly rare to get summoned as a Blade of the Darkmoon now, but in the off chance you do, it will almost certainly be into the world of longtime players that have crafted specific builds for PvP in these areas. Meaning unless you are very into Dark Souls PvP, you probably will get stopped. These items being dropped by normal enemies is FromSoft's way of making the Covenant rewards attainable regardless of how active the player base is. It's a compromise. While attempting this grind, I had the Blade of the Darkmoon Covenant insignia on throughout and got pulled into an invasion a grand total of three times. There are a few things I could have done to make it a bit more likely to get summoned, but it never would have outpaced the farming approach. And honestly, based on looking back at old posts, even when the game was more active, it seems like getting summoned still would have been the slower choice. With all of this said, I do think it would have been a lot more fun to get all the proof of concords kept through PvP. It would have pushed me to engage with a system that I haven't really put that much time into. To learn the meta, to hone my skills, to be truly challenged. The thing is, even if the PvP method was more reliable than it is, I have a feeling I probably still would have chosen to farm enemies instead of other players. With invasions, there is so much more out of my hands. It relied not just on my skill, but also on the skill of whoever I'm facing, as well as the number of players who are in the invasion, as these almost always are gank fights. Not to mention, it also rely on our connections to the internet. And while I'm sure I would get better at Pv

The reason I keep playing games I love in an unfun way despite feeling like I am kind of ruining them is due to the human instinct to dredge meaning from any experience, regardless of how much it sucks. It is, in fact, pure cope. Now, I do think that term gets used in a way that is far too dismissive. Most things in life do not go exactly our way, and it is in our ability to cope that allows us to not be miserable every waking minute. Being able to find enjoyment in wasted time and missteps is part of being human. Ultimately, while I do think it is a good thing that I am able to do this, I don't think it is necessarily always good when I do. There are plenty of instances where I think I would be better off disrupting the patterns I naturally fall into, and I hope this reflection of me clearly pointing out to myself and to you the ways in which I approach games in unfun ways, whether it be just on a normal playthrough or on a 100% playthrough, will get me to do that a bit more. Just because I can make meaning doesn't mean I should, and I think I need to get better at knowing when to back down. I have my doubts, though. For instance, a tiny yet not insignificant part of me wants to 100% Dark Souls 3. Again. It annoys me that I 100%ed Dark Souls 1, Dark Souls 2, and Bloodborne on PlayStation, and Dark Souls 3, Elven Ring, and Night Reign on PC. It'd be nice to have all of them done on one platform, and that's really only possible on PlayStation. Also, frankly, Elven Ring and Night Reign weren't all that hard to 100%, so the worst part about getting the Platinums would really just be doing the Dark Souls 3 grind again. And look, it wasn't that bad, all things considered. Now, this would mean doing Sekiro 2 as I'd want to complete the set, and that'd be tough as I've heard it has almost as bad of a grind as Dark Souls 3. And also, I'd want to do the original Demon's Souls, which unfortunately calls for more grinding than all of the Dark Souls games combined. And then, I don't know, maybe I should do Scholar of the First Sin to get the full DS2 experience. And the Demon's Souls remake, as I've heard they changed the trophies from the original. And Armored Core 6, as I might as well do it if I'm doing all the rest. I don't think I will do this. I really hope I don't do this. There is a non-zero chance that I will do this. What's more likely is I will get swept up again in the way I did with Dark Souls 3 or Claire Obscure or the dozens of others before it. I will become so focused with the result that I won't properly address the process until I've sunk too much time in it. It is who I've been and who I am and who I will be. And in fairness, it has worked out pretty well. I love games, and I love talking about games, and because of that, regardless of what an experience entails, I always will get something out of anything I play. The mere existence of this channel has acted as a way for me to add value to every game I try. And now that it is my job to talk about games, that is more true than ever. I'm in a unique position where a bad experience with a game can lead to me making something just as interesting, if not more interesting, than a good experience with a game. Frankly, this platform kind of incentivizes it. I try not to let that affect how I personally approach games. I don't go into something with a negative mindset hoping I can farm it for content. But I also don't always go into stuff with the intentionality that I probably should. I do like the sentiment of playing games in the way that is most fun to you. And maybe it is just that easy for many of you. But I at least have not found it to be that simple. It is hard to always be aware of the habits and patterns you subconsciously fall into when actually playing something. And even when you are, the way games are designed to bring about so many variables that can get in the way. With that said, while I don't know that I can just play games in the way that is the most fun, I would like to play them in a way that is more intentional. To not always get swept up in how I tend to approach them, which in one way or another always is about me focusing too much on the goal. Whether it comes in the form of mainlining content for progression's sake, or hyperfixating on completion criteria that is neither interesting or fun, I want to move away from it a bit. To be better at making sure I am actually getting the most out of everything I play. To go against my instincts sometimes, and instead try to play games in the way someone else might, in order to see what my playstyle might be missing. It could be that this in itself is a bad idea, that it will lead to me having a terrible time in entirely new ways. But if this grind taught me anything, it is that I will find a way to make it matter nonetheless. Ugh. Oh my god. I still have to beat the game two more times. This is stupid. Through all of this, I have been thinking a lot about all of the games I have 100%ed over the years. So I decided to put together a video where I go over every single one I've done, and give them a rating based on how enjoyable or annoying they were to complete. It has been a while since I've played many of them, and there honestly ended up being way more games than I would have guessed. I had a lot of fun reflecting on my gaming history, and I think you'll be surprised by some of them. I did also give out one 10 out of 10 for a game that I actually think is worth 100%ing, and you might too. If you'd like to watch the video to find out which one it is, even though you already know it's Outer Wilds, you can check it out right now on Nebula. I've been a part of Nebula for a good while now. You've almost certainly heard me talk about them before, and will again, because it is the best place online to watch videos from many of your favorite creators, like me, Game Maker's Toolkit, Jacob Geller, KingK, and tons and tons of others. You not only get the best versions of these creators' main videos, but you also get tons of bonus stuff exclusive to Nebula. I'd recommend checking out the video I mentioned already, as well as a conversation I had with Jacob, Iron Pineapple, and Eurothug4000 about Claire Obscure Expedition 33 and all of our thoughts on it. We actually recorded that before I had started to 100% it, so it is an interesting little time capsule that shows the differences between how I felt right after rolling credits to how I feel now. Along with that, there are Nebula original shows like Abolish Everything, which is sort of a panel presentation show where guests make pitches for things they think should be abolished. It is a lot of fun. Nebula just has a wealth of things to watch and listen to made by many of the most thoughtful people out there. For those interested in being more intentional with what they watch, I can't recommend a better place to go.
