## Even More Indie Games You Missed (if i had to guess...i can't be sure though)
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1rfVJdYt_zI

I love indie games, and every few years I like to share some lesser-known ones that I really enjoyed in the hopes that you all check them out and enjoy them too. So, I'm doing it again. Now, every time I make one of these, I get a bunch of comments saying that I didn't pick obscure enough games, and yeah, that's probably fair. The last few have had some sort of popular ones on it. This time, though, I'm only going to be talking about titles that have a thousand or fewer reviews on Steam, and one of them isn't even on Steam, so take that. I know the number of Steam reviews something has isn't the best metric for this sort of thing, as it doesn't perfectly reflect sales or account for major releases on other platforms, but it is better than nothing. I also cross-checked each game on Backlog to make sure none of them are wildly popular outside of Steam. The point is, I tried. And you know what? I think there is a good bet that you haven't played or even heard of most of these games, unless you have, which, you know, is out of my control. So, with that, let's talk about some indie games you haven't played. Probably. The first one I want to talk about, and frankly, it is the reason I decided to make another video like this, is Burgeist. If I'm being honest, it is kind of a hard game to describe. Not because it doesn't fit into a genre, but because when I say it's an open-world, real-time strategy tower defense game, I worry that your ears are going to shut off. But I promise you, this game is awesome. The core premise is that you are trying to build a tower that reaches the heavens in order to save your wife. But whenever you start building one, monsters come to try to tear it down. The gameplay loop pretty much becomes partially building towers around the world to get experience and unlock new abilities so that you can more effectively defend the towers and eventually get one as high as you need to. Of course, you aren't doing this entirely alone. You also have the help of a Burgeist, which is a big monster with a slab of stone on its back that you can place cannons and other things on. The effectiveness of many abilities and the Burgeist are often influenced by height or distance. So whenever you're defending a tower, you really have to understand the general area so you can place yourself and the Burgeist in the most optimal spots. The slate of abilities the game offers are great. Some are damage-focused, others are movement-focused, a couple are a combination of both, and I found myself regularly using everything in my kit to efficiently move around the battlefield so I could get proper leverage. In case it wasn't clear from this description of the gameplay or the footage itself, this game is really weird. But all of its systems somehow tie together nicely, and it does a great job of making the moment-to-moment gameplay, both when in combat and out of it, feel engaging in one way or another. The world itself is mysterious and a lot of fun to try to make sense of. I loved exploring every inch of it and using my wide range of abilities to try to get places that seemed impossible to reach in the hopes that there may be a secret there. And I was almost always pleasantly surprised by what I found. While the story and characters are a bit off-kilter, both are wildly intriguing, and I found myself wanting to engage with every side quest not just for the rewards, but also to learn a little bit more about the world and those within it. Burgeist is the kind of indie game I wish we had more of. It is specific and singular in its vision and feels so incredibly fresh. Girion Studio is also largely a one-person team, which given the scale of this game is wild. Above all, though, it's fun to play, and I think a lot of you would like it. So if any of this sounds interesting, spend the $12 to get it. When I started working on this list, I assumed Burgeist would be the weirdest game on it, but then I came across Basilisk 2000, and it makes Burgeist seem tame by comparison. Developed by Kira, who you may recognize as the developer of Lunased, Basilisk 2000 is presented almost like a found-footage game. According to the store page, a fan came across the files for the unreleased sequel to the unreleased SNES game Basilisk, and they have created a tool so that you can view the various levels of it to see the game that could have been. If you've played Her Story or really any Sam Barlow game, its framing device feels similar to those. Through using the game engine tool, you'll act as a sort of detective to learn both about the game and the story of why it never came out, both of which are fascinating to uncover. The only way to load a new area is by knowing its name, and discovering these names sometimes comes down to just paying attention to context clues in the levels you do have access to, but other times it will require using every potential trick at your disposal to get more information. I don't want to go into any more detail than that, as this very much falls into the category of games where the less you know, the better. I will say, compared to things like Her Story, this is definitely more about the exploration than the puzzle solving. That's not to say there is nothing to solve, there are many things to solve, but the moment-to-moment fun of the game will come less from aha moments and more from piecing together the story through the things you discover in each level. It's also worth noting that it can be pretty obscure. There are clear connections to be made, but it is fairly esoteric with how it makes many of them, which I imagine for some of you will be exactly your kind of thing, and for others will be a bit harder to latch onto. Ultimately, what I love about it is that it uses a very cool framing device to tell a story in a way that only a video game can. It's weird and creepy and really unique. For those of you who love liminal spaces, this should be right up your alley. You can get it for $2 on itch.io, and you can also play its predecessor Basilisk for free, which I'd say is a great companion game if you find yourself enjoying Basilisk 2000. This is one of those experiences that feels so rare to come across, and it plays with the medium in such an interesting way that I would say it's worth checking it out for that alone. Moving into the world of far more conventional games, the next one I want to talk about is Prodigal. If it wasn't obvious by simply looking at it for a few seconds, Prodigal draws heavy inspiration from The Legend of Zelda, specifically the more classic 2D games. Frankly, while I like the direction Nintendo has taken the series, I do often find myself wishing they do more in the 2D space, and while Echoes of Wisdom scratched a bit of that itch, it still wasn't exactly the kind of structure I was hoping for. And that is why I am very thankful Color Grave exists, and that they decided to build on the Zelda formula in their own way. It has good dungeons, some cool bosses, unique items, and a lot of charm. One thing that I think makes it stand out is that it has a strong focus not just on being the hero of the village, but also on creating relationships with the people in it, of changing your reputation from someone who abandoned the town to someone who is an integral part of it. This takes the form of friendships you can build, as well as romantic relationships, which I never thought I'd want in a game like this, but it works well. I don't know if it feels this way with all the characters, but at least with the one I ended up with, the relationship added a new layer to the wider story that I think benefited the narrative in a handful of ways. While the core of the game is solid in its own right, I think what really makes Prodigal shine is how much optional stuff there is to do that feels worthwhile, especially in the post-game. Like, I spent more time playing after I rolled credits than I did before, and there aren't a ton of games that I find myself doing that with. By and large, Prodigal is a fresh take on a classic formula that does a lot to get you to care about the place you're saving, and I found this super refreshing as so many games kind of expect you to want to save a place because that's what heroes do, and don't put in the work to establish reasons beyond that. There's lots and lots to love here, and I think it will be a great time for anyone who misses the days of playing stuff on their Game Boy Color. The next title I had originally planned to talk about actually passed 8,000 Steam reviews at some point between me buying it and making this video. So in order to skirt around my arbitrary rule that no one is actually going to hold me to, the game I'm going to recommend is Sheepo, a 2D Metroidvania with smooth movement and a good sense of humor developed by Kyle Thompson. And now that I think of it, everything in this game really set the groundwork for Kyle Thompson's follow-up game, Islets. Islets sets you in a world that has been fractured into multiple floating islands, and you are tasked with bringing them all back together. Like most Metroidvanias, you'll unlock new abilities that recontextualize the places you've been and unlock new paths forward. But what makes it stand out a bit from its contemporaries is that as you bring the pieces of the island back together, that also opens up new paths and secrets. So you go from exploring each island in its separated state to exploring it in its connected one

## The Best Games Are Kinda Bad
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QREUmhrZ95c

I'm going to start off by saying something that, judging by what I've seen on YouTube over the past year or so, is a pretty controversial opinion. That being Tears of the Kingdom is a good video game. Great, even. Nintendo took the open-air concept they built Breath of the Wild around and expanded on it beautifully, offering a slew of new mechanics that all prioritize player freedom. I can't think of many titles where the moment-to-moment gameplay feels as fun for as long as it does here. There are just countless ways to engage with the world as well as the challenges it presents. With enough effort and iteration, any stupid idea you come up with can become the solution to whatever's in your way. I put in just over 100 hours, and aside from a small chunk of time where I was just standing on a dragon's back to farm materials, I can't think of many dull moments. Simply put, I loved playing it, as it offered hours and hours of compelling gameplay and jaw-dropping spectacle. So to now see video after video focusing on all of its shortcomings, showing disappointment at how it turned out, belittling something that provided me with one of the most enjoyable gaming experiences I can think of... Well, it makes sense, because I think a lot of them are right. I've watched a ton of critiques on Tears of the Kingdom, and while I don't agree with every take about it, because that's not how existing works, I do think the vast majority of criticisms levied towards it hold a lot of water. There is an annoying amount of repeated content, the Sky Islands are too sparse, there aren't enough unique encounters throughout the world, especially in the depths, the dungeons lack gravitas, and the reward for completing them is terrible as the companion's abilities are unreliable, and also having them out kind of tanks the frame rate. The major rewards in general are underwhelming as there aren't nearly enough things that feel unique, the sages' cutscenes present the exact same information every time and don't progress your understanding of the world or story in any meaningful way, there's barely any narrative continuity between it and Breath of the Wild, the amount of menuing is out of control, and due to the flexibility of the mechanics, it's incredibly easy to trivialize most puzzles. Like Ultra Hand into Recall into Ascension clears over half the game. Pulling it off is fun the first few times, but when it becomes a solution to almost everything, the player no longer needs to really engage with what the game is putting out in front of them, and instead just has to execute a simple chain of commands. These are all things I feel about Tears of the Kingdom now, and honestly they were things I felt while playing, as I was having some of the most fun I've ever had with a game. It was a weird cognitive dissonance. I frequently found myself wishing it was better than it was and thinking about some of the ways it could have been, all while being regularly impressed by what it did have to offer. And this seems like a pretty common experience. Most praise of Tears of the Kingdom has always come with a caveat. An incredible game that annoyed me to no end. A disappointing masterpiece. A frustrating 10 out of 10. It's near impossible to talk about Tears of the Kingdom without talking about the ways in which it fell short. Now, it'd be easy to say that Nintendo should have simply fixed all the game's issues to make the perfect title, but the thing is, I think a large portion of its problems are a consequence of the thing that makes it so special. It's immense scale. By scale, I don't just mean world size, even though that certainly is part of it, as Tears of the Kingdom more than doubles Breath of the Wild's total area. But I also mean scale in terms of abilities, activities, items, and the near countless ways all of these things can interact with each other. There is just so much to all of it. The possibilities of just Ultra Hand and the Zonai parts feel endless, and it only gets even wilder when taking into consideration the hundreds of materials that all have multiple purposes. The world is so densely packed with things to do and ways to do them, giving players constant opportunities to utilize the overwhelming amount of mechanics offered. The game is a behemoth, and its promise of possibility gives it a depth that few titles ever even have the potential to reach. But there are costs to this. There's a GDC talk I think about a lot by Alex Jaffe called Curse Problems in Game Design. The premise is that some design ideas have unsolvable problems that are a result of their core promises being in conflict with each other, and a lot of the issues in Tears of the Kingdom fall into that camp. Like with its freedom over mechanics. It wants to allow players to be tactical in combat and utilize Link's massive arsenal, but it also wants fights to feel fluid and frenetic and exciting. However, in order for the game to offer full freedom, the action has to be disrupted. So players are kind of forced to choose between fluid gameplay with more restrictions in what they can use, or more fractured gameplay with free reign over every potential option. At the end of the day, as it is a controller-based game, the way the mechanics are incorporated are limited by it. There really isn't a wasted button, but even then, in order to create all the interactions they wanted to have, menuing and contextual inputs were unavoidable. With the massive range of options the game gives, it also creates balance problems, as the devs want to give players endless ways to overcome any obstacle, but also want those obstacles to feel challenging. The problem is, not every puzzle can account for every solution, and some solutions will be inherently easier than others. This means for players to maintain a decent level of challenge, they'll have to limit themselves in what they use, taking away some of the freedom. Doing this also requires some amount of self-control from the player, and that's kind of asking a lot, as sometimes it is hard to ignore the call of the simplest path, even when it isn't the most fun. Another example is that for Nintendo to fill the world with things to do around every corner, certain activities had to be reused. Given slight twists, of course, but still always similar to whatever came before. It could be argued that it didn't have to be this way, and that they could have taken more time in order to have every encounter feel entirely unique, but to achieve the scale and density they were going for, that would have required far more development time, which I don't think anyone wanted, as it would have kept us in anticipation for longer, ballooned the budget even further, and probably inched Nintendo even closer to charging $100 for it instead of the already increased $70. Regardless, the promise of Tears of the Kingdom's design is that players will always have something to do on a moment-to-moment basis. However, this approach, while great for people who aren't focused on exploring everything but just want stuff to engage with regularly, can become wildly repetitive for those who want to see and do everything there is to do. And while I do believe that Nintendo did not design the game with the intent that players would engage with every last thing in it, if you create a finite collectible, people will be compelled to get them all. When it comes to cursed problems, developers either have to deal with the consequences or give up some element about it, shifting how it works in a way that doesn't yield as notable of an issue, which might not be a compromise they're willing to make. And of course, not all of these issues will affect players equally. The consequences will be far more severe to certain playstyles than others, so it falls on the developers to decide what they're willing to live with. Are they okay with making part of the playerbase be annoyed to let the other part have a great experience? Problems like these exist with all kinds of games of all kinds of sizes, but they do seem almost inevitable for ones with massive scales. Frankly, they exist within all of the most beloved open-world titles out there. The Witcher 3, Red Dead Redemption 2, Elden Ring, Skyrim. All of them are considered to be some of the best games ever made in large part due to their incredible worlds and the breadth of player options they offer. But like Tears of the Kingdom, their scales have a cost. Whether it be struggling to properly balance mid- to late-game encounters due to not being able to predict how powerful any given player character may be at any given point, or sacrificing player freedom in order to tell specific stories, or relying too heavily on the minimap to make it possible for players to navigate the world without it, or being Skyrim. At a point, once a certain scale is reached, there are just too many factors to account for, and that will lead to concessions in one form or another. To be clear, a game just being massive in scale does not make it good. In fact, I think a pretty common problem with many modern AAA titles is that they are too big. They try to do too many things to create the ultimate forever experience in the hopes of having the same impact that any of the massive games I just mentioned did, both in terms of sales and influence. But they tend to end up being too derivative or too stretched thin to have that impact. They lack the twists and polish that the best ones have, making the downsides of scale all the more noticeable. Now, even though big game does not equal good game, they do make up a large percentage of titles considered the best ever. Almost every top 100 list I've ever seen has The Witcher 3, Red Dead Redemption 2, Elden Ring, Skyrim, and Breath of the Wild in the top 25. The drive to make large-scale games, while certainly influenced by the market, does go beyond that. There are just some things that only big games can accomplish. There has long been

...to do with a person being tired of hearing about a game for the millionth time that they didn't find to be all that special, that they felt had fundamental flaws that led to them disliking it. Underrated also is never about scores, it's more so a stand-in for underplayed. So many times when I've asked for underrated games, people respond with titles that have incredible reviews, it's just that their fanbase is small and they don't get talked about that regularly in videos online. By and large, calling something underrated or overrated is a plea for people to care more about the things you care about instead of the things that already seem to have enough attention. And to be clear, that's not a judgment, I'm guilty of this too. It makes me fundamentally sad that in 2022, Stray won Indie Game of the Year over Tunic. And Neon White for that matter. And frankly, also Sifu. And you know what? Also Citizen Sleeper, which wasn't even nominated for the award, but that's a different crime Jeff Keighley has to answer for. I found Stray to be fine, and I've seen a lot of people talk about how it acted as a sort of gateway to get back into gaming or even into it for the first time, which I think is great. There is value in all types of games for all types of audiences, and we need introductory titles as much as we need weird sweaty ones. However, I can't lie and say that I don't wish games that did more interesting things. And yes, games that I really cherish got the same kind of attention Stray did. Stray doesn't take a lot of risks. It's a simple, polished action-adventure game with a cute, playable character. It's approachable, and in a lot of ways designed to appeal to a wide audience. As someone who is steeped in the side of the indie scene that offers weird and unique experiences, it's hard for me to look at Stray, which is touted by many as one of the best games in years, and not feel like it doesn't do all that much to actually deserve that praise. But of course, that's the point. What feels a bit stale to me is what makes it palatable to many others. It's what makes it easy to love and to recommend. I can spend all the time I want saying that games made to appeal to everyone appeal to no one, but that isn't really the case. They just tend to appeal less to folks like me who play too many games. And to Stray's credit, while it may be designed to appeal to a wider audience, it still manages to feel like it has a personality separate from whatever was selling well when it first went into development. It may not be groundbreaking for me or the industry at large, but it certainly does enough to be groundbreaking for a bunch of people in its broad player base. We are a world of different audiences, and the aspects of a title that makes it special to one makes it overrated to another. To bring it back to where we started, I don't know that there is a series that has been called overrated more often than The Legend of Zelda. And Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom have received that label more than any of the other titles within it. Frankly, it makes sense, as they are the best-selling Zelda games by a lot. Together, they've sold more copies than all of the other 3D games combined. They are talked about by more people, they are loved by more people, and so it is no real surprise that they are also hated by more people. Tears of the Kingdom, especially, is a weird game in that it does a decent bit to be palatable to an extremely wide audience, while also having a handful of systems with edges to them that will appeal greatly to some but annoy others. Ultimately, I get why people feel so negatively about Tears of the Kingdom. Instead of polishing and narrowing in on what Breath of the Wild established, it pulled things out, creating an ambitious yet messy game. The reality is, it could have been better. While I do think many of its issues were a trade-off of its scale, not all of them were. And there are some pretty simple solutions to some of its problems, which makes them even more frustrating. Like, they could have solved the majority of the game's narrative continuity issues with a handful of lines of dialogue, a side quest or two, and the reuse of a few Sheikah assets from Breath of the Wild. These things certainly would have taken some time, but they do feel like they could have easily fit into the development window. However, despite its flaws, both the avoidable ones and cursed ones, it also offered a level of player freedom within a structure that provided a clear sense of progression in a way I've never seen before. And getting to experience that was incredible. I think the phrase nothing is perfect often gets used as a way to hand-wave the issues with a thing. Like, obviously, the statement is true, and is something I imagine we all recognize as true, but the way it gets used often washes away some of the nuance it contains. Because it's not just that nothing is perfect. It is that the aspects that make something good are also often the ones that make it kind of bad. Game design is a business of trade-offs, and while there are certain problems with elegant and perfect solutions, many others are cursed and will always have a cost. How you view that cost will come down to your taste or ability to overlook a flaw in exchange for an experience, but no matter what, it is still there. Whether it be that a game appeals to the widest audience possible by sticking to safe conventions, or is designed for a small niche of players that it will really hit for while actively antagonizing anyone outside of it, or is so massive in scope that despite providing some of the most innovative and intriguing gameplay out there, also contains unsolvable issues as a result of that, the best games will always be kinda bad. To some at least. Even though it is easier than ever to find things that appeal to our unique tastes, whether it be games, films, or online videos, it still is pretty common for creatives to stick with safe ideas. These can still feel personalized to your interests and be great, but creatives are often limited by the platform their work is consumed on. This is something I see all the time with videos and personally experience. It is hard to justify making things that are weird or experimental or different from what any specific creator views as safe for their channel. But like, what if you want to see Jacob Geller make a lasagna recipe from Wanted Dead with his fiancee? Or watch me take a script I wrote 12 years ago, turn it into an actual video, and then provide commentary throughout it? These sorts of things are fun to make and watch, but normally don't get made because it's a bit too different. However, these two videos do exist, along with many others, because of Nebula. Nebula is a streaming service that I've been a part of for a few years now. What drew me into it in the first place is how they empower creators to make more cool things, and the current catalog over there is a testament to that. And honestly, I think it is safe to say now that Nebula is for gamers. Aside from me and Jacob, there's also Game Maker's Toolkit, Liam Triforce, King K, Curious Archive, Cursed Judge, Eurothug 4000. It's just a great lineup of thoughtful creators that you probably already watch, and you can get the best versions of their videos and more over there. If you go to nebula.tv slash resbuten, you can get 40% off for the year, which comes out to just $3 a month. There's so much incredible work there to enjoy, so go start with Jacob making a lasagna, or me talking about talking about Kirby Air Ride, and then keep checking out everything else the site has to offer. Anyway, thanks to Nebula for sponsoring the video. For everyone still here, I appreciate you. As always, a big thanks to my patrons for making this channel possible. The support means so much more than you can ever really know, and I say that every time, but it is true. With that, I hope you have a great day and or night, and I will see you in the next one.

## The Games That Got Me Through 2024
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Es6Zi342eGE

We've made it through yet another year, and like the last few, it has been a pretty life-changing one for me. Most notably, I've gone from being a dad of one kid to a dad of two, and this shift has brought about whole new levels of confusion, exhaustion, stress, and joy. There is just so much in my life now, and when I look back at the year, it's hard not to see it as one big blur. I'm sure some of that feeling can be chalked up to the various sustained periods of sleep deprivation that comes from having a newborn, but in general, as I've gotten older, I've found that if I'm not intentional with grounding myself in moments in time, they will get away from me. And so, like most years, playing games has been one way I've grounded myself, and now I want to take some time to reflect on the stuff I played in order to ground my experience even further. These aren't necessarily my favorite games I played this year, but they are the ones that helped me through it in one way or another. Also, as this series generally goes, the focus will be more on how these games impacted me rather than the games themselves, but if you're curious to see more typical reviews of everything I played, I've been doing that on my second channel this year, so maybe check that out. Normally, I like to start with the first thing I played last year, but this time that's kind of hard as I was playing multiple games at the same time. However, there is one title from that general time frame that has stuck with me more than the others, so that seems as good of a place to start as any. And that game was Unpacking. Unpacking is a simple title where you organize a main character's belongings as they move from place to place. The story is told through objects and locations and how those two things mix together. Everything you need to know about the main character is learned through the act of unpacking her things, and it is wild how easy it is to understand her from just this. But I guess it makes sense. Moving's very nature is transitional, and that makes it a deeply revealing process. As someone who has moved nearly ten times since becoming an adult, I felt intimately drawn in by this energy. I know the excitement of fresh starts, the anxiety of figuring out where it is you fit in, the frustration of setbacks, and the comfort of being in the space you'll hopefully be in for the long haul. I didn't need to see all the moments that happened in between, the ones that fueled each move, in order to connect with the character. Simply seeing where she went and what went with her meant so much more to me. How we use and fill our space is a reflection of who we are. And honestly, these changes happen whether you're moving or not. Even though I am now in a home that I don't plan to leave anytime soon, the way even it has changed over the years because of shifts in the stuff that takes up the most space within it has made it feel in some ways like a new house every year. As the spots that used to only be occupied by mine and my wife's stuff have slowly but surely been overtaken by our kids, our house has taken on new meaning, new functions. And maybe those things will only serve us for a short time, but they will still serve us. Unpacking acted as a good mindsetter for the year. I don't know how often I will look back at it moving forward, but at the very least it was a reminder to appreciate the space we live in and how it changes, and that the transitional periods of life can be just as impactful as the results that come from them. Around this time I was also playing Elden Ring Reforged, a mod for Elden Ring that among other things adds a difficulty mode made exclusively for multiplayer. Frankly, it was a nightmare as it wasn't balanced for the amount of people we had, but it is still an experience that I look back at fondly. I played through it with Iron Pineapple and Yakko for a video Pine wanted to make, and going in we were far more confident in ourselves than we should have been. It ended up taking us over 100 hours, and there were so many times that it felt like we would never be able to get past some obstacle. And unlike typical games where you're pretty certain that they're balanced to be beatable, you just have to figure out how to do it, given Reforged status as a mod designed for a bigger group, success wasn't necessarily guaranteed. This made the process of actually overcoming the challenges wildly satisfying, and also it was just a lot of fun to see Pine do Pine's thing in real time of examining every ability in the game and coming up with off-the-wall builds for us to try in the hopes that it would solve our problems. I'm one who often falls into using strategies that I feel the most comfortable with and sticking to them even when they're not optimal, so it was nice to be pushed out of my comfort zone a bit, especially because I was alongside someone who's so good at doing that sort of thing. Now, while I do think Reforged is solid, it wasn't the mod itself that mattered to me. Some years I know I would be tempted to say it taught me that I can overcome hard things by looking at them in new ways, and there is some truth to that, but that's not something I found myself internalizing with this playthrough. What did have a lasting impact on me, though, was just the act of playing a co-op game with friends. Since starting to do this as a job, I've primarily focused on single-player titles, and while I love doing that, it has meant moving away from the more social side of gaming that made me fall in love with the hobby in the first place. I think for a while I mistook me not loving competitive multiplayer games as me not loving multiplayer games, and that mindset cut me off from a part of gaming I really value. Honestly, so much of what I love about this hobby is sharing experiences with friends. Whether it was couch co-op or LAN parties or taking turns on single-player titles, most of my fondest gaming memories are with other people. Part of why I started this channel in the first place was because opportunities to share games with others were becoming fewer and further between due to the realities of getting older, and it acted as a way to continue to share my experiences and thoughts with both friends and strangers. So getting back into co-op games at all has been really nice, and specifically getting back into them with Pine and Yakko has been especially great. Throughout the course of the year, we played through a handful of games together, and every time it was a blast. Not only are they really fun to be around, but as they love talking about games as much as I do, I found discussing what we thought worked and didn't work about whatever we played to be just as, if not more, enjoyable than actually playing it. Also, our playthroughs have all turned into videos, and like not everything needs to or should be content, but I gotta admit, I really like having these curated versions of our playthroughs to look back at. I think they capture an energy that is nice for me to relive and easy for anyone else to connect with. They also show off a different side of me than these essays do. Like all humans, I am multifaceted, but I sometimes struggle to convey all of those facets here, so having the chance to try to be entertaining in a much different way than people expect from me has been a nice exercise. Not that I plan to move away from essay content, but it has been a solid outlet and gotten me to want to find more ways to express the fuller scope of who I am. Along with sharing games with friends, I also shared games with my toddler for the first time. Or, a game, really. Near the beginning of the year, my wife and I reset our Animal Crossing island as we wanted to experience the early parts of it again. Not wanting her to fully zone out and be hypnotized by the lights, colors, and sounds, I narrated everything I was doing and tried to get her to do the same. Every few days, she'd watch me play for 10 to 15 minutes, and once she had an understanding of what was going on, as I played, she'd talk about what bugs I caught and exclaim, uh-oh, net broke, every time one ran out of durability. It doesn't really matter to me if it works, but that's how I want to model my hobbies. So with that, I fully understand that as small as this is, it might be the peak of us gaming together, and that's okay with me. It was a fun way to spend some time during a handful of afternoons, and I appreciate the ways it forced me to view the game as a parent instead of as just a player. Figuring out how

## Video Game Cities Are Weird
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VRWDq2Xu7I0

When I first played The Witcher 3, I thought I had the full measure of what it was capable of after a dozen or so hours of playtime, but then I reached Novigrad and it kind of blew my mind. I had played plenty of massive open-world games by that point in my life, but while some had incredible and expansive wilds to journey across and others had dense and detailed cities to explore, I had never played one that did both convincingly. In the ones that tried to, the cities never felt realistic. For instance, take Skyrim. While each of the cities are intriguing and impressive in terms of theming and visual design, they don't really feel like proper cities. They are far too small and singular in focus, and their populations are minuscule, with each city having the amount of people you'd historically expect to find in a small village and not a place with a fortified keep. I don't know, like when Nazeem asks if you've been to the Cloud District lately, it's a bit baffling because how could you not, as there is barely any separation between it and the rest of Whiterun. Now, the choice to have smaller cities makes sense given the general design goals of Skyrim. They want you to feel like you can interact with anyone and anything, and creating bigger cities where most of the inhabitants and buildings largely act as set dressing would take away that aspect of the game. Also, trying to scale the cities to something that more closely resembled reality probably would have broken Skyrim's engine irrevocably. Regardless of it being the right choice for the game, it does still have the effect of making the world feel smaller in a way. It makes it all the more obvious that it is just a representation of a city and not an actual one. Novigrad, however, really feels like a city. There are people everywhere you look, all going about their business. And more often than not, it isn't them just doing one task in one place for all time. They move around, they seemingly have schedules and jobs and important places to be. Along with that, there are more buildings than you can reasonably keep track of, the majority of which tower over you, making it feel like the city is a world of its own. It can't be understood in just one glance and is as easy to get lost within as the vast marshes and mountains of the world outside of the walls. Novigrad feels alive. There is an energy to it that's undeniable and makes the game far richer because of it. The city matches the scale of the rest of the world and the way it operates as well as the fact that it exists within a larger context provides a sort of realism to it. There's a sense that it could be a real city in a real world. Now, of course, in reality, it couldn't and it isn't meant to be. Major cities are made to accommodate hundreds of thousands of people and they require countless considerations in order to build something that supports those who reside within it simultaneously. In games, however, the design goal generally is to support just one person, the player. The infrastructure of a video game city doesn't need to provide anything for anyone living in it because their needs don't exist. It doesn't matter that new ships will never come into Novigrad's harbor or that these carts in Assassin's Creed 2 are always stationary or that the power lines in Liberty City don't really make any sense. Although it does make for a fire any Austin video. Actually, in that video, he makes a point about how video games are top down representations of real spaces. The aim of developers is to capture a vibe, not create a functional space. So they aren't focused on creating practical cities. They're focused on creating something that feels close enough. We use the word simulation a lot when talking about video games, but with the exception of stuff like City Skylines, the vast majority of video game cities aren't truly simulations. They're simulacrums, a word I only know from Dungeons and Dragons and therefore am almost certainly missing its full philosophical context. They're imitations that don't have the components to truly operate, but when viewed from a certain perspective, they are able to convincingly fake it. Novigrad is not a functioning city. However, it has all the trappings of one that is making it extremely easy to suspend disbelief and feel that sense of immersion we so often hope to find in games. This illusion only takes a tiny amount of investigation to shatter though. If you spend time following different people in the city, you'll find that each is not an individual. They are an archetype. One who is assigned a zone to operate within and then move around interacting with environmental prompts that align with whatever their assigned tasks are. She'll clean clothes in any washtub she comes across. He'll pick up boxes to take from one spot to another. He'll count the inventory of every pile of stuff he sees, but there is no rhyme or reason for any of it. Doing these things doesn't give them new clothes to wear or earn them money to help support their lifestyle or change the resources the city has. Because why would it? Who cares about a nameless NPC's ability to meaningfully change their life? What does matter is that at a glance it seems as if whatever they're doing could. And in all likelihood you'll only ever give them a glance. In the game you're a witcher and have better things to do than watch this guy saw this piece of wood without ever making progress. You've got a daughter to find and monsters to slay. So while you may take a moment to appreciate the moving pieces of the city, the game is designed in a way where you're most likely just going to run by these people. Because what you have going on is more important and interesting than any single person's mundane life here. The game doesn't need to do anything more because all that matters is that it adds to the player's sense that this could be a real place. Giving more weight to the aspects of the gameplay and story that actually do matter to them. When Ciri feels like a missing part of a place with a sense of life to it, it makes finding her feel even more important. Designing a city in a way that enhances the player's experience obviously goes beyond how it operates or seems to operate. It also can be seen in its layout. Historically, major cities in the real world sprung up near various water sources that best allowed for agriculture and trade, and then had to take the natural environment into account when developing their infrastructure. In games though, devs aren't having to figure out how to build around the natural landscape. They're making the landscape. Every aspect can be developed together to match the architect's vision and not have to compromise to account for reality. The existence of a river might be used in the lore to justify why a city is there, but the actual reason is to give the player something to interact with. So whether it be Novigrad's rivers, terrain, or placement of buildings, they all exist for the player and have the dual purpose of seeming like a plausible feature while also being engaging to play around. Now this can all be a hard line to walk, especially when certain goals may be at odds with one another. For instance, it seems pretty clear that CD Projekt Red wanted Novigrad to feel like a maze of a city that anyone could get lost in. But at the same time, as the game puts a lot of emphasis on exploration, they almost certainly wanted it to feel navigable as to not create constant friction for players whenever they tried to go from one spot of the city to another. Depending on the quests the player pursues and choices they make, they can spend an inordinate amount of time in just the city alone. So making sure that moving through it didn't feel worse than moving through any other area of the game mattered a fair bit. To their credit, as confusing as Novigrad may seem at first, it is one of the few areas in The Witcher 3 where I feel like not using a minimap is extremely viable. And this is done through the inclusion of clever landmarks and terrain that help guide players. For instance, a few branches of the Pontar River cut through Novigrad in different ways, creating distinct sections of the city. To the south are the docks and various gang-controlled neighborhoods. In the center is the market district, which is also alongside some gang-controlled neighborhoods. And to the north is Temple Isle, which is controlled by the worst gang of them all, the Church of Eternal Fire. There's a lot of space to get lost within, but the various water features around Novigrad tend to make it easy to get your bearings. Finding the lower river gives you a straight shot to the docks and out of the city. It is also right by Hierarch Square, which is where many shops and quests are based out of. Following the coast gives an easy path through the docks and also to St. Gregory's Bridge, which can take you to Temple Isle. And even when further away from the bay, the sails of the ships docked in the harbor can be spotted from many different places across the city, giving players an easy way to orient themselves when feeling a bit lost. As for how it uses the terrain, there are exceptions to this, but generally when going north, the elevation increases and when going south, it decreases. I imagine this choice stems from how we tend to associate north with up and south with down, so having that reflected in the topography feels pretty natural. Or maybe I've just spent too much time thinking about this. They also tie different social classes to the various elevations, with the upper class being at the top of the hill and the lower class being at the bottom. This has a fair bit of historical basis, as nobles and royalty were often settled at the top of hills as they offered more protection from potential attacks, but here it mostly serves to further create a distinction between the various spots in the city. Quest design even plays a role in making the city more manageable to navigate

They want a city that feels alive and is intuitive to move through. They want one that enhances the core gameplay. They want one that allows them to experiment in ways they never could in real life. They want one that enhances the story being told. Video game cities are weird because if they weren't, they wouldn't support the vision of their respective games. Ultimately, as much as we may say we might, I don't think we really want realism, at least not to its fullest extent. It's limiting, and in the context of video games, often pointless. What I think we actually want, whether it be in relation to cities or any other part of a game, is the illusion of realism. But as recognizing that something is an illusion often breaks the illusion, I guess let's just keep saying we want realism. And maybe we'll believe it. And while we're doing some pretending, let's pretend like this transition is good. I have a pair of headphones that I really love. My ears have fully adjusted to them, so everything else kind of sounds like trash now. They are what I plan to use for the foreseeable ever, but the downside to them is that they are just headphones. ## Games That Feel Like Dark Souls (that aren't like Dark Souls)
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SYT7ttYvCcE

Few games are as consequential as FromSoftware's 2011 breakout hit, Dark Souls. It came out at a time when many major developers were becoming more and more focused on streamlining their games to create smoother experiences for a wider base of players, and while its release didn't halt that trajectory, it did disrupt things enough to prove that there was still a sizable audience for titles that have rough edges, where obscurity and struggle aren't seen as things that need to be fixed, but instead as features. Its success helped carve out a space for so many titles, both indie and AAA, that feature frustration as a central mechanic, and tons of developers have taken inspiration from it in one way or another. Dark Souls' influence continues to ripple across the industry to this day, it has become one of those all-timer titles that will be referenced forever. And its impact obviously isn't just contained to game devs, it's also spread to players. For me personally, it has shaped my tastes and the lens I use to look at games as a whole more than any other title I've played. Even though I thought I knew what I liked about games, playing it unlocked a new appreciation for them, and that first playthrough is something that has stuck with me for 13 years. And this isn't a unique response, it's why there are so many videos where people talk about how Dark Souls changed their life. Honestly, you have a better chance of winning the lottery than of finding a gaming essayist who has never mentioned Dark Souls in a video. The game just hit different, providing a product that hearkened back to the oldest of old school games while also feeling entirely fresh. Now this isn't to say I'd never been challenged by a game before playing Dark Souls, of course I had, but it wasn't quite to this same level. At that time of life, I was much more likely to quit something if it was giving me that much trouble, so it was rare to ever build up the necessary amount of tension to have the relief of success be all that notable. This made it so sticking with and getting through Dark Souls felt so much more personal. At the start of it, I felt powerless, making every victory however small it was feel like something that mattered. And the struggle wasn't exclusive to combat, it also was felt with navigation and trying to parse how various mechanics worked and what the different stats and effects actually did. Every aspect of the game provided some sort of challenge, and there were many times where I thought I would never be able to get past it all. The most prominent example of a moment like this, and I wouldn't be surprised if many of you experienced this same thing, was when I hit Blighttown. By this point in the game, I had strung together a few successes. I'd beaten some bosses, gotten a weapon I felt confident with, and started to figure out what stats would help me out the most. Little did I know, I was making a huge mistake by feeling confident. A feeling that evaporated very quickly. Once I opened the doors to Blighttown, I struggled to make any meaningful progress with the early sections, so I decided that my best bet would be to just make a mad dash through to see if I could spot the next bonfire. And after a few attempts, I was able to. But reaching this bonfire didn't really help at all. Now I was just stuck in the middle of Blighttown and didn't know how to navigate its tangled scaffolding and ladders. I was lost, and the idea of going back from where I came seemed just as daunting and improbable as moving forward. So all I could really do was try to trek through Blighttown. And there is no area in the game that beats you down quite as bad. From the narrow platforms, to the enemies hidden around every corner, to the status effects that can whittle your health down to zero in just a few seconds, it felt suffocating. And that's not even to mention the frame rate issues, which made all of these things even more deadly. There was a good while where I thought I'd be stuck at that bonfire forever. There was just too much to navigate, too much to fight, too much to overcome. But then there wasn't. I worked my way through slowly and systematically. I did my best to have patience and understand the full layout, and I found a path forward. And it felt incredible. While it's not a straight line, the game takes you from feeling powerless to powerful. And while some of this has to do with getting higher stats and better weapons, more than anything else it has to do with learning how the world, the enemies, the bosses, the weapons, and the movesets work, and then executing on everything you learned. All of the success from this struggle gets highlighted by the way the game offers a lot of space for reflection. There are so many tense moments, which makes those calm ones, whether it be looking out at a beautiful vista or sitting next to a bonfire, feel so valuable. These breaks give you time to bask in your successes, as well as time to consider your failures and how to overcome them, cementing a connection with what you've done and what you still need to do. In a weird sort of way, this all made me feel vulnerable, which, especially at that point in my life, was an extremely rare thing for me to feel from playing a video game. But man, did I love it. It made me feel so immersed and created an unshakable bond to the game. And this feeling is one I've come to covet. I understand that if every game gave it to me, it would stop feeling special, but whenever I try something new, well, part of me always hopes it does. As FromSoft has now released a ton of games, and plenty of other developers have created titles that fall into a similar vein, you'd think this is a feeling I'd be experiencing a lot. But the reality is, that hasn't been the case. Honestly, pretty much nothing FromSoft has put out has come close to making me feel the same way I felt while playing Dark Souls. Like, while I actually did play Demon's Souls before it, I relied far too much on cheese to feel any true sense of accomplishment. As for the rest, they largely just felt like an extension of what Dark Souls established. They're all different in their own ways, and the difficulty has certainly ramped up from title to title, but playing Dark Souls gave me the tools to beat everything that came after. I'd probably even argue that most of the games FromSoft has put out since Dark Souls are better, but none of them have clicked with me in that same way. Playing them gave me an echo of what I felt from Dark Souls, and that echo is enough to get me to play FromSoft games until the day I die, but it's not the same. The only exception to this has been Sekiro Shadows Die Twice. So while stuff like Ashen and Liza P, and I'd even argue Hollow Knight, scratch a similar itch in terms of gameplay, for me at least, they didn't have the same kind of profound impact that Dark Souls did as even those felt like challenges I had already overcome before. I'm not going to try to define the Souls-like label in what games should or shouldn't fit into it, only Iron Pineapple can do that, but I will say I think part of why the label has stretched so much further than it arguably should is due to games sharing a similar design philosophy regardless of whether or not they have similarities in gameplay. Recently I watched a video called There Will Never Be Another Rain World by UK that helped put some of this into perspective for me. And it's these titles that share a similar design philosophy but apply it to different types of games that actually get me to feel the same way I did when playing Dark Souls. ## ...Why Skyrim?

Skyrim is one of the biggest games of all time. It has received high acclaim from reviewers and players alike, been re-released so many times that I've lost count, and sold over 60 million copies across all platforms. Not all sales data for games is exact or public, as it's on the publishers or devs to report it, but of all the information that's out there, this makes it the 8th best-selling game of all time, and what's most impressive about that is that it's one of only two games in the top 10 that's single-player only. Since its release, it has been a force to be reckoned with, and has changed the gaming landscape forever. Throughout the years, it's inspired countless artists, memers, video essayists, game developers, and of course modders, all of whom have kept the game alive in various ways. It is beloved in a way few games ever are, and I often find myself wondering, why? The answer I expect a lot of you will have to this question is simply that it's a great game, and okay look, I'm not going to claim that everything about Skyrim is terrible, it's not, but there's a lot in it that's really not great. What makes this notable is that some of the stuff that I would say are the worst aspects of the game are also arguably some of the most important. For instance, the combat. It is one of the main pillars of the title, and it's kind of a mess. Melee feels floaty and unresponsive, making it so landing a hit doesn't even feel satisfying. And as enemy AI is pretty bare bones, fights largely boil down to just spamming the attack button in the hopes you'll outdamage whatever you're going against. You may occasionally need to block or take a few steps back to avoid a hit, but even then it still ends up being pretty mindless, and can be further trivialized by making or buying a lot of health potions. Magic also feels unsatisfying due to scaling issues, and can be incredibly frustrating because of how easy it is to accidentally do damage to allies or just any person hanging around. The latter can be especially annoying as in some instances it leads to people attacking you. Like when I was doing the vampire quest near Morthal, I had Fawnir join me, and whenever I would use Bane of the Undead, the area of effect would hit him too, giving me a bounty and causing him to go after me as if there wasn't a master vampire right in front of us. All in all, while your attacks may get stronger and your defense is more effective, you're never really challenged to engage with the combat any differently by the end than you are at the beginning, creating a flat experience. Another rough spot with the game can be seen with the roleplaying itself. While you do have tons of choices in terms of what quests you engage with, more often than not there aren't all that many interesting choices once you've started a questline. And in the instances where you are given a choice, it often ends up lacking nuance and suitable options. One of the first quests players will likely come across is a prime example of this. Upon reaching Riverwood, you come across Sven and Feindal, two inhabitants of the village who are in love with the same woman, Camilla. Whichever one you talk to first will ask you to deliver a fake letter to Camilla filled with rude and heinous things and then tell her it was sent from the other. From there you can give her the letter and either lie or tell the truth about who wrote it, or you can show it to the suitor you haven't talked to yet who will then give you a fake letter of his own to give to Camilla and also tell you to say it was from the other. Now once you have both letters, you have to make a choice between who you want to sell out, Sven or Feindal, and this sucks. The quest makes it clear that both these guys are scumbags, but once you reach the point of figuring that out, there is no way to tell Camilla about it. So you either have to pick a side and let her continue to spend time with someone that's manipulating her, or you just do nothing, neither of which feels like a satisfying end if you are trying to play as a moral character. And these kinds of decisions are pretty commonplace. More often than not, you are extremely limited in the responses you can have to any given situation, and the options you are posed with often don't account for information you've uncovered, all of which makes it hard to develop any sort of personality for your character. Most of the time, you have to pick between two bad choices. These two aspects of the game design feel especially noteworthy because Skyrim is an action role-playing game, yet its action and role-playing are both fairly lackluster. I know some people will point out that Skyrim is a 13-year-old game, so it obviously is going to be rough around the edges in some ways, and yeah, sure, that is true to a degree. But these specific issues don't really have much to do with limitations in tech or design knowledge. There are plenty of titles from that era that did these elements much better, and a bunch of them were published by Bethesda. For example, Dishonored dropped just a year after Skyrim, and it provided exciting and satisfying first-person melee combat that allowed for tons of player expression due to its movement options and Corvo's supernatural abilities. Even a few years before that, Dark Messiah of Might and Magic had an incredible combat system that rewarded creativity and observation of the environment while also having solid and varied swordplay. As for the role-playing side of things, Fallout New Vegas released in 2010 and has long been praised as one of the most well-written, interesting, and robust role-playing experiences of all time. The point is, they had the ability to create deeper and more fulfilling combat and role-playing systems. They just chose not to. My list of issues with the game goes on and on, ranging from the overly simplistic puzzles to the level scaling to the tedium of travel to the annoying encumbrance system, and it all adds up to an experience that's easy to look back on as one defined by missed opportunity. Now, despite all of my criticisms, Skyrim became Skyrim, a title that will forever be seen as one of the most important games ever, that people will keep coming back to regardless of how much time has passed, that means something more to those who love it than most games could ever dream of. It doesn't matter that I have issues with it, because it's reached people in a way that few titles ever have or will. And again, that brings me back to the question of, why Skyrim? Despite how it may seem, I'm not trying to be a hater for the sake of being a hater. This isn't meant to be me arguing that game people love bad. I don't want to try to prove to you that Skyrim never should have reached the heights it did, or that you didn't even really like it, actually. I just have long felt a disconnect with the game, and genuinely want to understand how Skyrim, a title with so many shortcomings in aspects working against it, succeeded in spite of them. So for the past few months, I've immersed myself in all things to do with the game, reading interviews, researching the release, and replaying it. And I see things a lot clearer now. Of course, it's not the sort of thing that can be boiled down to a single answer. It's a confluence of factors, some circumstantial and some intentional, that enabled Skyrim to become the behemoth it is. And I think it all begins with the audience Bethesda was aiming to capture. Most games out there have a wide range of types of fans, but I've noticed this is especially true with Skyrim. Obviously, there are plenty of long-time fantasy nerds who fell in love with it, as well as RPG lovers, but it also grabbed the attention of a much more casual audience. This is anecdotal, but over the years, I've had many conversations with people who lean on the normie side of the spectrum where we get on the topic of video games, and I end up asking what their top three favorites are. And the majority of the time, their answers have been along the lines of Call of Duty, FIFA, and Skyrim. There are so many people who have played Skyrim that you wouldn't have expected to play Skyrim, that don't play anything else remotely similar to Skyrim. Yet, despite it being a single-player fantasy game, it appealed to these kinds of players anyway. One major reason for this had less to do with the game itself and more to do with the cultural landscape of 2011, primarily how fantasy was moving into the mainstream. Fantasy is an interesting genre in that it feels niche in a lot of ways, and for a while it was, but over the past 20 years or so, it has become no longer just for the nerds. One of the biggest contributors to this shift was the Lord of the Rings trilogy, which released in the early 2000s and achieved levels of success that no one could have ever expected, creating a demand for more stories that felt like it. This gave fantasy games a much larger target demographic to aim towards, helping many titles in that space become even more relevant. Now, the success of Lord of the Rings definitely helped Skyrim in some ways, but a different fantasy series played a much more impactful role in its success, that of course being Game of Thrones. The show premiered in April of 2011 and was an immediate success. There were nearly 10 million average viewers per episode, not including the many more people who pirated it, and that first season laid the foundation for the cultural phenomenon it would eventually become. Its grounded story filled with multifaceted and relatable characters

accentuate my favorite bits of the game. For instance, it does a lot of stuff that cultivates a powerful sense of place. Every object in the game is a physical thing that can be interacted with. They can be picked up and moved around, which doesn't really serve much of a purpose, but the interactivity feels nice regardless. Presenting items in this way often makes it slower to collect them, as they aren't just bundled up in a glowing light that you know will be worthwhile to grab. Instead, you need to sift through things, picking them up one by one, which in some cases, like when there are a dozen gold pieces on a table, can feel excessive. But it also creates an almost tactile sense to the things you're engaging with. You have to spot what you might need and decide what's actually useful and what will just waste space in your inventory. Honestly, the encumbrance system in general pushes you to always think about the items you're carrying. I do have issues with how it's incorporated, but at the very least it prompts some level of thoughtfulness about what you're grabbing. I think it could be argued that the game's reliance on menuing also adds to this feeling, as even with hotkeys, there are so many items and abilities you'll likely cycle between that you'll never cover them all. So whether it be the favorites menu or the main menu, you'll be pausing the action regularly and scrolling through everything you have, as there is no real way to sort stuff to get to the things you want to use. In theory, reminding you about all the other things you have at your disposal. While these breaks in action can be annoying, they also lead to some incredible moments where you notice something far more useful in your inventory than what you were looking for that helps you overcome a challenge. Furthermore, even though the game scales to your level, there are some enemies placed around the world with set levels and others who start at a much higher level than the Dragonborn before they start scaling. This leads to some big difficulty spikes where you need to figure out how to deal with an enemy that you don't have a good chance of defeating by typical means. On this playthrough, I was given a quest from the Companions to take out some vampires, and it all felt like an appropriate challenge until just before the end where a master vampire blocked my way. As I was far under his level and had no shot of out damaging him, I instead kited him over to a ledge, charmed him so he wouldn't be hostile, lined things up as best as I could, and then somewhat messily knocked him off. And it felt so good to do. Admittedly, more often than not, these spikes will probably push players to just run away, but they can also spur creative thinking, which makes them valuable. The dragon attacks are another example of this. When they pop up, your travels become far more treacherous, and it can lead to some interesting interactions. Like when a blood dragon attacked me as I was running by a giant and the two of them started fighting, so I stood from a distance doing what I could to support my new giant friend. This all adds a layer of excitement to what can often be just a dull walk. Honestly, even the fact that the game doesn't have interesting movement mechanics means your focus will mostly be on just looking around, helping you get a better lay of the land and appreciate the beauty of the place you're in. I'm not saying all of these things are perfectly done. I'm not even saying that Bethesda incorporated every single one of them with this exact result in mind. But I do think their friction has an effect, and for the most part, that effect makes players consider the space they are in and the various things that are in it in a way a lot of games don't. Skyrim's major mechanics are soft, making it massively approachable, but many of its minor ones are spiky, creating a thorough connection between the player and the world without running the risk of them getting stuck. This mixed with Skyrim's massive scope creates a unique kind of immersion, one that is more concerned with the small moments than the big ones. But as there are so many small moments to be had, it all adds up to something more substantial. There are so many interactions to experience. You can explore almost any place you see. You can grab a fish from a line. You can pick up a mug from a table. You can find ants crawling on tree stumps. You can drop something on the ground and it will still be there 20 hours later. There are roaring rivers, lush forests, and northern lights that paint the night sky. Characters go about their lives regardless of if you are there, and have conversations with each other about insignificant things. And every moment is accompanied by impeccable sound design and an all-timer soundtrack. Frankly, a lot of this stuff doesn't really matter in terms of what could be considered the core of the game. They aren't part of the gameplay loop, and most don't even serve a functional purpose. But they are still there, and can be encountered everywhere. Even though the combat and roleplaying don't feel like they have much weight to them, the world itself does. It feels alive, and while the game does frequently show its seams and break the powerful sense of immersion it builds so well, it never takes long to slip back into it by coming across something new. In the documentary You're Finally Awake, nine developers recount the making of Skyrim, there's a quote from Denis Mehiones, one of the game's character artists, that I keep coming back to. Which is, it's not that we did any one thing first or any one thing better, it's that we did it all for the first time. The thing is, it's not just that they did it all for the first time, it's also that no other game has really done it all again since, at least not to the same degree. And this is the other major reason I think Skyrim continues to be so popular to this day. No other game feels like it. Sure, plenty of open world titles have incorporated ideas from Skyrim, but the vast majority of them have taken far more influence from the likes of Assassin's Creed and Grand Theft Auto. Most are action focused, have third person perspectives, and offer far less unnecessary interactivity. This makes leaner games that are often more fun to play on a moment to moment basis, but they lack the slow burn that makes Skyrim, Skyrim. What I've come to realize through replaying Skyrim and talking to others about it, is that for a lot of people, the reason they keep coming back isn't because they want to defeat Alduin or become the head of the Thieves Guild. It's not because they care about maxing out their armor or getting the most powerful spells. It's that they just want to recapture the wonder of being part of a fantastical world that feels realized in a unique way, that isn't always concerned with every aspect adding to the gameplay. They might want to experience this for just one hour, or they might want to for a hundred. But ultimately, it is less about the experience of playing through the game than it is about playing in it. For these reasons and more, Skyrim has created a loyal following. By appealing to a massive audience but delivering an experience that feels deliberate in significant ways, they hooked millions of people. And many of those people are willing to buy multiple versions of the game so that they can keep stepping back into an experience only it really offers. Many also have the desire to regularly mod it in order to get a fresh experience of what they first fell in love with. Honestly, Skyrim is kind of the perfect game to be modded because it has so many systems with the potential of being far more interesting than they currently are. And Bethesda deserves a ton of credit for recognizing that their fans would want to mod the game and providing tools to help them do it more easily. Skyrim rides an interesting line of being for everyone and for no one. I can't say examining it in this way has made me fall in love with it. I do still find myself wishing it was a much better game, or at least more suited for my tastes. But also I think there is a ton of value in it being an entry point to video games, or at least these kinds of video games, for so many people. Skyrim came out at a perfect time to reach a new audience, and Bethesda did a stellar job in grasping that audience and designing a game that wouldn't push them away, while also putting in enough jagged edges to make things feel meaningful. The world is worth revisiting because in ways it feels like a real place, a place you'd be lucky to see with your own two eyes, a place that begs the question, why not Skyrim? A little while back, I replayed God of War 2018, and ever since, I've been thinking a lot about the Valkyrie side quest. It involves a challenging and engaging series of fights where you're pushed to learn the unique patterns of each Valkyrie and master new skills to overcome them. And not only is it satisfying to just get good enough to beat them, but they also provide players with a lot of materials and items that will make them far more powerful. The quest culminates with the best and hardest fight of the entire game against Seagren, the Queen of the Valkyries, whose moveset is comprised of all the moves of the previous Valkyries, and she unleashes them against you at an overwhelming rate. What makes the fight so cool is that you already know how to beat her before going in. It's just about getting used to the pace of the fight and making as few mistakes as possible.
