After the adrenaline wore off, though, I looked over the spoils of the battle, which included the Retribution Pommel, a solid enchantment, and some crafting materials, all of which would help me become more powerful, and thought, huh, what's the point of this shit? The progression of the Valkyrie questline is partially tied to progressing the main story, so even though not every player will face Seagren at the exact same point, no matter what, it will happen pretty close to the end of the game, meaning these pieces of gear will mostly be used for just the final fight. The mileage of these rewards will be better for those who play New Game+, but as I am not one of those people, their usefulness was super limited. And what makes things worse is the final boss isn't even that hard. It is way easier than the Seagren fight, and honestly, easier than a lot of the Valkyrie fights. It has multiple checkpoints throughout, and no section is that long, so even if you do die, you're not going to lose much progress. Not to mention, in order to get strong enough to take on Seagren, you'll almost certainly have to find and level up some of the best gear in the game, so mix that with the strong abilities earned from beating her, and it leaves you wildly overpowered for the main quest, causing the final boss to be a bit trivial. And to be clear, that isn't necessarily a bad thing. Being able to decimate anything in your path because you did a ton of optional content can make you feel powerful, and like the extra work you did paid off, and that certainly is appealing to a lot of folks. Personally, though, I feel let down when what should be a huge challenge isn't. It ends up feeling a bit anticlimactic. The final boss of a game doesn't need to be the hardest, but when they are one of the easier ones, it lessens their overall impact, and here that was caused by the rewards I got for doing the Valkyrie questline. Rewarding players seems like such an easy thing to do. You just give them something better than what they had before, but if done incorrectly or at the wrong time, it can throw off the balance of a game and lead to players feeling unsatisfied with the stuff that should make them feel great. It's not just about giving players something cool, it's about making them feel like they got something cool, and that might sound the same, but it is different. A lot more goes into the latter. Now, rewards come in all shapes and sizes. Sometimes they are things you collect, sometimes they are things you use, sometimes they are stats you gain, sometimes they are progress you make, sometimes they are moments you experience, and within each of those categories there are many different levels of importance. Collecting a coin in Mario will give you a brief moment of feeling rewarded, but that will sustain you for about as long as it takes to grab it. But getting a star will make you feel better for longer and have more of an impact on how you move forward. Small rewards beget big rewards, and big rewards beget bigger rewards. Together, all kinds of rewards are used as breadcrumbs to help usher players along in a way that ideally leaves them feeling satisfied. And it's the question of how to make rewards actually feel satisfying that is so tough to answer. For the most part, rewards can largely be split into two categories, intended and optional, although there is some overlap between the two. Intended rewards are the things you are supposed to get. They're typically tied to the mainline of progression and are composed of stuff the developers don't want you to miss. They come in the form of abilities that make up the core mechanics of the game, items that have a significance to both the story and gameplay, experience points earned from taking out the enemies on the primary path, and all sorts of other things. These rewards aren't necessarily mandatory, as many titles are a bit more open-ended than that, but more often than not, they are, and the ones that aren't are still pretty hard to miss. As developers can generally count on players receiving these rewards, games are often balanced around them, whether that be adding new challenges to account for new abilities or introducing stronger enemies to match higher-leveled players. On the other end, optional rewards are things gathered by the player that aren't necessary to complete the game. These often contain similar things as the intended ones, like weapons and experience points and upgrades, but developers can't guarantee players will encounter them, so they tend to play less important of a role. Optional rewards are obviously tied to optional content, so it is much harder to balance the core part of the game around them, as it's impossible to predict how much of it any given player will engage with. For instance, if the developers balance a game for those who only do the main objective and nothing else, the main line of progression will become far too easy for those who get a handful of optional upgrades. And if they balance it for those who spend all their time treading off the beaten path, it will make the game extremely difficult for those who stick close to the main quest, essentially turning all optional content into mandatory content. So developers are faced with the task of picking a spot on that continuum that will feel satisfying to either the most amount of players possible or to the demographic they are primarily aiming to appeal to. The most common approach seems to be where games are balanced in a way that doesn't require doing specific optional content, otherwise it wouldn't be optional, but does call for doing some optional content in order to not fall behind the demands of the main part of the game. For example, in every Zelda title, you don't need to collect any one heart piece, but if you don't get any, combat will be much harder because of it. And unless you're really good, you'll probably die a lot and maybe not be able to beat the game, so you'll need to gather a handful of them at some point. With any optional reward like this, the strategy is to scatter so many across the world that even the least observant player will be able to stumble across a few of them. These can be done for big rewards like heart pieces or small ones like crafting materials, and the amount the player will need to collect of either will depend on their own skill as well as the scope of the game. But for the most part, things lean on the side of not needing to do a ton of optional stuff. It's meant to present the game in a way where players will have somewhat unique experiences by delving into different optional content, but not be pushed into spending a wild amount of time on things that aren't the main story. Given that the majority of people who start a game are unlikely to even finish it, this sort of approach that has a more casual feel makes a fair bit of sense as it lowers the risk of creating friction that might make the player abandon the game. So while this isn't universal, many titles end up containing a mixture of intended rewards, optional rewards that the developers intend players to collect a certain amount of, and purely optional rewards. And if this all sounds like it must be a nightmare to balance, that's because it is. At a glance, it may seem like optional rewards are the source of all this trouble, and it certainly does add a complex layer to it all, but to be honest, intended rewards on their own are a hard thing to get right. Like, how often should players be rewarded with something? Does it need to be an upgrade, or can it just be story progression? What sorts of things will even feel like a worthwhile reward? That collecting too many optional rewards can make things too easy. Especially in Elden Ring, optional content acts as a way to essentially augment the difficulty. While this is great for those struggling, it acts almost as a consequence for more skilled players who like to explore and also want things to always feel challenging. This leaves some players having to choose between one experience or the other. And to bring it back fully, this is why the Valkyrie quest in God of War 2018 left me feeling so conflicted. I lost out on a certain experience by engaging with optional content. Now there are ways developers try to address this. For instance, with God of War 2018, even though doing the Valkyrie quest line makes you overpowered for the main part of the game, you do still have to take on the Valkyries, who are extremely challenging. So those looking to be pushed to their limits might not get that from the main game, but will from the side content. Which is something, even if the timing for it is kind of off. To Sony Santa Monica's credit, the sequel, God of War Ragnarok, improves things a bit by placing the hardest optional fights in the post-game. So the rewards you get from them won't impact anything in the main part of the game. But it does also make the gear you get feel even more pointless, as these fights will probably be the last things you do. To be honest, both feel like half measures. I much prefer when games take the next step of rewarding the completion of side content with unlocking a new challenge that is tied to the main content. The prime example that I've talked about in the past, and will talk about again in the future, you can't stop me, is Hollow Knight. Doing the optional stuff will get you more abilities and charms and health and soul, generally making the main bosses easier. But also doing pretty much everything unlocks the true final boss, who is a considerable challenge. In some ways, it ends up being the best of both worlds, because to access the true final boss, you still have to fight the original final boss. And for those who have taken their time to collect everything to get to this point, he will be kind of a pushover. Allowing you to live the power fantasy while also still being challenged by what comes next. The last thing you do will also be the hardest thing you do, and the reward of relief from being done with it feels better than anything else could. And you also get a more satisfying ending to the story, which is great as well. I do get why God of War 2018 didn't follow this exact approach. Having the Valkyrie questline change the main questline in a meaningful way would most likely require the game to have a significantly different ending for the new path. And as the title is very intentional with the story it is trying to tell, a split like this would work against creating the impact it's aiming to make. I do still think it would have been a more interesting way to do it, but they clearly didn't want their best emotional beats to be missable, as that would make the climax not hit as hard and the sequel be more confusing for those who didn't do it. This is understandable, but I do find myself wishing more developers were unafraid of whether or not people encountered the best parts of their game. That is the beauty of optional content and rewards. Not everyone will experience them. They are something the player has to work to uncover, and as they're not just readily handed over, it feels exclusive and special. It feels like forming your own narrative. It has to be earned, and when the reward is something that feels substantial, that isn't what you'd normally expect to be rewarded with, there is something about being a player who earned it that feels spectacular. And I don't even think it's about other people missing it. Instead, it's knowing that you so easily could have that makes it hit so hard. I think with a lot of games, the type of player who would most enjoy pursuing optional rewards, that being those who love a challenge, who revel in uncovering mysteries, who want to get the most out of a game, aren't who they are designed for. And even though I think that is a bit of a shame, I do struggle to say that they should be designed for that kind of player, because at the end of the day, it makes sense why devs would focus more on the experience of the average player rather than of this relatively small subsection. Developing a game involves spinning many plates, and while it is easy to say that every title should have meaningful optional content that elevates the experience and gives players a new challenge to engage with, that can't and won't be a priority for every developer. To get made, games need to be able to sell, so design and balance decisions will always be impacted by that. Rewards are a necessary but flawed part of games. They can help signify the importance of a task, offer ways to evolve what a title is about, and motivate players to play more. However, they also can trivialize the core gameplay of a title, provide you with something you'll never actually use, and become predictable and stale to collect. Making rewards feel good is a delicate balance that goes beyond the pure function of a thing and into the player's perception of a thing, which is immensely difficult to manage. However, when devs get close, the immediate positive feedback that comes from doing a thing and getting something for it is an amazing feeling to experience, especially as it isn't something we typically get in our daily lives. You generally don't get paid the moment you're done doing a task, you don't find cool and useful stuff that's also free by just looking around for it, and you can't just put a point into a skill to master it. You need time and patience. Rewards in real life are often delayed, but rewards in games let you know that you're doing the right thing right as you do it. And that is immensely appealing, which is why I love when titles get it right. I don't expect my issues with how many games do rewards to go away. Like most aspects of game design, it is impossible to balance perfectly for each and every player, but I do hope to keep seeing titles that push the boundaries of what rewards can be, so that I can feel surprised and delighted when I earn them. Sometimes though, the best reward you can get is the one you give yourself. Like, I don't know, a backpack with more hidden pockets than you could imagine, or a sling that lets you have a fanny pack without having to admit that you have a fanny pack,
or a tech kit that can cleanly carry your Switch or other small bits of equipment. And of course, you can get all these things from this video's sponsor, Bellroy. Bellroy makes a ton of awesome products that are all focused on keeping you organized and looking stylish. They provide functional yet sleek ways to carry your stuff, and they do a lot to minimize the environmental impacts of making things by using sustainable materials like ecotan leather and recycled mylon. I genuinely use Bellroy products every day, and I've bought from them in the past, and I will buy from them again in the future, which is about as good of a recommendation as I can give. So yeah, if you're like me and love quality bags and cool little accessories, click the link in the description to get 10% off anything at bellroy.com. Whatever you go with, I bet it will help you out in one way or another. Also, they make great gifts to give to other people

## What Baldur's Gate 3 is Like For Someone Who Doesn't Really Play Games
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SvrY9xlgAr0

Over the past few years, I've been running a series of informal experiments for my wife, also known as TheLadyILiveWith, where she tries out various video games in order for me to see what they're like for someone who didn't grow up playing them. Throughout that time, she's gone from a complete non-gamer to someone with a growing knowledge of how games work, and I want to keep seeing how that knowledge grows. Now, while she has tried a wide sampling of games, she hasn't gotten all that deep into the vast majority of them. For the most part, that hasn't mattered a ton. She's been able to get a sense of what a lot of the games are like by just playing a couple hours. But with some of the titles, I don't think she got far enough to really see what they were about. And because of that, there are a few games and genres I've wanted to see her revisit for a while now. And at the top of that list are CRPGs. In general, they offer players such a wide range of approaches for any given situation, and as my wife typically has done better with games that offer her a lot of freedom, I want to see how she does with one that provides an unparalleled amount of it. For a while, I didn't know the best way to have her revisit the genre, but then luckily for me, Larian Studios decided to create a wildly ambitious CRPG that not only has appealed to longtime fans of the genre, but also to people who never thought they would be interested in a game like it. And that, of course, is Baldur's Gate 3. I do know my wife well enough to be sure that Baldur's Gate 3 is not really her type of game, but as it's had a way of appealing to many people who would say the same thing, it's made me wonder if it might at the very least help her enjoy the genre a bit more than she did the last time she gave it a try. For the informal experiment on roleplaying games, I had her play a bit of Disco Elysium and Divinity Original Sin 2, neither of which went all that well. Disco Elysium was a bit too out there and dark for her liking, and Divinity proved to be especially overwhelming. As it is a robust game with loads of intricate systems, there was so much for her to figure out in a short amount of time, and she felt bombarded by how much information there was. To her, it seemed as if every step was accompanied by a tutorial prompt, which not only annoyed her because she doesn't like getting interrupted, but also stressed her out due to how much stuff the game seemingly expected her to keep track of. Each new piece of information made things seem more complicated, and instead of her feeling as if she was gaining a stronger understanding of what the game was about, she felt as if she was only getting further away from having a grasp over it. This, of course, was not helped at all by me, who was just sitting back doing my mostly silent observer thing. With both games, she thought they were more trouble than they were worth, and had no interest in continuing with them. And as that video was focused on a bunch of different types of RPGs, instead of pushing her to play more, I figured it'd be best to just move on to a different kind. But since then, I've always thought it was a bit of a shame that I didn't have her play more, because while the starts of these games give a taste of what their greater systems are like, they open up in so many interesting ways as they go on. So, to see whether or not Baldur's Gate 3 could draw her in enough to get past her issues with the genre, I decided to run another informal experiment. As I wanted to ensure that she got well beyond the tutorial, I chose not to just sit back this time as a mostly silent observer. I did my best not to lead her too much, and I generally waited a bit to see how things played out before giving guidance. But I did walk her through some of the major mechanics and reminded her of how stuff works as she went along. As there are so many ways things can go in Baldur's Gate 3, I didn't set a specific goal or endpoint for her to reach. Instead, I just let her dive into the world and hoped the current would take her somewhere interesting. So, this is how it went. At this point of her gaming education, my wife has experienced a handful of character creators. Of all of them, this was easily the one she spent the most time in, and that was mostly because of how many impactful decisions it asked her to make. As a longtime D&D fan, the classic races and classes just feel like common knowledge to me, but as her exposure to D&D has mostly been hearing me yelling in bad accents from another room, she was immediately lost as there was so much information to sift through. There are 11 races, each with unique abilities and benefits, with the majority of them having subraces to choose between with even more abilities, 13 backgrounds that offer different skill proficiencies, and 12 classes that all play very differently from each other, and within all those classes, there are 46 subclasses, providing even more variety to what a character can be like. Understandably, she felt overwhelmed by the cascade of information, and found a lot of it hard to parse as she is not familiar with the game or 5th edition D&D. So reading ability descriptions didn't give a ton of insight on how stuff would actually operate in game. You get advantage on your next attack roll. That would be good for me because I'm a bad player. When most titles are teaching the player about a new ability, they have them just do that ability. But at this point, she hadn't even seen what combat looked like. So without any sense of framework, it was hard for her to make decisions. There are ways to change the main character after starting, so players are not completely locked into whatever they go with in the creator, but it does still ask people to make a lot of important decisions that will have a pretty huge impact on their experience before they know how the game works at all. I kind of wonder if players like my wife who just have no idea about how this type of title works would have benefited from there being a playable section before the character creator where players do a combat or two as the origin characters in order to get a sense of what combat is like. This not only would teach the basics before asking them to build a character, but it also would show off a few different classes so they can know a bit more of what to expect. As her guide, I found it tough to succinctly explain all the options to her in a way that didn't seem confusing. Like for instance, what is the best way to differentiate a warlock, a sorcerer, and a wizard to someone who sees them as synonyms and doesn't know enough about the core mechanics of the game to have a grasp over the implications that come from their different spell slot situations? They all sound the same. And in some ways, it felt like this with all the classes, as a lot of them, despite feeling unique from each other, are only a step or two away from others in terms of function, so it was hard to effectively differentiate them without giving her a history lesson that would almost certainly bore her to a point of having no interest in playing at all. So my solution was to pitch the classes roughly by how focused on magic they were, which was a bit difficult to do because of how many martial classes have subclasses that allow for magic, but I think I got close enough. And then I just asked her if she'd like to be more focused on hitting stuff with a weapon or with spells. She said she wanted to be a magical character so that she could attack stuff from a distance and not always be in danger, but didn't want something too confusing. And after pointing her towards the bard and warlock, she went with the latter for one very solid reason. Well, I like this person's outfit. That's as good a reason as any to pick them. Regardless of the why, the warlock felt like a pretty great option as it has a lot of versatility in terms of melee and spellcasting, and most of her abilities would be replenished from short rest so she'd get to be close to full power for most fights without needing to spend a bunch of time going back to camp. Eldritch Blast is also just really freaking good. Boom! What? Once settled on warlock, I went over the subclasses, evocations, spells, and cantrips she could go with, and during that, she was reminded of something about me. So there's one where you can be in service to the fiend. You sound like a nerd. Bro, I run a YouTube channel about video games. What do you mean? You just forget sometimes. Yeah, with all my Chad behavior, how? How do you forget? I don't know. You don't usually tell me about spells and demons and things. Yeah, it's pretty cool, isn't it? On the spectrum of degen to normie, my wife obviously skews to the normie side of things. She doesn't have an issue with nerdier things. For instance, this entire series started because she wanted to engage with one of my interests, but most stuff that falls under the umbrella of nerd culture has just never been her go-to form of entertainment. While she's been able to latch onto some things within it since marrying me, others have not been as appealing to her, fantasy settings being a major one. For whatever reason, she finds magic and made-up worlds hard to connect to, so being inundated with so many details about spells and elven ancestries and otherworldly patrons right off the bat before getting the chance to engage with more grounded elements like characters definitely created a bit of a disconnect. To be clear, fantasy

Her plans were just outside of what the game could accommodate, but others, like burning the door down, were on the right track. It's just her character wasn't really capable of doing it with her current abilities. However, she couldn't really tell the difference between the two types of failure, as she didn't pick up on the subtle ways the game was trying to communicate that something might work, making her feel limited in terms of how she could overcome obstacles. Eventually, I decided to show her it was possible to do stuff like break down the door by having Laezel do it, but that mostly led to her feeling disappointed that her character was ineffectual with this type of stuff. Now, she did appreciate the things her character was good at, which was mostly talking, and she liked that it meant there were solutions to problems beyond just fighting. For instance, after failing to sneak past some goblins, she was able to talk her way out of a situation by intimidating them.
Nice!
I'm powerful. I am very powerful.
She ended up doing this a handful of times, and as she didn't want to engage with the combat that much as she didn't really like it, there was always a nice bit of tension whenever these checks came up, as she felt like there was something to lose, and this led to her being really excited whenever she would succeed. One thing that did feel weird to her with a lot of the skill checks, though, was that her character never actually talked. This made it so there would be times where she succeeded in a persuasion or intimidation check, but didn't find the scene to be satisfying because it didn't feel like her character was actually doing anything.
I'm so confused. Was I talking for him?
No, you're talking for you, and you're kind of in the conversation. You would prefer if...
Yeah, that's stupid.
To be honest, this is something I struggled with too when playing Baldur's Gate 3. There are times where the created character doesn't really feel like a part of the world. You do see what they say and think through text, but them never vocalizing it does create a bit of a disconnect. I do get it from a logistical standpoint. Having voice acting for the main character would either require an unreasonable amount of lines, or for them to scale back on the amount of dialogue options there are, neither of which are good solutions. At some point, a game of this scope is going to have to make some sort of concession that won't work for everyone, and having a non-voice acted protagonist is an understandable one, even if it can be a bit jarring at times. Anyway, despite her successes with intimidation, she found talking her way through things to be less effective than she would have liked. This was especially true during the section where she was tasked with finding Halcin. She figured her best bet would be to talk to people to see if they'd have any information, and as every NPC in Baldur's Gate 3 can be talked to, she assumed there'd be a lot of information to gather, but most don't say all that much, and very few had specifics about Halcin, so my wife ran from person to person trying to learn something, and got annoyed that she couldn't just bring up Halcin with anyone she talked to. Now, I imagine there are many reasons to not add a dialogue option like this to every NPC interaction, but as my wife's primary focus was finding this druid who might know a cure, it didn't make sense to her that her character could only ask certain people about him. Every other conversation felt like an unnecessary distraction, and it eventually led to her assuming it wasn't worthwhile to talk to anyone even though that would have led to answers. All of this is to say that while Baldur's Gate 3 does provide a tremendous amount of flexibility with its major mechanics, whether that be in the form of dialogue or abilities, she still ran into the issue of the game not letting her do things that just made sense to her. Another aspect that hampered her enjoyment that I didn't really expect was how grossed out by the game she was. And in fairness, that was a massive oversight by me, as there is a lot in this title that a normal person would rightly be grossed out by.
I, like, uh...
I can't do that!
Oh my god, what the hell?
Oh my god!
Oh my god!
Oh my god!
Oh my god, dude, I don't...
This is disgusting.
This game's gross.
What about it?
Ugh.
This is terrible.
Well, then don't do it.
I don't want to!
Then don't do it.
I don't want to do it.
Oh my god!
Please don't put that in the video.
This isn't to say that these examples of violence didn't register as intense to me at all, but I definitely am desensitized to fictional violence in a way my wife is not. Every time something came up, it pulled her out of what was happening, and just wasn't something she wanted to engage with. This is far from the first time she's been grossed out by a game, but as this is probably the most amount of hours she's put into something for this series aside from Animal Crossing, and it is very deserving of its M rating, it is easily the most violence and gore she's experienced from a single title. I imagine there are a plethora of reasons that all the grossness in Baldur's Gate 3 bothered her far more than it bothered me, but I have to imagine the biggest factor in that is my exposure to these kinds of elements from years and years of playing video games. It's the sort of thing that is easy for me to compartmentalize, but for her, it just felt uncomfortable. Aside from these aspects making her less interested in playing, it also had some gameplay consequences, the biggest of which being that she didn't really loot bodies as she was weirded out by the idea of taking stuff off dead people. This meant that she had way less stuff to work with and missed out on gear that definitely could have helped her and her party. Honestly though, she didn't have a ton of interest in helping her party, as she kind of hated all of them.
We clearly move in different circles.
He's just like a jerk.
She just tried to hurt me.
Yeah, but then she didn't.
But she tried.
I suppose the finer details are lost on a creature like you.
She's kind of a bitch.
Personally, I really like all the characters in Baldur's Gate 3. They are fun and interesting and layered, but not all of them are all that lovable right off the bat. And really, Lazeal, Astarion, and Shadowheart are probably the three who leave the worst first impression. They aren't nice, they don't come off as all that trustworthy, and Lazeal and Astarion literally consider killing you when you first encounter them. So for her, the idea of traveling with them felt off, as she fundamentally did not align with what any of them were about. I do think it's worth noting that she missed Gale entirely, and by the time she met Will, she pretty much was over the companion. So I do wonder if she had met these two first whether or not her opinions on them as a whole would be different, as they are far less abrasive. After a while, she expressed wanting to leave the companions behind, as she was tired of controlling them and dealing with their weirdness.
It would have been quicker to kill them.
No, it wouldn't have. What do you mean?
Knowing that it'd be difficult for her to take on the wilderness alone, I figured it was time to see if she'd have more fun playing some form of co-op. So I rolled up my own character and joined her adventure. As I don't have an extra PC, we opted to play split-screen local co-op, which worked decently well, although there were times where it was a bit visually overwhelming, and also we lost out on some functionality like having a minimap during combat. Also, the screen is always split regardless of how close you are to each other. This is a departure from how Larian's last game, Divinity Original Sin 2, did it, and I'm not entirely sure why it's not the same here as being on one screen creates a much cleaner look. With that said, I think my wife probably benefited from just being able to focus on her part of the screen and not having to deal with transitioning between the two modes. Anyway, given that it would only be the two of us moving forward, I chose to play as a Paladin so that I'd be able to tank hits, deal solid damage, and keep us healed as best as possible. But honestly, I wasn't needed that much for a decent chunk of time as she kept talking her way out of fights. So I mostly just followed her around as she looked for the safest path to the Goblin Camp.
Oh, is there a difference?
Once we got to the camp, she struggled with figuring out where to go next. As I mentioned before, she kept trying to talk to people who might give her information, but almost always ended up having to engage in unrelated activities that she found pointless. I found them to be pretty funny though. My favorite came up when one Goblin ordered her to kiss his feet, and after we beat the crap out of his gang, she turned the command around on him. Then, in a moment of morbid curiosity, she decided to show no mercy and finish him off, causing the entire camp to attack us.
Yeah, I didn't like that. I don't know.
I don't know. I don't know. I don't know.
I didn't do this on my playthrough, so I didn't know it would happen. It obviously makes sense that hitting a defenseless Goblin would make other Goblins pretty mad, but she thought it might make them respect her out of fear, which I think tracks decently well, even if it wasn't the case here. Unfortunately, or maybe fortunately, depending on which one

## The Games That Got Me Through 2023
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rs89EaMayyk

It's been another year, and despite the fact that I've long understood that time feels like it moves faster as you get older, I am still at a loss as to where 2023 went. A lot happened throughout the year. I made a handful of videos I'm really proud of, I started a second channel that I've actually managed to be kind of consistent with, I watched my baby grow into a toddler, which is something I am still trying to grapple with, and I played a ton of video games. While the way I engage with games year to year, and honestly even game to game, is ever-changing, I do always find myself benefiting from them in one way or another. And as it has become a tradition for me at this point, I want to talk about the ones that helped me get through this year. These aren't necessarily my favorite games I played in 2023, but they are the ones that have made my life better in some way. So, as always, the best place to start is at the start, with the first game I played last year. Bioshock Infinite. I'm really not sure why I wanted to replay Infinite. I probably needed b-roll for a video, but regardless of the why, I chose to. And that choice has led to it being the single game I spent the most time thinking about in 2023. I've touched on it in other videos already, but Infinite used to be my favorite game ever, and replaying it confirmed that it very much no longer is. To be honest, there's not much I even like about it anymore, but at the very least, it still has the ability to grab hold of my brain and make me want to analyze every bit of it. And as a person who has found a way to turn over analyzing things into a job, there is a lot of value to that for me. It's just a bit sad that it came at the cost of tarnishing what used to be a game I really cherished. There is a silver lining here, though. Upon finishing Infinite, I decided to also revisit Bioshock 1 and 2, and I had a blast with both of them. Rapture is such an iconic and enjoyable place to explore, and the core mechanics of both, but especially Bioshock 2, are just a lot of fun to mess around with. However, what truly made it all worth it was that I finally got around to playing Minerva's Den, and it is now by far my favorite entry in the franchise. It melds the best aspects of Bioshock 1 and 2 to make something really special, and I hope this is the blueprint the next Bioshock game works off of. Coming back to the series so many years later has been a bit weird, because my ranking of the games now is pretty much the exact opposite of what it was a decade ago. With that said, I think starting the year with such a dramatic shift in opinion benefited me in a handful of ways. It was a reminder that my taste is ever-changing, and while it's sad to go back to a game I used to love and walk away wondering how I ever loved it, it's exciting to know that a game that once didn't leave much of an impression has the potential to resonate so strongly with me now. I like knowing that I'm still capable of change, and I think a lot of joy can be found in challenging opinions that once felt like they were etched in stone. Obviously, there are too many things to play, both new and old, to justify revisiting everything in the way I did with the Bioshock series, but it is something I think is worth making time for as I enjoy finding the ways in which I look at things differently. Life is about constantly growing and figuring out who you are. Not long after finishing all the Bioshock games, I actually played a trio of titles, all within the month of February, that explored just that, and unsurprisingly, they ended up being three of my favorite games I played last year. Those being Citizen Sleeper, Kena Bridge of Spirits, and Sable. All three, in some form, are about characters searching for their place in the world, and their relationship to their respective worlds is a pivotal one. Kena communes with spirits and rot to clear the corruption that has taken root within a mountain village and its surrounding areas, the Sleeper connects with both the people of the derelict space station they are stranded on as well as the station itself in order to survive, and Sable treks across the dunes of her sandy planet to figure out what parts of it she is most drawn to. Obviously, plenty of games put a lot of importance on the world they take place within, but something about these three really vibed with me. The settings of Sable and Citizen Sleeper are both desolate locations that seem unsurvivable, and neither were really meant to be permanent spots to settle, but with nowhere else to go, the people found a way to make it home. In Kena, life has largely left the village and the surrounding regions, and it's on her to guide those who have been lost in order to restore peace in the forest. They are all places that so easily could be given up on, yet whether it's through the actions of the character you play as or those who came long before, life in these desperate locations finds a way. Ultimately, these are games about finding the good within places that on the surface seem devoid of it, and as someone who lives in a state that is frozen for four months out of the year, it shouldn't be a huge surprise that I connected to these worlds. Home is a weird thing that can be hard to truly find, but when you do, you end up seeing the place you live in a way that no one outside of it can really understand. You truly get why it's special and also why it sucks, and there is a sort of pride in having that knowledge. No one will ever hate it and love it as much as you do, and playing in these worlds that, despite being nothing like my home, still reminded me of it, made me care about them in a way that most titles don't. They didn't make me feel better about how I had to shovel snow in the freezing cold every other day during that time of year, but they did reinforce why I'll never leave. While the games I played right after these three weren't as meaningful to me, they still were a ton of fun. Pizza Tower felt pretty close to a perfect game, absolutely nailing what fast platforming should feel like. The Resident Evil 4 remake took a game I didn't think needed to be remade and proved to me that I was wrong as hell, and The Case of the Golden Idol made my brain buzz with excitement for solving little mysteries in a way that really only Outer Wilds and The Return of the Obra Dinn have been able to do. I got through as many games as I could during this stretch of the year, as I knew one title was about to take over my entire schedule, which it very much did, and that, of course, was The Legend of Zelda Tears of the Kingdom. Tears of the Kingdom is how I spent the month of May and, honestly, most of June. For that span of time, it was the only game I thought about. Hours would pass in the blink of an eye as I made my way across this familiar yet fresh version of Hyrule, and I found myself endlessly enthralled with the scope and versatility of Link's core abilities. I can't think of many games that I've had more fun with than this one, and while I certainly had a lot of issues with it that I plan to talk about more in a future video, the stuff I loved about it outweighed any problems I had by so much that it never got in the way of my enjoyment. Once I stopped playing it, though, I barely thought about it anymore. Despite putting in 100 hours and having a blast the whole time, it didn't leave much of a lasting impact on me. It was fun and had a lot of cool ideas, but it didn't feel revolutionary. It didn't change the way I look at games like Breath of the Wild did. And obviously, that's an unfair expectation to have. Nintendo's goal was to iterate on what Breath of the Wild established, not to redefine the series again. Regardless, while this led to a very enjoyable title that I think is better than Breath of the Wild, it doesn't matter to me nearly as much. Had I played Tears of the Kingdom first, I imagine I'd feel very different, but there's no way to really know for sure. And it's an odd spot to be in, because while I did love my time with it, a part of me obviously wishes it had meant more to me. I wanted it to be my new favorite game of all time, but it's just not. I don't even know if it's in my top 20. This sort of thing is just part of life. You can't always predict what is going to matter to you, and if you expect every game you're looking forward to playing to redefine the medium or teach you some important life lesson, you're setting yourself up for disappointment. And I definitely did here. Sometimes a game is just a good way to spend a few weeks, and maybe one day my thoughts on it will shift, but for now at least, that's all Tears of the Kingdom was for me. After wrapping it up, I moved on to some more really solid games. Prodigal scratched the itch that's come from a lack of any new 2D Zelda titles, while also having its own spin on things that made it feel wholly unique. Remnant 2 got me playing games with friends for the first time in a while, and aside from the game itself just being a lot of fun, it was incredible to spend a ton of time hanging out with friends in voice calls who I normally only communicate with through text. And then, I finally played Metroid Prime for the first

## What Tears of the Kingdom is Like For Someone Who Doesn't Really Play Games
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bKfkXdawhnI

Over the past few years, I've been having my wife, more commonly known as the lady I live with, try out a bunch of different video games in order to examine how someone with little to no gaming experience engages with them. These informal experiments have given me a better understanding of some of the barriers that exist for inexperienced players and the opportunity to observe what the process of someone becoming proficient in the language of video games looks like. From these experiences, she's gone from someone who knew nothing about games to someone who knows some things about games, causing the name of the series to be less and less accurate with each additional entry. Oh well. Regardless, as the series has become more about her transition from a non-gamer to a gamer, I've been interested in having her play titles that share similarities with ones she tried early on in order to see how having more experience has changed her approach to playing them. So obviously, as soon as Tears of the Kingdom was announced, I knew I would have to run another informal experiment. Breath of the Wild was one of the earlier games she played for the series, and it was pretty much the first time where she actually felt successful while playing something. The freedom the game offers allowed her to solve problems and overcome obstacles in different ways, so even when she didn't pick up on what the game was nudging her to do, she was still able to find her own path. Where in other games she'd get frustrated when doing the thing that made the most sense to her wasn't possible, in Breath of the Wild, the vast majority of things she tried actually worked, rewarding her creative thinking and never making her feel stupid for not getting something. Tears of the Kingdom takes the base of Breath of the Wild and adds all sorts of new tools designed to increase player expression, and while I found this to be a welcome shift, I am curious as to how these additions will feel for an inexperienced player like my wife, as even though having more options increases flexibility, it also increases complexity, which may prove to be more annoying than helpful. So, in order to find out, I had her play through the core of the tutorial, stopping once she got off the Great Sky Island, as I figured that'd be enough to give her a chance to engage with the majority of the primary mechanics and get a decent feel for how exploration works. Like always, I sat back as a mostly silent observer, only providing occasional reminders of things she had already learned and advice on what to do when she got stuck for a substantial amount of time. So, this is how it went. Tears of the Kingdom gives control to the player quicker than any other 3D Zelda game, and this was something my wife appreciated, as she likes it when she doesn't have to spend a ton of time waiting before actually being able to start playing. This feeling was short-lived though, because the control the player is given at the start is pretty limited. Every few steps, Zelda would stop her to say something, and it got on her nerves quickly. These interruptions seem to be a way to characterize Zelda as an excitable nerd while also providing some information about the lore of the world, but my wife found it to be far more annoying than endearing or informative. With games in the past, she's always found being stopped in this way to be jarring, as when she's playing a game, she really just wants to play the game, and losing control out of nowhere feels kind of bad. So it happening so many times in a row left a sour taste in her mouth. After all that, things did pick up a little as she came across a brief yet thrilling fight. But then that was followed by a fairly long cutscene that was followed by another fairly long cutscene, and she wasn't all that interested in any of it. In general, the intro is filled with a ton of exposition about the Zonai and the history of Hyrule, and while I found this to be intriguing because I'm invested in Zelda lore, for her it was just a massive info dump about a world she knew next to nothing about. It just didn't mean much to her, and she ended up zoning out a bit. I've noticed this happen with cutscenes in other games she's played, but certainly not all of them. Really, her investment in a scene typically comes down to whether or not it is character focused. For instance, with The Last of Us, she was drawn in right away by Joel and Sarah's banter. The scene is about people connecting with each other, making it easy for her to care about what was going on in a way that hearing about a war that happened 10,000 years in the past never could. While there are certainly a few great moments in these early cinematic sequences in Tears of the Kingdom, they largely fail at being compelling scenes for a more general audience. What matters more, though, is that she went from thinking she'd get to start playing right away to sitting through 20 plus minutes of dialogue and cutscenes that she struggled to connect with, providing a decent bit of whiplash. And unfortunately, it would be a little longer until she got into the game proper, because upon arriving in the Room of Awakening and grabbing the decayed Master Sword, she spent about five minutes searching every corner of the room for something to help her get out. To her, the Master Sword looked too blunted and brittle to be an effective weapon, and she assumed it would break before anything she might hit it with would. And in fairness, she wasn't that far off about that, but it did lead to her drawing the wrong conclusion. She overthought what was being asked of her, causing her to ignore the most obvious approach. After not finding anything, she eventually gave the Master Sword a shot, despite not thinking it would work. Throughout all of these experiments, I've noticed that my wife doesn't test things nearly as much as I do when playing a game. For her, if an action doesn't make sense, she rarely gives it a second thought. So when she got a sword that looked like it was about to fall apart, in her mind, it stopped being a viable answer to the obstacle. As she's played more and more games, she's gotten better at interpreting the information presented to her, but it does still trip her up sometimes. And this was not the only instance of it happening during her playthrough of Tears of the Kingdom. The first, and funniest, at least to me, happened at the very start, with her not knowing what button to press when the first text box showed up. Can you help me? How do I follow the thing it's telling me? It's got a little down arrow! Press A. Why would that be the answer? And this is pretty much exactly what happened when she played Breath of the Wild for the first time. What'd you hit to interact with it? A. Well, okay, it had a little triangle facing down, so I was looking for that. In fairness, it has been years since that first experience, so I'm not surprised it didn't stick with her. Also, the majority of the time, both games show button prompts for various actions, so having the arrow is visually inconsistent with how they present most other information. Another example came up during the Fuse Shrine, where she noticed the green coloring of the locked door, the green light on the front of the chest holding the key to it, and the green light of the Zonai Charge in her inventory. Because of this, she thought they all must be connected, leading to a good chunk of time being spent on her trying to get something that would never work to work. Are you kidding me right now? Are you kidding me right now? That didn't do it? Ultimately, there will always be visuals that are misunderstood by players, even by ones who play games all the time, and while I do think developers should always consider the many ways the information they put out there may be interpreted, there is no way to control for how every player's brain will process information. That's why one of the best lessons an inexperienced player can learn is to just test everything, even if it doesn't make as much sense to them as the idea they originally started focusing on. Frankly, even I should do this more. Anyway, bringing it back to how things started, once she figured out that the Master Sword wasn't completely useless, she made her way through the next bit easily enough. And after a brief freakout about how high up she was... She made the leap into what I would say is the true start of the game. All things considered, it took her about 30 minutes to get to a spot where things actually opened up, and around two-thirds of that time was filled with text boxes and cutscenes. By comparison, it took her just 10 minutes to get to Breath of the Wild's title reveal and into the core of the tutorial, giving her the chance to immediately get a feel for the gameplay and what was expected of her. The frequent stops and starts of Tears of the Kingdom's opening sequence is a sharp contrast to this near-immediate freedom, and it definitely left her feeling less engaged and a little frustrated. Having a hot start can go a long way for both experienced and inexperienced players. As games are an interactive medium, gameplay is the best way to connect someone to what's going on, so the sooner the player can get to that, the better, especially when they have no connection to the source material. It's also tough when a title relies so heavily on cinematics, despite them not being an important part of what the game is trying to do. Tears of the Kingdom's slower intro set up a rocky start for her, and while things did get smoother once she made it into the game proper, the design of the Great Sky Island proved to be a challenge for her in ways that the Great Plateau of Breath of the Wild did not. When it comes to games that center around player freedom, there generally are a ton of mechanics and ideas to figure out, and finding the best way to introduce those elements without getting in the

My wife ended up liking them all way more, especially as I mentioned before, Ultra Hand. This is not surprising as the games she's enjoyed the most throughout these experiments typically include building in some capacity. In general, she finds it fun to create stuff, but it also gives her a sense of control that makes it easier for her to feel invested. When she can manipulate items or even the environment itself, it gives her more opportunities to do things in a way that makes sense to her instead of having to fully conform to what a game wants her to do. This type of sandbox approach allows her real-world logic to be more effective within the game space. Of course, the actual process of using Ultra Hand did take her a while to get used to. Getting objects rotated in the direction she wanted involved a lot of trial and error, and due to all the conditional controls, she'd sometimes mistake what mode she was in and move things in ways she didn't mean to. In turn, this sometimes led to her attaching things in suboptimal ways, and she often found herself wishing that the game just knew what she wanted to do. All of this was done in a way that made the building in Tears of the Kingdom less versatile and interesting. Given that most of the things she constructed were relatively straightforward, I do understand her desire for it to auto-correct to a position that actually makes sense. It being so particular with how attaching objects together works led to her spending a lot of time trying to get things just right, and as in her everyday life, she's a bit of a perfectionist, she always wanted things to be aligned as perfectly as possible, which added even more time. All of this did give her a ton of practice though, and she started to get a pretty good grasp over how it worked. And due to it being a mechanic she enjoyed, she didn't mind the time it took to figure it out. The other ability she got a decent bit of use out of was Ascent. She liked being able to get to the top of things quickly, especially as she was prone to falling off stuff. As for the other two, she barely engaged with either, pretty much only ever using them when it was mandatory. In fact, she actually skipped past a few puzzles that I thought required them. The first happened in the Fuse Shrine with the puzzle I mentioned before where she hyper-focused on the green of the chest matching the green of the construct core instead of looking at the wood plank and leaves surrounding the chest. By the time she started to search for a different solution, the firefruits she had picked up earlier were a distant memory, so instead of using Fuse, she found a torch, placed an arrow in it, and shot it up there. Her goal was to burn the chest, but even though the plan was off by a bit, it still worked, which is all that matters. The next major instance was just before the fourth shrine. To get to it, the player has to fast travel to the starting room and then use Recall to traverse these gears. But when she got to the room, she ran right past them towards the waypoint on her minimap. At first, she looked around to see if there was a way to climb up, but then remembered that she could use Ascent, which got her right into the room. The last notable instance happened in the fourth shrine itself. It ends with a puzzle where the player has to use Recall to align the hands on the clock in order to open the door, but instead she used Ultra Hand to get them aligned and then attached them together. All of these were really awesome to see, because they aren't how I did them or would have thought to do them. With all three instances, it seems pretty clear that Nintendo designed them with these approaches in mind. While the devs definitely heavily guide the player throughout the tutorial, their goal still is to get them to be as creative as possible with the tools they have, and creating challenges that can be solved through the use of different abilities is one way to get players to do that, and it certainly worked for my wife. It just took being pushed to learn the ins and outs of the major mechanics. Even though it took longer to get there, she was eventually able to have a similar sense of freedom with Tears of the Kingdom that she had had with Breath of the Wild. I'd even argue that in some ways it was a more meaningful form of freedom, as most of the freedom she felt in Breath of the Wild came from being able to find her own path to a destination, which had more to do with the world layout and ability to climb almost anything than having a solid understanding of the core mechanics. Here though, the freedom came through clever uses of the core abilities. She was able to apply what she had learned earlier in order to progress, even when it was not the intended or optimal approach, and this made her feel good at the game in a way that not even Breath of the Wild did. All things said and done, Tears of the Kingdom proved to be a much more challenging game for her than its predecessor. For the majority of the time, she felt limited with how she could approach each obstacle and confused by the complexity of the various abilities, but by the end, it did successfully get her to a place where she understood the mechanics well enough to use them in a way that made the most sense to her. And that's the beauty of Tears of the Kingdom's approach to game design. It gives players the tools to do things in a way that makes the most sense to them. There are almost always multiple solutions to a problem, and I'm sure Nintendo planned for many of them, but the mechanics are so versatile that players have found ways to do things that Nintendo could've never fully anticipated. Now, I don't think every game should do this. I love when a title pushes me to think in the way it wants me to, but it is incredibly liberating to play a game that gives players this much agency. And I think titles that do this are especially valuable for less experienced players. Not having to conform to a single approach lowers the barrier of entry. The hard part is getting those players to a point where they have a grasp over the many things there are to learn, and I don't think Tears of the Kingdom fully nails it with how it onboards newcomers. In some instances, it leaves far too much up to chance, and in others, it directs the player in a way that almost feels at odds with the game's ethos. With that said, it did do just enough to prepare my wife to engage with it in the way it was meant to be engaged with, by learning to break the quote-unquote rules. Tears of the Kingdom is far too massive and combat-focused for my wife to be interested in playing a whole lot more of it, but the mechanical freedom it offered did help build her confidence as a player. She gained an understanding of the game that felt unique to her. Like Breath of the Wild, it met her in the middle in a way most games haven't, and I think titles that do this are some of the best for turning non-gamers into gamers. As my wife has now played through the first hour or so of a bunch of different games, I figured it was about time to check in with her to see which ones she's actually enjoyed playing, so I had her make a list of her favorites for us to go over, and you can watch us talking about them right now on Nebula.
