## When Should A Game End?
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PEad2KJ5RaE

How do you decide when you're finished with a game? That you've done everything you want to do and are ready to move on to the next one? For me, and I imagine a lot of others, the obvious answer is hitting the end credits. Occasionally I will have the terrible idea to go for all the achievements, but typically once the credits roll, I'm done playing the game, regardless of whether or not there are more things I could do. While credits seem like a formality, there is a fair amount of mechanical power to them. They provide a moment of reflection to look back at what you just played, and they signal that you've completed the main content of a game, the stuff the developers viewed as the core experience. Hitting the end credits provides that sweet sense of satisfaction that comes from accomplishment, and seeing them roll always gives me a nice final hit of dopamine. However, the sense of finality that comes with end credits makes it really hard for me to jump back into a game. Leveling up and getting new abilities feels great when it's helping me progress to that main goal of taking out the final boss or solving some grand mystery, but once that goal is reached, I don't see the point in doing that stuff. When I don't have something I'm working towards, progression systems become meaningless. Like, yeah, I can do all these quests to get a cool weapon, but why do I need it if I've already accomplished what the developers wanted me to accomplish? As my motivation stems from the desire to beat a title, continuing after doing so always feels hollow. And look, I'm sure a lot of people are able to find motivation in just having fun with a game instead of needing to work towards some goal, and there are also lots of folks who find tons of value in how much extra content a game has. And, you know, good for them. But I'm not built that way. I need to be working towards something greater. For the most part, I'm fine with not having the drive to continue with a game after beating it. Especially with more story-centric titles, there isn't even that much to do after the credits roll except play it again. So more often than not, I don't feel like I miss out on all that much. But sometimes games introduce important content after the credits roll, and I always struggle with how to approach it. Most recently, this came up with Pokemon Legends Arceus. After the end credits, players are given an entire new questline centered around capturing various legendary Pokemon. Out of all the story missions in Arceus, about a third of them happen post-credits. And while not every mission takes the same amount of time to complete, this still makes up a huge chunk of the game. Between those missions and filling out the Pokedex, players could easily spend more time with endgame content than the actual game itself. Of course, as I'm sure you already can tell, I didn't do any of that stuff. There were new things to progress towards, but they didn't feel as important as what I had already completed. This sort of thing isn't inherently bad. Having a substantial amount of post-game content give those who adore a title more time with it, and those who have enjoyed it but are reaching their limit and easy out where they can stop playing yet not feel like they have left the game unfinished. It is understandable why the developers approached it in this way, and I'm not positive they were wrong to format it like this. Especially given the fact that the game is designed with kids in mind, many of whom may not have the attention span to beat a 50-hour game but can manage something shorter. It's also possible that the gameplay of the post-game is designed with a more niche audience in mind, and if they had made that content a part of the main game, it would have alienated a large portion of players by making the core of the game feel like too much of a slog. Nevertheless, the choice to place it where they did led to me and players like me who are motivated most by beating a game to miss out on some content. Which is a bit of a shame as I have heard from multiple people that the endgame of Arceus contains some of the most interesting story beats and moments in the game. Regardless of whether or not it was the right choice for Pokemon Legends Arceus to roll credits when they did, it does highlight how the placement of the credits can influence player behavior and satisfaction. As it defines the core experience most players will have, developers have to be cognizant of what they want that experience to entail. Take Slow Clap's kung fu beat-em-up, Sifu. The game consists of five levels for the player to work through, where they will take on hordes of enemies and tough-as-nails boss fights, both of which take considerable skill to overcome. Sifu's difficulty revolves around its resurrection mechanic, where every time the player character dies, they get older. And once they hit a certain age, they can no longer be revived and the player needs to restart the level. On a first playthrough, this will mean replaying each level over and over again to master the mechanics and finish at the lowest age possible. Which is easier said than done. While playing, there were times I thought I'd never be good enough to get to the final boss at a reasonable age. But I kept trying, and kept getting better. And after enough practice, I was able to not only get to the final boss, but also beat him. I felt that sense of pride and relief that comes from finishing a hard game. However, and I'll be as non-specific as possible so I don't spoil anything, right at the moment I expected the credits to roll, a cutscene played instead that indicated there was a slightly different way to approach each of the levels. And then it set me back to the start again. Even though the story hit a natural and satisfying conclusion, due to the credits not rolling, I felt like I needed to keep playing. So I jumped right back in and went through all the levels again. This time, instead of struggling for the slightest bit of progress, I used everything I had learned from the countless times I had gone through the levels before and beat all of them with ease. After dominating the final boss, I felt like a gamer god. And then I was finally met with the credits. The true ending of Sifu feels like the sort of thing that would normally be optional post-game content. There for dedicated players who want an additional challenge, but easily skippable for those not interested. However, by holding off on the credits, Slow Clap made it a part of the core experience. As the credits rolled, I knew with complete certainty that had they come after beating the final boss for the first time, I would not have kept playing to see the true ending. And that would have sucked because I would have missed out on the amazing experience of witnessing how far I had come as a player. To be honest, until this experience with Sifu, I never spent much time thinking about how motivated I am by reaching a game's end credits. But now I can't stop thinking about it. And I find myself questioning whether or not I would have stuck with certain titles if their credits had rolled earlier. Like, would I have kept playing Hades had I seen the credits after the first time I beat the final boss instead of the 10th? Would I have played the epilogue of Red Dead Redemption 2 if they had separated it from the main game? Would I have searched for more endings in the Stanley Parable if there had been credits after every single one instead of just the not Stanley ending? As these are all games I really cherish, I'd like to think that I would have continued with each of them. But given my track record, it doesn't look great. Ultimately, where to place the end credits ties into one of the great challenges of game design, determining which parts of a title should be mandatory and which should be optional. And as it turns out, there isn't an easy answer. If developers opt to make most content in a title mandatory, it could throw off the pacing, leading to a lot of bloat. Also, especially with less linear titles, if nearly everything is mandatory, it may take away some of the joy that comes with exploration. There is something special about uncovering secrets, of finding things that not everyone will find. It rewards curious players with new things to encounter and creates experiences unique to their playthrough. Of course, the downside to not making things mandatory is that a portion of players will miss these things. And sometimes they may be an important part of what makes a game great. For instance, let's look at the ending of Hollow Knight. Hollow Knight is a massive game with tons of secrets from items to bosses to entire areas. On my first playthrough, I did some of the optional stuff, but was more focused on beating the game than anything else. So once I beat what I thought was the final boss and got to the end credits, I stopped playing. At the time, I knew there were more things I could explore as I hadn't cleared the map, but I didn't really know what those things entailed. A lot of it centered around collecting enough essence to improve the Dream Nail, which seemed a bit tedious. I had already gotten my dopamine hit and didn't want to tarnish that. So I convinced myself that whatever was left wasn't worth my time because I was able to beat the game without it. And while I do think that the Hollow Knight ending is fine, it doesn't hold a candle to the true ending. The real final boss, along with the steps it takes to get there, contains some of the most enjoyable and iconic moments in the game. When I went back to replay it last year and finally did everything, it launched Hollow Knight from being just a title I enjoyed to one that sits firmly in my top five. The thing is, I wouldn't have known that there was more worth doing if people hadn't told me. Obviously, I understand

## Reading In Video Games (and why I barely do it)
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Fe8Itezy5P4

Alright, be honest here. When playing a game that has optional text entries, do you actually read all the ones you come across? Hell, do you even read like half of them? Because for me, the answer is a definitive no. I typically will check out the first couple I find, but after a few hours, my extent of interacting with them is doing a quick click through to get rid of the notification. The thing is, there's often a lot of really good writing in these optional text logs. Take Control. The various entries explore the secrets of the game's main location, the Oldest House, and examine the paranormal and supernatural encounters experienced by the Federal Bureau of Control. These stories are highly influenced by those of the SCP Foundation, a wiki that documents the anomalies observed by the fictional group. Control essentially takes the kinds of stories that you find yourself reading in pitch blackness at 3am and spreads them across its game world. They're well written and often unsettling, and they add even more layers to the space you're exploring. With that said, there are also a lot of them, and while they don't take long to read, it is still a notable interruption from the main gameplay loop. Despite being interested in what they had to say, I felt like I was constantly pausing to read some new note, and after a while it started to seem like I was reading almost as much as I was actually playing. It threw off the pacing, and even though they were enjoyable to a degree, interacting with them almost felt separate from the core of the game, so I just started to skip them. And this happens to me with nearly every game I play that has these kinds of text entries. Regardless of if they're well written or interesting, a lot of the time they hurt the game's pacing, so I stopped finding them worthwhile to engage with. In general, pacing is one of the hardest things to get right when designing a game, as it is impossible to account for how each individual player will approach a title. There are so many different elements to games that are competing for the player's time. Devs not only have to think about the pace of gameplay, like how many combat encounters there will be in any given stretch or when to throw in a puzzle or a boss, but they also have to consider how things like watching cutscenes, having conversations with NPCs, and navigating menus to do anything from leveling up to changing or buying gear to reading text logs will impact the pacing of a game. It is an imperfect science because no two players are the same, making it near impossible to balance. So with there being so many aspects competing for the player's time and attention, when things start to feel slow, the obvious answer is to stop engaging with optional elements like reading text logs. And that's okay. Frankly, it's already hard enough to get everyone to read what would be considered mandatory text, as some people just hate reading anything in a game, to the point where they won't even play a title if it doesn't have voice acting. In the grand scheme of game design, finding the best way to incorporate optional text entries is not that important. However, it also isn't entirely inconsequential. For instance, a lot of games use various kinds of logs as an incentive for exploration. They're a type of collectible for players to find, with the reward being a little piece of lore. From what I've noticed, more often than not though, that is the extent of the reward. Unlike many other forms of collectibles, there isn't a greater bonus for gathering a certain amount of them. So with games that use them as the primary collectible, if players hit a point where they no longer care about reading optional material, it takes away one of the main reasons to explore, which depending on the title could have a massive negative impact. Because of that, I think there's value in considering how best to implement them, despite the fact that they're largely optional. So what is the most effective way to incorporate them? Obviously, the answer differs greatly depending on the game in question. And a part of that comes from expectations we have of certain genres. Like, where I almost always stop looking at optional logs in open world games, I find myself reading almost everything in narrative exploration games like Gone Home or Firewatch, as it's kind of the core of these types of titles. I go in knowing that I will be spending a fair bit of time reading, so when I come across notes, I'm more likely to want to read them, because that was the plan from the start. Whereas with something like Horizon Zero Dawn, text entries feel more like an obstacle in the way of me fighting a radass robot dinosaur. Action oriented titles are always going to have a harder time of convincing players it is worthwhile to interact with these things. But it isn't impossible. If developers want players to engage with optional readings, they have to make them feel like a part of the core experience. A title that does this really well, and I promise that one day I'll make a video where I don't use it as a positive example for whatever topic I'm talking about, but it's not my fault that Mobius Digital made a masterpiece, is Outer Wilds. One of the main things players do in Outer Wilds is search for text logs left behind by an ancient alien species known as the Nomai. These writings contain all sorts of information about the solar system, and they give players both lore about the discoveries and lives of the Nomai, as well as clues for how to solve the mysteries of the different locations. All of the logs are optional, as it is possible to beat the game through sheer force of will, albeit highly unlikely. The importance of this though is that interacting with the text is technically a choice, and it's one players are happy to make, because the information in the logs is valuable both narratively and mechanically. The best way to find the answers needed in order to progress is by reading everything. A fair amount of the text logs only advance the lore, but as players become desperate to find any hint that might put them on the right path, they're far more inclined to engage with any text they come across. It doesn't matter that not every piece of writing has an answer in it, what matters is that any of them could. Now I'm not saying that every game should follow this path and make optional text logs feel mandatory, as that just wouldn't work with a lot of titles, but I do think most games could benefit from having them be important both narratively and mechanically. The most efficient way to do this is simply by giving players tangible rewards for collecting a certain amount of text logs. Lore is a great motivator for some players, but cool new weapons and abilities is one for far more, so having text-based collectibles amount to something greater helps keep players searching for them. A pretty solid example of this can be seen in The Ruined King. Collecting lore entries found throughout the world rewards players with rune shards, which can be used to upgrade various characters' stats. So the more notes the player collects, the more powerful their team can be, incentivizing them to keep collecting logs regardless of whether or not they're interested in reading them. Alongside this, a handful of entries have information that can lead players to even more valuable rewards, which makes it worthwhile to read them. What I like the most is that these entries aren't just quick notes placed right next to whatever the player is trying to find that say something like, ah no, I forgot the code, so let me write it down right here so I don't forget it. Instead, they're actual additions to the lore that help build out the world while also giving hints of how to solve certain puzzles. Sometimes it even takes finding multiple connected notes to figure something out, making it even more important to engage with all of them. The Ruined King could stand to have more text entries that players need to interact with to uncover hidden rewards, but it is at least heading in the right direction by making entries valuable to read for both lore enthusiasts and reward chasers, while also encouraging players who don't want to read anything to still collect them. With games that do this sort of thing, I'd love to see the majority of entries tie into a reward somehow. Along with rewarding players for interacting with text entries, another important factor in getting folks to read them is how they're presented. Personally, I'm far more likely to read a note I find in a game if it is a physical thing within the world. It helps make reading it feel connected to the core gameplay. It is more immersive to read a note while hearing noises from the space around you and seeing your immediate surroundings than it is to read one from a menu screen that has almost nothing to do with the note you're reading. Actively pausing a game to look at text is an inconvenience, where reading something native to the world feels like an extension of gameplay, despite them kind of being the same thing. Alongside this, the amount of text plays a role as well. I wish I wasn't this way, but when I see a huge block of text when playing a game, my brain goes into full, I ain't reading all that, I'm happy for you though, or sorry that happened mode. However, if text is presented in smaller chunks, I'm far more likely to read it, even if it ends up being just as long as a massive block of text would be. This is why subtitles are the way they are. By just giving out two or three lines at a time, it makes it easier to digest. This kind of presentation doesn't work with every game or kind of text log, but when applicable, it can go a long way. Placement also matters a fair bit. It's impossible to know how fast players may get from one spot to the next, so getting the perfect spacing is unlikely. Putting too many entries next to each other quickly becomes overwhelming. Like, Horizon Zero Dawn clumps a lot of text entries together on the main quest, so whenever I'd go to these important locations, I'd be met with the option to do a solid ten minutes of reading when I just wanted

## The Future of This Channel
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mKnJkEi0hTc

This is my first video. I released it over eight years ago and it's pretty bad. There are a ton of forced jokes that aren't funny, it doesn't do any meaningful analysis of the topic at hand, and despite being an adult when I made it, I sound like I'm 15 years old. It's embarrassing to watch back, but it is also how I got started with all of this. I wouldn't be here without it. I've spent a fair bit of time recently thinking about beginnings, looking back to the person I was when I first started this channel and the expectations I had going in. To be honest, at the time I was pretty confident I would make it as a YouTuber. I had experience editing from years of creating home movies with friends, I felt competent as a writer due to majoring in English, and I held a deep passion for games, which I was sure would shine through and pull tons of viewers in. I still vividly remember a conversation I had with my then girlfriend, now wife, a month before putting out my first video. We had just moved to a new state and I had no job prospects at all. Concerned a bit for our ability to pay bills, she asked the very fair question of what I would do for work. And in what I think is the single cringiest moment of my life, I held up the Elgato capture card I had gotten earlier that day and said, this could be my future. And, you know, I was eventually right, but that moment was far from me calling my shot, because I had no clue what I was talking about or doing. I had a lot to learn. After releasing my first video, I not only realized that my work wasn't anywhere near the quality I wanted it to be at, but also that getting views on YouTube is stupidly hard. Yes, there is skill involved, but it takes a lot of luck. In the span of an upload, I went from completely believing YouTube would become my job to being pretty sure it never would. Thankfully, though, it did. I've been doing YouTube full time for a little over two years now, and just saying that makes my head spin. Because to be honest, while I have learned a ton from making stuff over the years, I still have no clue what I'm doing. I try my best to wade through it all looking as together as possible, but there's a lot I don't know and that I just can't know. It's the nature of the beast. And being the anxious person that I am, the thing I find myself most unsure about is how long I will keep doing this. There isn't a clear career path with YouTube. It isn't a job where you get annual raises or a retirement package. There isn't a set endpoint. It is something most people do until they've either raked in stupid amounts of money and can retire at an early age or fade into irrelevance, making it impossible to continue doing it for a living. Based on the kind of videos I make and the ones I want to make in the future, I could assure you that I will not be retiring early, which means that the likely scenario for how this will end for me is kind of bleak. I don't think I'm anywhere close to that point, but I also don't think YouTube is a job people do forever. Who knows? Maybe folks will still want to hear my takes on why open world games are bad when I'm in my 50s, but I'm not counting on that. I've worked to come to terms with the idea that only certain aspects of this job are in my control, and trying to predict or influence the things that aren't will only lead to me being miserable. And right now, things are going really well, and I've been putting a lot of effort into building from what I have instead of preparing for some future I can't know. It's easy for me to wax poetic about how this channel started or delve into anxieties of how it might end, but it sometimes feels weird to just talk about how things are going. Like I may be divulging too much information about how the sausage gets made. However, that is probably the most valuable thing for you all to know. So as it has been a long time since I've done any sort of update on my current plans for the channel, I want to talk a bit now about where stuff is at and the direction I'll be taking things over the next few months. Currently, I feel comfortable with where the channel stands. After Gaming for a Non-Gamer blew up, I waited for a while to see where stuff would settle because I knew the numbers I was getting around then would not last forever. And now that things have leveled out some, I've fell into a pretty consistent pattern of growth. Some months are better than others, but what's largely important is that the channel has not been stagnating. And I think that goes for the actual work I've been putting out as well. Over the past two years, I've definitely shifted my focus towards longer videos that examine my personal experiences with games, opposed to quicker pieces that try to present a topic in some sort of objective light. That isn't to say I'd never want to make a video like The Color of Corruption again, as I love that one, but in general, the approach to making videos I've been taking more recently is the one I enjoy doing the most. Also, it isn't a secret that YouTube prefers longer watch time and seemingly aims to condition creators to make longer videos through how it presents analytics, a tactic I have certainly fallen victim to. For example, when I put out my piece on Holocene, my dashboard had a comment about how the video was underperforming because my watch time on it was significantly lower than average. It had really high viewer retention, but the video itself was only six minutes long. Even if it had 100% retention, it still would have been below my average watch time. So I was hit with a lot of negative reinforcement for not making a video long enough. Luckily, for the most part, my interests in what works on YouTube largely seem to align, but sometimes I do feel limited in what I can make. Experimenting on YouTube is tough, as taking any sort of risk can affect my income. And to be frank, that's why Patreon is probably one of the best things that's happened for my channel. AdSense can be incredibly volatile depending on time of year or subject matter of a video, and there are certain pieces that I just don't want to put a sponsorship on. So Patreon makes it possible to maintain consistency even when experimenting with different kinds of videos. I don't talk about it all that often because I feel weird about self-promoting, which is probably to my detriment, but backing the Patreon goes a long way. Simply put, the more support I get there, the more I am able to make what I want to make without worrying so much about a video's widespread appeal or how long it takes to make it. So now that I'm fully into a Patreon pitch, if you'd like to see me branch out with what I create, whether it be diving into more niche topics that don't perform as well on YouTube, or making longer form and bigger budget essays that take way more time to create, consider tossing some money to the Patreon. You get cool perks like access to videos a day early, a monthly podcast, and director's commentaries on every piece I put out. It's a good time and does help a ton. The dream is to one day be able to primarily rely on Patreon so I don't need to worry at all about AdSense or sponsorships, giving me the freedom to make cool shit for the people most interested in seeing it. And to be clear, if you don't want to or can't support the Patreon, please know that is entirely okay. I appreciate you just watching and I hope you'll continue to watch as I move forward with whatever I make. My primary goal currently is to keep being able to do this as a job for as long as I can. I love making videos and it's a profession that feels like it was made for me. And while it certainly is stressful, I wouldn't want to be doing anything else. So my main focus is to protect my ability to keep doing it. My secondary goal is to expand what I do, whether that be experimenting with vastly different approaches to videos or even doing things outside of YouTube altogether. I've already started this a bit with my show Once Upon a Roll, which is a D&D podcast where I have a new guest on each episode and run a one-on-one adventure for them. It is one of my favorite things to make as I get to play D&D with a ton of awesome people and I love being able to tell stories. If it sounds interesting to you at all, please check it out. One thing that's great about the show is that as each episode is a contained story, you can pick up with any of them and understand what's going on. Although listening to every episode will obviously give you a much deeper understanding of the world and the people in it. Alongside Once Upon a Roll, one day I would love to write up a module of one-on-one one-shots based on things I've run over the years if there's interest in it. Similarly, I'd also love to make a game someday. I have a handful of ideas for potential board games and while I'm not ready to move forward with any of them yet because I can't afford to put substantial time into them, it is something I am actively building towards. There's more things I want to do, but I don't want to overpromise and then underdeliver, so I'll leave it there for now. Many of these things are going to take a long while to get to because I don't want to stretch myself too thin and potentially lose this flame I have burning right now, but I am doing what I can to build something bigger. That's all down the road stuff. For the more immediate future, there will be a few changes. Hopefully none of them impact things all that much. Mainly,

## The Games (and other things) That Got Me Through 2021
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kpjsmkw6mgI

2021 has been another year. Parts have been good, parts have been bad, and through it all I've continued to try to figure out how to move forward in this world and life that I barely understand. If it wasn't obvious by the mere existence of this channel, I look to pieces of media to help me navigate different things I'm going through. Games, shows, films, music, and really every art form I engage with give me things to pull from whenever I need it. Whether it be while going through a tough time or celebrating successes. And as we have somehow reached the end of another year, I wanted to reflect on a few things from it that have stuck with me the most. Last time I did this I solely focused on games, and while that certainly will be the core of this video because that is the media I consume the most of, I'm also going to touch on some stuff outside of the game sphere that has shaped my year. So without any further ado, these are the things that got me through 2021. And as always, I think the best place to start is the start. That's going to be the first game I played this year, which somewhat unsurprisingly was Outer Wilds.
Anyone who has played, and especially beaten Outer Wilds, knows that it isn't really the kind of game you can replay. Progression is tied to player knowledge, so once you know the secrets of the solar system, beating it takes barely any time at all. Playing through the core of the game is really just going through the motions for the sake of it. However, at the beginning of the year, I was craving that sense of wonder that Outer Wilds had given me when I first experienced it. So I decided to jump back into it and approach the game in a way I hadn't before, by going for all the achievements. I've talked extensively in the past about my issues with 100%ing games, but the achievement list in Outer Wilds is actually pretty good. The vast majority of them ask players to engage with the game in unique ways, whether it be trying to land on something that you're really not supposed to land on, or getting to places in an unintended fashion. Going through the game this way didn't provide anything close to the feeling I had when I first played it, but there was a sense of familiarity there I found comforting. It was nice to be back in that world with a new purpose, even if that purpose was short-lived and in some cases a bit silly. All in all, it just felt good to be replaying a game that I loved, even if I wasn't getting nearly as much out of it as I did in the past. And revisiting old favorites was actually a pretty common trend for me this year. I replayed Hollow Knight for the first time since it came out and grew a whole new appreciation for it, as now I had a better understanding of its mechanics and exploration, making the things that had once frustrated me not be a problem at all. This made it so I finally got around to all the things in the game I had missed on my first playthrough. And just like Outer Wilds, it was nice to be back with new purpose. I also revisited Majora's Mask, Uncharted 2, Wind Waker, and Portal 2. And while I can't say that all my old favorites held up in the way I hoped they would, I still found joy in just being able to re-experience things that once meant the world to me. Sometimes it can be hard to get into a new game because you don't know what to expect and don't know if it will even be for you. And because of that, for a while this year, I wasn't playing much of anything at all. I was stuck in a bit of a rut, but replaying games I knew I cared about helped break that. And on a personal level, doing victory laps through many of my favorite titles brought me a lot of solace, especially in times where I was struggling the most. Honestly, even looking at a lot of the games I connected to that actually released this year, many of them still had a sense of familiarity to them. For instance, Resident Evil Village felt like the perfect cross-section of the aesthetic and general campiness of Resident Evil 4 and the more horror-focused gameplay of Resident Evil 7. RE4 is one of my favorite games of all time, and I found RE7 to be a nice reinvention of the franchise. So Village pretty much felt like it was made for me. Bowser's Fury took movement and design elements from Super Mario 3D World, which I know this is a controversial take, is my favorite 3D Mario game. And it created a compelling, small open world that has me very hopeful for future entries to the series. Psychonauts 2 finally came out after me being positive it never would, and despite having become so disconnected from the property due to years of waiting, when I played it for the first time, I genuinely cried a bit because I was so overwhelmed by the fact that I was actually playing a new Psychonauts game after all that time. Life is Strange True Colors provided the comfy vibes that the series is famous for, while also serving a solid story with far less hello fellow kids energy than earlier entries. And to bring it back to where I started, Echoes of the Eye released, and it gave me that sense of wonder I had been craving when I went achievement hunting all the way back in January. It let me actually relive a feeling I never expected to have again, which was incredible. Generally, I really enjoy branching out and trying games that I know nothing about, as it is how I found some of my favorite titles. But having the chance to replay old favorites and also experience new content within familiar properties helped steady me this year. I live with a lot of uncertainty. I constantly am second-guessing every aspect of this job I've lucked into. So often I feel like I'm teetering on an edge, ready to fall at any moment. So as silly as it may sound, playing familiar games gave me a sense of security. They acted as a sort of comfort blanket I could cover myself in when I just needed to feel good. And now that I'm at the end of the year looking back at my list of every game I've played, I guess I needed that a lot. Of course, I did play plenty of new and fresh IPs that left massive impressions on me, most of which were in the indie scene. One definitely stands out among the rest though, as I haven't stopped thinking about it since playing it. And that's Before Your Eyes.
As I've gotten older, time only seems to move faster. Days melt away, and especially when I get caught up in a project, weeks can go by without me processing the passing of time. Like mentally, I'm still in August. Also, as I look back at my life, every year I remember less and less from when I was younger. The gaps between memories only grow with age. So playing Before Your Eyes, which centers around a mechanic where if you blink in real life, time in the game moves forward, unsurprisingly ruined me. Every moment in Before Your Eyes is fleeting, and that idea is explored through the story, which is all about doing enough with the life that you're given. This isn't the first time I've played or seen something that explores that theme, but there was something about having an involuntary human function, like blinking, controlling the pace of the game that connected me to that theme in a profound way. No matter what I tried, at some point, I had to give up and blink. There's a sort of hopelessness to trying to slow things down and gain complete control over the movement of time in the game. And that's real shit. For any of you who have watched a few of my videos, you've probably picked up on the fact that I struggle immensely with living in the moment. I'm often looking at who I could or should be instead of who I am. And not only does that create an unrealistic expectation for myself, it also has me living in a constant state of unfulfillment. While I do believe that people are never meant to stop growing, it's also important to take pride in the steps we've made. I am awful at recognizing the achievements I've reached, and Before Your Eyes was a good reminder that there is just as much, if not more, value in the things we've done than in the things we may do. Thinking about the other games I've played in this vein, it was a pretty great year for existential dread. Inscription toyed with the format of roguelike card builders, examining the life of a game in a way that only Daniel Mullins could. Unsighted presented a world where each of the characters' lives have a time limit, creating an experience where every action felt like it mattered, and I was incentivized to use every tool in my arsenal to save as many people as I could. And Disco Elysium The Final Cut dropped, so I finally got around to playing what everyone kept telling me would become one of my favorite games ever. And yeah, everyone was right. It's very good. Being set in a desolate city armed with a shocking amount of approaches to every situation, most of which just lead to getting into more trouble, provided an experience about as close to a tabletop RPG that I've ever seen in a video game. It's thought-provoking, and one day I hope I'm smart enough to make a longer breakdown of everything it accomplishes. Jumping between familiar titles that comforted me and newer ones that made me feel deeply uncomfortable was the prevailing pattern for me this year. Ultimately, I think approaching games in this way helped recharge me when I needed it, and then got me to reflect on life when I was ready to do so. In the most surprising twist of the year, I started to get interested in the dangerous world of League of Legends. Don't worry, I stopped short of actually playing it, but with the release

## How Sound Design Makes Games Feel Lonely
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mt5SKnUGHOY

What's the loneliest sound you can think of? For me, it's...

*train horn*

There's something about a train horn in the distance, especially when heard at night, that makes me feel alone, regardless of whether or not I'm around other people. The way it cuts through the quiet darkness and echoes through the night from miles and miles away, hanging in the air like a whisper on the wind, resonates with something deep inside of me that I don't fully understand. Every time I hear one, which is a lot as I live right next to a railroad, I feel a pang of emptiness. And it's been that way for decades. Sounds have so much power to elicit strong and specific emotions from us. Our brains are hardwired to recall experiences and feelings that we associate with the things we hear. No reaction to a sound is universal, but there are definitely common responses many of us have. And when looking at games, and really any type of media, that is one of the biggest challenges sound designers and composers face, finding a way to evoke a certain feeling through sound. They have to find answers for what various emotions sound like, which is fascinating to me. And of course, the one I find myself thinking about the most is what does loneliness sound like? The answer I imagine a lot of folks would jump to is that it sounds like silence, but I think that misses the mark. True and complete silence can be unsettling, but it isn't something most of us actually experience all that often. So people's association between silence and loneliness probably isn't that strong. The feeling of loneliness seems to come more from sounds that break silence, ones that remind us of the space we're in. One of the most common sounds that do this in games is wind, whether it be whipping around the player or brushing up against a building they're in. While wind exists almost everywhere, it is strongest in high up and remote locations, creating an association with secluded places. Wind cuts through silence and shifts in intensity in an unpredictable fashion. Personally, hearing it reminds me of late nights where I couldn't fall asleep, and the only thing I could focus on was the wind trying its best to get inside. Honestly though, tons of sounds when isolated can be used to evoke that sense of loneliness, whether it be rain, the ticking of a clock, the static of an old radio, or even...
*train horn*
In most public situations, we are so bombarded with noise that it can be hard for any one thing to really stand out. So in place somewhere quiet where there are only a few sounds loud enough to hear, those noises become more memorable. Often times though, the loneliest sounds are the ones made by the player character, the most common of which being footsteps. Whether it be exploring an old house or moving through deep caverns below the ground, footsteps when paired with relative silence create a sense of isolation. To sell it further, designers typically make footsteps, and any noise really, far louder than they'd actually be in real life in order to make them stand out even more. When the primary sound a player hears is one they're making, the message being communicated is that they're alone. For now at least. Footsteps in this context also usually have a decent bit of reverb on them in order to match the natural sound of a space. Reverb and echoes both give a lonely quality to sounds. They occur most in big, empty rooms and long hallways. So when we hear sounds that have them, we are reminded of being alone in those places. The way sound travels and bounces off things defines the feeling of a space. This technique is used to great effect in Disco Elysium. When the player steps out into Revachol proper, the first thing they hear is a sad and slow horn playing in the distance, echoing across the city. It reverberates off the near empty streets and run down buildings. Revachol not only looks like a city on its last limb, but it also sounds like one. Through simply adding a bit of reverb to the horn, it gives far more depth to it. It becomes part of the scenery, sticking in the air, making the city feel desolate and lonely. So in general, it isn't just sounds that can create a sense of loneliness, but also how those sounds are heard. For instance, proximity to a sound can also greatly augment the feeling it evokes. Continuing with Disco Elysium, when the player enters the whirling in rags, the bar's theme plays diegetically from the speakers. If the player goes upstairs, the song continues, but now at a distance, and with the floor blocking part of it, making the song more muted. Hearing music, conversation, and really any sounds of socializing through a wall can feel surprisingly lonesome, especially when hearing a social situation that you're not a part of, because there is a sense of missing out, of other people having fun and feeling connected to each other, and you just being on the other side of it, alone. It's a loneliness fueled by a sort of envy. And while it seems like knowing other people are close by should bring some comfort, it often does the opposite. The same technique is used to a slightly different effect in Hades when entering Eurydice's chamber. Upon arriving, the player can hear her singing off screen, seemingly on the other side of a wall somewhere. As you approach, her voice gets fuller, and you can even move past the wall as to not have any separation. But even then, there is still a lonely feel to it, as her voice reverberates around her big, empty chamber in hell. The difference here is instead of the loneliness being directed at the player character and in turn the player, it feels attached to Eurydice. She's trying to come to terms with death, and as the game continues, we also learn that she has been separated from Greek mythology's most famous sad boy, Orpheus. While she's a warm person who is capable of living in solitude, she's been cut off from everything she once knew, and that loneliness can be heard in her singing. By having the player first hear her from a distance, it sets the tone for her character moving forward. Of course, creating a sense of isolation isn't always just about how something sounds. In fact, one of the most effective ways to make a sound feel lonelier is through juxtaposition. Take a game you've never heard me talk about before, Outer Wilds. When flying through space in the ship, a calm yet driving theme plays in the background that manages to be both reflective and adventurous, which pretty much perfectly encapsulates the tone of the game. However, if for one reason or another the player is separated from their ship while traveling through space, they are met with this.
Within the silence of space, the only notable noise is of the player character breathing and the occasional propulsion of their jetpack, both of which not only illustrate how isolated they are, but also that their two most important resources, oxygen and fuel, are being used up. When comparing it to the lively theme that plays while in the ship, it is clear that this is not the way to travel. While there is always a bit of a melancholy feel to adventuring in Outer Wilds, it's moments like this that hammer home the feeling of being alone more than any other. Another solid example of this can be seen with The Wind Waker. While sailing during the day, the great sea theme plays, which is bubbly, heroic, and makes me want to stand on the bow of a ship and look out at the horizon. However, once night rolls around, there's no music at all, just the soft sound of waves, the blowing of wind on your sail, and the creak of your boat as you change directions. The shift in tone accomplishes a lot. For instance, it helps keep things fresh, as despite the great sea theme being a certified banger, it would become less effective if heard constantly. The vast contrast between the soundscapes of the two times of day makes each far more distinct. Where the momentum of the daytime section seems to be pushing players to move to their next objective, the quiet of night asks for reflection, to slow things down a bit, to remember why you're doing this. It also reminds players that not every aspect of adventuring is glorious, and that sometimes it can be quite lonely. Each section serves to highlight the other, always nudging players a bit off balance so they don't get too used to either. In general, music is a great tool to use in order to set a tone, especially a lonely one. Admittedly, I know almost nothing about music theory, and in my attempts to research it for this video, I walked away feeling more confused than when I started. So this examination of what makes music feel lonely will be through the very academic lens of vibes. Some of the loneliest tracks I can think of in video games come from titles focused on exploring worlds that have largely been abandoned, and many of these soundtracks reflect that sense of barrenness by being stripped back in terms of instrumentation. For example, Breath of the Wild relies heavily on the use of piano, sometimes accompanied by a flute or a few violins. As you walk around various areas, fragments of melodies play, causing the vast, broken world to sound broken too. While almost any instrument can sound lonely, I'd argue that the piano is one of the loneliest. Not only can its easy-to-reach high register create a haunting feel, functionally, it is one of the few instruments where a single person can play both a song's harmony and melody, making it an instrument for people who play music by themselves. And I think that gives the soundtrack a lot of power. My favorite piece in the game comes when riding a horse across Hyrule at night. A piano plays what feels like a haphazard assortment of as many notes as possible. As it goes on, it feels just on the edge of formless.

## Should Games Be Frustrating?
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xMNTNDRcQJI

Red Dead Redemption 2 is weird. Especially for a AAA game, where many titles in that space aim to appeal to as wide of an audience as possible, Red Dead Redemption 2 really doesn't. In a lot of ways, it's uncompromising. I'd go as far to say that it isn't even concerned with being all that fun. Of course, there is traditional video game fun to be had. We get shootouts and chases and... But between all that, there's a lot of slowness. Rides across multiple state lines, lengthy conversations with members of the gang, five-hour-long animations of skinning an animal. Large portions of RDR2 are intentionally tedious. That's not to say they're bad, but the main goal of those moments doesn't seem to be traditional fun. At its best, it's type 2 fun, which is when something isn't all that much fun in the moment, but is fun to look back on. Even then, though, there are parts of the game that seem to be designed expressly to be frustrating. And no section of Red Dead Redemption 2 exemplifies this better than its fifth chapter, Guarma. After a few dozen hours of becoming familiar with the various territories of Red Dead's America and trying to find a foothold for the gang somewhere in it, chapter 5 takes Arthur and a few members of the gang to an entirely new part of the world. They have a job go wrong, hop on a ship to escape, get caught in a storm, and find themselves stranded. This whole part of the game is hard to play. I don't exactly want to call it bad, but yeah, it's kind of bad. There isn't all that much to explore or do on the island, so pretty much the only option is to mainline the story missions, all of which are not super interesting. Mechanically, most of them revolve around moving from shooting gallery to shooting gallery. The non-stop combat gets exhausting pretty quickly, and on top of that, the section doesn't even have all that interesting of a narrative. The gang gets wrapped up in a local rebellion aimed at the owner of a sugar plantation, as they see it as the only way to be able to get off the island. And none of it ever really feels like it matters, because it's so separate from the world and story the player has spent the past 30 or so hours caring about. Furthermore, the members of the gang who are with Arthur are all the worst, those being Micah, Dutch, Bill, and Javier. Micah is cruel and unpredictable. Every time he has a plan, it ends with Arthur having to kill people who don't deserve to be killed. Dutch has fallen deeper and deeper into delusions of grandeur and can't seem to help himself when it comes to putting the gang into terrible situations. Bill is reckless and rough around the edges, almost always having something to complain about. And Javier, while probably the most likable of the bunch, has a fierce loyalty to both Dutch and Bill, meaning he fully buys into the horrible plans that those two cook up. For folks who have played the original Red Dead Redemption, there's far more baggage here, as Dutch, Bill, and Javier are three of the primary antagonists. And during the time between the two games, they've become even more brutal and unhinged, making it hard to connect to them in any sort of positive way. To be clear, I think at least in RDR2, they're all interesting and well-written characters, but I don't like being around them. And I especially don't like being stranded on an island with them. All things considered, this section only takes 2-3 hours to complete, which really is nothing in this game. But while playing it, I swear it felt like it took 5 times as long. At first, I thought it was a failure in the game's design. Rockstar had presented me with a world and characters that I had grown to care about a fair bit, and then they pulled me away from it all right when the tension was highest, just to funnel me through a handful of boring fights with stakes I had no connection to. And honestly, it's still hard for me to look back at that section with anything other than frustration. However, it ended up having a pretty huge positive impact on how I approached the rest of the game. Before even getting to the Guarma section, I had started to rush things a little bit. After putting in so many hours, the exploration and side activities had lost a bit of their luster. Also, I could sense the game wasn't too far off from ending, although it definitely was further off than I thought, so my natural instinct was to keep moving forward with story missions so I could see how everything would resolve. By the time I hit chapter 4, I was ignoring most things that didn't progress the story, and without those quiet, slow moments between missions to help recenter me, a sense of fatigue with the gameplay was starting to set in. When I actually got to Guarma, the pace sped up even more, and that sense of fatigue skyrocketed. Along with that, I wasn't even enjoying the story anymore because I didn't care about what was happening in Guarma or what stupid plan Dutch had to get us out of there. I was miserable. So when I finally got off the island, the last thing I wanted to do was more story missions. Especially ones from a D or an M. I needed a break from the constant grind of dealing with Dutch's bullshit. So after reuniting with the members of the gang I cared about, I went off to do my own thing. I explored the land again for the fun of doing it. I met new people for Arthur to befriend. I took a breath for the first time in what felt like a dozen hours. And I started to have fun again. Mostly the type 2 kind still, but either way, I was enjoying taking things slow again. Honestly, more than I ever had before. Chapter 6 of Red Dead Redemption 2 is all about self-reflection. It has Arthur questioning what matters. And for the chapter to work, I think it's very important for players to take their time with it. To soak in the world that is so easy to just ride through. To engage with the things that you've started to take for granted after countless hours of playtime. That is how I experienced the chapter. And it's honestly one of my favorite sections of any game ever. I can pretty confidently say that if it weren't for how much I hated playing through the one before it, I would not have approached it in the same way. Guarma made me aware of how tiring my approach to the game had become. And it disrupted the pattern I had fallen into. This led to my playstyle shifting in a way that mirrored the themes being presented in Chapter 6. Making everything hit harder. When looking at the use of frustration to highlight certain themes or playstyles, things get a bit murky. For starters, when looking at these moments, it can be tough to tell what is an intentional choice by developers to try to elicit a certain response from players and what is just flawed game design that inadvertently works for some folks. Unless the devs come out and say what their intention was, it's pretty much all guesswork. Additionally, there's an argument that intention doesn't even matter. Because if a player has an enjoyable or terrible time with a game due to some frustrating aspect or mechanic, the player's experience doesn't change based on whether or not it was intentional. Personally, I think intention largely matters, because every developer goes in with the vision of the experience they want players to have. So if a design choice accidentally shifts that experience, even if some players view it as for the better, it is a failure of sorts. Granted, players finding unintentional enjoyment is just part of gaming, so it's not the biggest failure in the world. In Red Dead Redemption 2's case, I think Guarma's frustrating design was an intentional choice by Rockstar. Certain aspects of this are easier to support than others. Like the fact that Arthur is stuck there with Dutch, Micah, Bill, and Javier can't be a coincidence. Between some of them being villains in the first game, and all of them being assholes in this one, I can't imagine that Rockstar didn't want to agitate players with this choice. The vibe of the section would have been far different if Arthur had been there with, say, Charles, Sadie, Lenny, and John. Having the characters with him all be antagonizing forces had a purpose. I also think taking away the ability to explore is meant to make players recognize how important it is to be able to wander. The section takes away player choice, which goes against everything the open world has represented. While in Guarma, you're supposed to feel trapped. It's harder to determine if things like the missions being boring was an intentional choice or just bad missions, but given the pace, they seem like they're supposed to stress you out. Either way, all of this added to a mood that it seems like Rockstar wanted to cultivate. That being, an intentional feeling of frustration used to make players appreciate the slowness that is so easy to speed past. And I found it effective. But the way a lot of people talk about Guarma, I don't think everybody did. And of course, that leads to the biggest question that pops up when looking at the intentional use of frustration in games. Is it worth it? Like any creative medium, there are countless emotions games can evoke from players. And frustration is one of the most powerful that a title can tap into. For those willing to push through the frustration and come out the other side better for it, it can create a massive emotional connection between the player and the game. One of the most obvious examples of this is Dark Souls, which has bred a community of diehard fans through the shared experience of suffering. They trudged their way through trapped corridors and poisonous swamps. They clawed through each area, learning

off, which comes out to less than $15 for the year. On its own, CuriosityStream is awesome. And it was fascinating to hear different stories from brewers as they're so incredibly passionate about making beer. Anyway, for less than $15 a year, you can get all the great stuff on CuriosityStream as well as tons of extra content from awesome creators over on Nebula. ## The Pain of Waiting For Games
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6ZUtuRPZyGU

In February of 2019, Team Cherry officially announced a sequel for their beloved cult classic, Hollow Knight. What originally was a stretch goal on their Kickstarter for a second playable character in the base game morphed into a full-fledged follow-up titled Silksong. And since then, no one's really talked about it. Few games have produced a community as dedicated and passionate as Hollow Knight's. And for anyone who's played it, it's pretty easy to understand why. From the sense of wonder and curiosity that comes from exploring Hallownest, to the triumph felt when besting extremely difficult yet still fair bosses, the game is filled with fulfilling design that respects those playing it. It's a $15 title with more polish and quality playtime than 99% of games out there. And when considering that it was developed primarily by four people, it's hard not to be awestruck by its existence. Playing it feels like being a part of something special because it kind of is. So because of all of this, fans obviously wanted a sequel. While it has only been two and a half years since Silksong was announced, due to knowledge of the second campaign from the Kickstarter, as well as just general excitement for those who finished Hollow Knight still wanting more, for many, it has felt closer to a four and a half year wait, which is kind of a long time. Now in terms of game development, it's really not that long, especially when considering the size of Team Cherry. But for fans who really want more Hollow Knight, it has felt like an eternity, leading folks to grasp onto any crumb of information in hopes that it will give some indication of when it might come out. This sort of response certainly is not unprecedented. Recently, both Elden Ring and Breath of the Wild 2 had long periods of fans anxiously awaiting some sort of announcement of a release date or year. Really, while some communities are louder than others, this kind of anticipation comes with pretty much any property that people are attached to. I think there's a lot of value to waiting. It allows you to feel excitement about what's to come, which sometimes can be almost as enjoyable as the thing you're waiting for. The wait allows it to feel like an actual reward, making it stand out more and giving you a sense of fulfillment. I think this is part of why I find yearly releases to often be underwhelming. There's never a long enough wait to get invested, and as it leads to a series having so many games out there, it's hard to care about any individual title because they all kind of feel the same. A good wait helps put you in the best mindset to experience something. It gives time to actually care, to be invested. And that goes for pretty much everything in life, whether it be waiting for a game to come out or waiting for your dinner to be ready. That reminds me... Okay Google, set a reminder to take the enchiladas out of the oven in 10 minutes. Okay, a 10 minute timer called Take Out the Angelina's. Thank you. Of course, there are downsides to anticipation too, namely that it can often end in disappointment because we don't have enough information. Waiting for stuff when you have no idea how long you'll have to keep waiting kind of sucks. When everything is out of your control, it can be hard to temper your expectations and excitement. Looking at these long, unknown waits, there seems to be a pattern with how folks generally respond. It starts off with earnest excitement, but as the wait gets longer and longer, that excitement slowly shifts into either resentment or indifference. There's an oft-quoted passage from Patrick Rothfuss's first novel, The Name of the Wind, that relates to this idea. When you wait a few span or months to hear a finished song, the anticipation adds savor. But after a year, excitement begins to sour. While the timeline for every individual will always be different, it's hard to maintain excitement forever, and eventually most people's interest will fall off in some way. It's natural, but unfortunately it can lead to a fair bit of toxicity. This passage in particular comes up a lot for fans of Rothfuss's series, The Kingkiller Chronicles, because it has been over a decade since the last entry came out. In that time, many have gone from eagerly awaiting the third book to attacking Rothfuss anytime he does anything that isn't related to writing it. There's a sense of entitlement that certain fans feel. They put dozens, maybe even hundreds of hours into reading and re-reading the books. They spent time thinking about its themes, characters, and mysteries. They invested themselves in the series. And because of that, they feel that Rothfuss owes them. And unfortunately, some people lash out because of that feeling. Which, by the way, just don't do that. Personally, I don't think that Rothfuss owes his fans the third book. He's a creative person with many interests and callings, and he should be allowed to live his life how he wants. Just because he started something doesn't mean he has to finish it quickly, or honestly, even ever. Although I would be devastated by that. While readers may feel some sense of ownership over his work due to how they connected to the material, at the end of the day, it's his story, and he can do what he wants with it. So, if he thinks it's best to take his time, that's what he should do. With that said, I do understand and have personally felt the disappointment that comes from having no idea when a thing you care so much about will be released. It's painful when that anticipation you once found joy in begins to sour. Because if you can't be excited right now for a thing you've been looking forward to for years, who's to say you'll feel anything at all when it actually comes out? Regardless of whether or not folks pass through the resentment stage, after a long enough wait, the vast majority of people will end up in a place of indifference or even complete apathy. Interests change, and at a point, there's only so much energy you can spend on waiting for something. I imagine a lot of us have plenty of upcoming games, shows, movies, and books that at one point were all we could think about. But now, almost never give a second thought. And, I don't know, it's kind of sad, but it's also just how things go. In the past few months, two properties I used to adore finally released projects that I had long convinced myself would never happen. The first was Psychonauts 2. I played the original around the time it came out in 2005 and immediately fell in love with it. I found the humor, the characters, and the general concept so intriguing. As soon as I finished it and it ended with a tease for a potential follow-up, I was completely on board for a sequel. I brainstormed potential directions the series could go and what types of minds you might be able to explore. I thought about what the Psychonauts organization might be like and how they might help or hurt the world. And then, a few years passed. Occasionally, there'd be a rumbling that a sequel was coming, but nothing ever materialized. And then a few more years passed. And then I didn't care. Even when the crowdfunding campaign launched, I still wasn't convinced that it'd actually come out. Because especially at that time, a successful Kickstarter or FIG wasn't a guarantee that a game would actually be made. So it wasn't until about a month or so before it came out that I actually believed it was coming out. The second was the TV adaptation of Brian K. Vaughn's comic, Why the Last Man. I got into the series near the end of its run during a time when post-apocalyptic fiction still seemed fresh. The humorous yet terrifying tone interested me. And after finishing it, I thought it would be a great comic to adapt into a movie. And apparently, so did other people as New Line Cinema acquired the rights. I spent countless hours thinking about what they might change to fit the film format. I even did a bit of fan casting. Which, by the way, my pick for Yorick was James Roday Rodriguez, who played Sean Spencer in Psych. But then a few years passed. Every time there seemed to be progress with the production, it inevitably stalled. Then a few more years passed. And my casting choices had almost all aged out of the roles. And then I didn't care. I only realized that it even existed because of a promoted tweet I saw the day the show dropped. As it turns out, both Psychonauts 2 and the Why the Last Man adaptation are pretty good. Psychonauts 2 might be the best 3D collectathon I've ever played, for whatever that's worth. And Why the Last Man is an intriguing modernization of the original story with incredible chemistry between its leads. At least from what I've seen so far. Who knows? It's early. It could still get bad. Or canceled, apparently. Both exceeded my expectations because by the time I experienced them, I didn't really have any expectations left. I thought they would never happen. And not only had I stopped caring about the possibility of them actually coming out, but also, as time went on, I stopped caring as much about the original thing I had fallen in love with. I became a bit disillusioned with each franchise and moved on to new passions. The versions of myself who couldn't stop thinking about Psychonauts 2 and Why the Last Man are strangers to me now. And in a weird way, a part of me wonders if that actually helped me enjoy them more. That certainly sounds backwards, but I do remember some of the wildly unrealistic expectations I had for each of them. I may have been too excited. And I think that's a potential downside of leaning too much into anticipation. You run the risk of falling victim to the hype. Whether it be expectations you set for yourself or ones introduced to you by others, when you spend a fair amount

## Have Video Games Gotten Worse?
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N38BRxJ0O_8

In the fall of 2009, a game came out that received universal acclaim. I didn't know much about the series it was a part of, but as someone always looking for a good game to play, I decided to buy it. Instead of playing it myself though, I ended up going over to a friend's house where I let him try it out as I'd be able to play it on my own whenever I wanted. And for the next 7 hours, I sat in complete awe as I watched him play Uncharted 2 Among Thieves. Everything about it blew my mind. The story, the performances, the characters, the set pieces, the music, the bombastic and constant action, the animations, the transitions from one scene to the next, the way it flowed seamlessly in and out of gameplay. I was enraptured, transfixed by this game I could hardly believe actually existed. The hours melted away, and it wasn't until 4am that I reluctantly went home to get some sleep. I rested for a few hours before catching up on my own to where my friend had left off, and then I went back over to watch him finish the game. As the credits rolled, I knew beyond a shadow of a doubt that this was the best game I had ever played. Admittedly, at that point in my life, this kind of experience was somewhat common. Every year I played a new game, sometimes multiple games, that for at least a brief moment felt like the best one I had ever played. In 2008, it was Fallout 3 and LittleBigPlanet. In 2007, it was Call of Duty 4 Modern Warfare. In 06, it was Oblivion and Twilight Princess. In 2005, it was Resident Evil 4 and Psychonauts. The year before that, it was Fable, and then the one before that, it was Prince of Persia Sands of Time, and I can keep going down all the way to Donkey Kong Country 2 in 1995. Some of these games fell out of favor for me somewhat quickly, but at the time of playing them, each expanded my understanding of what games could do in a way that felt revolutionary. They did things I hadn't seen before, and their mere existence was evidence of how far games would be able to go in the future. When it came out, Uncharted 2 probably wasn't the best game ever made. Not only is it impossible to truly determine that sort of thing, but also Shadow of the Colossus had come out 4 years earlier, I just hadn't played it yet. Regardless, in that moment, Uncharted 2 felt like the best game ever made. And even though I've played a lot of games since that I think are better, I still categorize it as one of the greatest of all time. And I don't think I'm alone in that. It often finds its way on lists of the top 100 games ever, and whenever I've seen people rank the games in the Uncharted series, it almost always finds its way to the top of the list. The interesting thing is that I think Uncharted 3, 4, and even Lost Legacy do pretty much everything Uncharted 2 does, but better. Their set pieces are more fluid and complicated, their stories have stronger moments that are supported by unbelievable performances, and their attention to detail in the animations and environments go so far beyond what Uncharted 2 was able to do. But none of those games made me feel anything close to what I felt when watching and then playing Uncharted 2 for the first time. I recognized the improvements they made, and I enjoyed each of them a fair bit, but they didn't have that same sense of importance to them. They didn't greatly expand my understanding of what games could be, and none made me think about how far they could go in the future. I've noticed as time has gone on that I don't walk away from games with that sense of having just played the best thing ever nearly as often as I used to. It does still happen. There's a reason you all never hear me shut up about Breath of the Wild and Outer Wilds, but what used to be a yearly occurrence has now maybe happened three times in the past decade. I can't help but wonder why that is. And of course, there's a bunch of reasons, many of which boil down to the ways games have changed over the past few decades. When comparing titles from 1991 to ones from 2021, it's easy to see improvements in terms of how games look, how they run, and how they feel to play. Hardware has accelerated at a rapid pace, giving developers more impressive tools to create games with and giving players the machines capable of running them. By and large, and I really don't think this should be a controversial statement, but I've been yelled at for less, video games are better now than they've ever been. Obviously, when it comes to things like design, gameplay, and art styles, everyone has different preferences and modern games might not always line up with what you like the most. But in general, due to tech and lessons learned from previous generations, games have more polish, grander scopes, and a better understanding of what the average player is looking for. With all of that said, over the past 10 years or so, these improvements have started to feel far more incremental than they did in the past. Like, yeah, there is a pretty big difference between the PS4 and the PS5, and once we get further into the PS5's life cycle, those improvements will be even more significant. But when you compare it to the shift from the Super Nintendo to the N64, it doesn't feel nearly as notable. The N64 added a new axis, paving the way forward for 3D games, which revolutionized everyone's understanding of what video games could do. It invented new genres and created a level of immersion that overwhelmed my 7-year-old brain. It changed everything. Whereas I can play almost every game that comes out on PS5 still on my PS4, which I need to because I still don't have a PS5, what the f- Super Mario 64 is and will always be remembered as one of the best games of all time. It became the blueprint of not just how to make a 3D game, but of how to make a good 3D game. It went far beyond anything that had come before it. While I do think its formula has been improved over the years by Nintendo and other developers, those steps forward have never been as notable as the one Mario 64 took in the first place. And I think this is where my recent disconnect stems from. The games that consistently blew my mind in the past were often the first of its kind that I had played, and many of them were seen not just by me, but audiences in general, as trailblazers. They did it like no one had done before, or at least they did it with a more substantial audience than those who had actually done it before. The improvements in tech, especially from the early 90s to mid-2000s, created a landscape rife with experimentation and risk-taking, leading to a lot of titles that set the groundwork for games over the following 15 to 20 years. And yeah, many of them don't hold up all that well anymore, but their influence is still clear. When looking at conversations about the best games ever and thinking about my own experiences, trailblazers are almost always at the center of the conversation. On IGN's most recent top 100 games of all time list, while they made an effort to not make their decisions just based on how influential a title was when it released, it definitely did skew in that direction. For instance, 13 entries in the top 20 all came out before 2005. A lot of them are games that have invented genres and moved the industry forward. Even today, they are referenced when talking about new titles. They're important. But I don't know, do most people who have played both Hollow Knight and Super Metroid really think Super Metroid's better? Because I definitely don't. Honestly, I think there are tons of modern games that do what most of the titles on this list do, but better. Like A Link Between Worlds is better than A Link to the Past, Titanfall 2, and I know I'm going to get eviscerated for this one, is better than Half-Life 2. Celeste, Donkey Kong Tropical Freeze, and Rayman Legends are all better than Super Mario World. But the thing is, and what it keeps coming back to, is that when I played Super Mario World for the first time, it changed everything for me. It was revolutionary. It expanded my understanding of video games. It made me think about how far they could go in the future. At that moment, I knew it was the best game I had ever played. And I can't say that about the platformers I now think are better than Super Mario World, because I simply didn't have that feeling while playing them. No matter how hard I try, I still can't shake the games that shifted the landscape the most, despite playing stuff that I enjoy more and think is better. And this isn't just because games are seemingly improving at a slower rate than they did in the past. It's also that back then, I didn't have as many games to play, so I didn't have nearly as many comparison points. Now though, the video game market is much more saturated. To be clear, that is largely a good thing, as it means there are so many more incredible games to play. But it does make it harder for an individual title to stand out, to change everything. There certainly are still plenty of developers experimenting with what games can be, but more recently, especially with larger studios, the focus seems to be centered on fine-tuning what previous generations started, instead of exploring entirely new realms of game design, most likely because a lot of what works has already been
