Between losing their primary source of electricity and having a far less effective police force, tensions in Republic City are high. Furthermore, in Republic City and other major areas, there have been strange attacks that are rumored to be caused by angry spirits. Blame gets tossed around in all sorts of ways, and a fair amount of it is directed at Korra, who hasn't been fulfilling the assumed responsibilities of the Avatar, as she has holed herself up on Air Temple Island, dedicating the majority of her time towards mastering airbending, although she doesn't admit it to Tenzin or any of her friends, this is all in an effort to distract herself from her hardships. She still has not accepted what happened. I imagine there would be a scene where she's standing by the ocean late at night trying to bend the water, but to no avail, signifying her reluctance to let go even after all this time. During the time jump, Mako pines for Korra, but she doesn't reciprocate his feelings. He joins the police force to help protect Republic City, and he rises through the ranks quickly, because with his bending, he's one of the more effective police officers. However, he's overworked and starts to feel the weight of being responsible for everyone else's problems. This, mixed with still thinking about Korra all the time, is not a good combination. Bolin joins him on the force, and Chief Beifong tries to teach him and the few other earthbenders remaining in the city how to metalbend, but he can't figure it out. This frustrates him a great deal, and he feels like a failure, establishing Bolin's deep desire to metalbend, and strengthening his arc for Book 3. Asami has been trying to keep her company afloat after the arrest of her father, but with very little support from former business partners, it's proven difficult. The group has grown apart a bit, as they each try to adapt to life in a post-revolution world. None of them are comfortable with where they are in life, and each worries that they will never get what they want. Korra starts to have dreams every night, similar to the ones she had in Book 1 that followed Aang's interactions with Yakone. But instead of dreaming of Aang, it's of a different avatar, one Korra has never heard about before. Avatar Wan. These dreams start cryptic, but soon Korra realizes that they're showing her how Wan became the first avatar. From these dreams, she learns the origins of each bending discipline. Waterbending from the moon, earthbending from the badgermoles, firebending from the dragons, and airbending from the sky bison, which sticks closer to the origins of bending that Avatar The Last Airbender first established instead of the direction The Legend of Korra took it. Each source has a spirit associated with it, and Wan seeks each of them out in order to wield the four elements. Korra realizes that the dreams are trying to get her to find the original sources of bending, and knowing the tales of how the princess of the Northern Water Tribe became the moon spirit, Korra heads north, in the hopes of restoring her bending. She tries to go alone, but Tenzin insists that he be there to act as her spiritual guide, and of course his family joins them, including Bumi and Kaeya. Lin, knowing the importance of Korra's journey, assigns Mako to help escort her. But Lin comes along hoping he might learn a thing or two about bending from the badgermoles, and Asami sets up a meeting with a very eccentric and extravagant businessman, Varric, who has a summer home in the Northern Water Tribe, because why not? Still on a Sato-made ship, the new team avatar sets sail for their first stop, the Northern Water Tribe. On the trip, Korra and Asami start to strike up an actual friendship. They bond not just over their grief of what's happened to them, but also over how no one knows how to treat them anymore. Both have gotten more pity than anything else, so it's nice for them to talk to someone who offers actual empathy. As they arrive at the Northern Water Tribe, they're met by Korra's uncle Unalaq, the chief of the tribe, and he expresses his concern about the mistreatment of spirits in the south. He fears that the great cities outside of the North Pole have lost respect for the spiritual world, driving many spirits from their rightful homes in the name of progress and science. With Harmonic Convergence approaching quickly, he urges Korra to open the Northern Spirit Portal as a sign of good faith to the spirits, a way to show that humans want to live alongside them. Korra tries, but she isn't able to open it. At some point, Bolin meets Eska, who he quickly falls in and out of love with, and Asami strikes a deal with Varric, who agrees to finance a new project for her company if he's allowed to document the Avatar's journey in a mover. So Korra goes to the Spirit Oasis and sits next to a pond where two koi fish swim around each other endlessly. She tries to connect to the Moon Spirit, but due to Tenzin laying his guidance on a little thick, distractions from Varric's film crew, and Korra's personal walls, she's unable to. However, Jinora makes a brief connection with the Moon Spirit, who tells her to bring the Avatar back later that night alone. They do this, and with Jinora's aid, Korra is able to communicate with the Moon Spirit. Yue, through spiritual energy, reconnects the severed link to Korra's waterbending, restoring part of her powers. The next day, frustrated that he missed the moment, Varric tries to recreate it, enlisting the help of Bolin. A funnier writer than me could come up with a lot of good bits for this. Korra has little interest in wasting her time with reshooting these events, meaning Varric has to cast stunt doubles and stand-ins to try to make a cohesive product. This remake continues throughout the entire adventure, as the film crew doesn't end up capturing most of the important moments as they actually happen. Varric's actual goal is to follow Korra to various spots with intense spiritual energy so he can purchase nearby land and commercialize it, essentially turning these spiritual spots into tourist traps, and he'd use his mover to help promote it. ## Items In Open-World Games Are Boring
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bto30zzdSN0

When it comes to open world games, getting items is boring.
And this is a bummer because it should be one of the most rewarding parts of a game, as, you know, items are the actual reward for doing things.
However, obtaining new stuff is often only exciting in the early parts of open world games.
Receiving those first few weapons or pieces of armor can make a character feel far stronger, and because players will be low on supplies, every little bit helps.
Over time, as acquiring items becomes more common and players create a nice little stockpile of resources, the excitement that comes from getting items fades away.
There are a handful of reasons as to why getting items in so many open world games isn't as fulfilling as it could be, and the easiest place to start is with presentation.
When I think about games where getting an item causes me to feel excited, the ones that have some sort of fanfare stick out the most.
Opening a chest in Zelda and hearing...
...hardwires the player's brain to think, I just got something cool.
And even when it isn't something that cool, the mental association tricks our dumb brains into thinking it is.
It feels like an achievement, it feels important.
On the other side of things, this is what getting an item in most open world games feels like.
It's efficient, yes, but it isn't exciting.
Now obviously a fanfare like the one in Zelda would not really work in an open world game, as there are so many more chests to open and items to get, so having it stop players to watch the same animation over and over would get tiresome quickly.
But there is a huge gap between...
...and...
So finding a middle ground could help make these moments feel a little more important.
I know this sounds like a surface level complaint, but being reinforced with visual or auditory flourishes can make a positive connection between the player and whatever caused those things to happen.
Turning something that would otherwise seem flat into a much more exciting and engaging experience.
Aside from how items are presented to the player for the first time, I also think it's important for games to present items in an interesting way when they're actually in the player's inventory.
I find myself feeling far more engaged with an item when it seems to take up physical space inside my inventory.
Games in series like Diablo, The Witcher, and Resident Evil do a pretty good job of this.
Being able to see items as physical objects in a set space makes them a little more tangible than just having them be a name written on a long list.
What I like even more is when these types of grid systems have a limited amount of space, pushing players to find the optimal way to organize it.
Admittedly, this is something I hate doing in real life, but playing inventory Tetris in games is something I find a surprising amount of joy in.
Players have to pay attention to what's getting put into their inventory and decide what is important versus what can be tossed.
Resident Evil 4 takes it one step further by having equipped items take up space in the inventory instead of there just being a designated spot for a weapon.
Making it so players have to decide how much they really care about the massive weapon that takes up the majority of their space.
The answer's a lot.
For me, this made any new weapon that I decided to keep feel more special because it came at the cost of other things.
And this ties into my next point.
For items to feel important, games need to make encumbrance systems that actually work.
Honestly, encumbrance systems in most open world games, especially ones made by Bethesda, are pointless.
The starting limit of what players can carry is typically super high, and when it is reached, there isn't a real consequence.
Sure, movement is slowed to a crawl and the ability to fast travel is taken away, but players still have the option to drop items to get just below the threshold, fast travel to a town, sell their stuff, fast travel back, pick up whatever they missed, and fast travel back to the town again.
It ends up taking five minutes, and no interesting consequences are given for being nearly over-encumbered.
And as soon as I mentioned fast travel, I could already hear some people saying, well, don't use it then.
But it isn't that simple.
Fast travel is a band-aid for bigger issues in a game, like stale movement mechanics or boring world design.
It doesn't fix the problems, it just covers them up.
So even if the player decides not to fast travel, they most likely will have a long, tedious walk, and it will really only make the player lose some of their time.
In my opinion, unless time is a key mechanic in a game, losing it is not a good consequence.
It's just padding.
I think traveling and transporting items in open-world games would be far more interesting if fast travel was only usable in specific locations, like the signposts in The Witcher 3 or the carriages in Skyrim, and if encumbrance systems had more gradual status effects.
A solid example of this is from a relatively unknown RPG called Dark Souls.
Depending on how much the player character is wearing, their overall speed and the types of rolls they can do change.
This drastically affects how they handle in combat.
I'd like to see something similar to this be implemented in more open-world games, but instead of consequences just being dictated by what the player has on, ideally they would be affected by everything in the player's inventory.
Changing the gameplay in this way would create a risk-reward system where players can take more stuff, but it would make things like combat become more difficult.
The consequences for hitting different encumbrance limits could range from making the player's stamina recovery a bit slower to them not having their full range of motion in combat, leading to them being less effective than when they are unencumbered.
There could even be some positive side effects, like if a character gets hit really hard while carrying a lot of stuff, they may be less likely to get knocked back because they're just that heavy.
This would cause the player to choose between whether it's better to collect a lot of loot or have full access to a preferred playstyle, creating a connection between players and the things they carry.
With all that said, even if items are presented in interesting ways and players are constantly asked to make decisions about if something is worth it or not, a huge problem with items in open-world games is that most of the things players pick up are boring in and of themselves.
For instance, I've noticed a trend where games will have items with the sole purpose of being sold.
While I can appreciate developers wanting to add flavor and a level of realism to a game by having things other than just coins be in chests, it ends up being a detail most people ignore, and it adds an extra step to getting that money.
Items like this work well when there is some sort of strategic value to holding them.
For example, in a game like Hollow Knight, where dying puts players at risk of losing all of their coins, items that can be turned in for cash are useful things to hold onto, and they force the player to consider when it would be best to sell them.
This heavily relies on Hollow Knight's death mechanic, which I can't imagine many open-world games adopting.
Although I do think having players lose something upon death that they could go back and get would be a really neat mechanic for open-world games to have.
It would not only give more value to the materials you don't lose on death, but it would also add a new layer of tension as you head back to get your stuff, making traversal across the world more interesting.
An easier approach for developers would be just adding better ways for players to lose their cash while they're out traveling.
Maybe NPCs could be able to pickpocket the player's coins, or there could be more scenarios where paying a fee is actually more viable than just killing everyone in the way.
However, this really only fixes a small part of the problem.
The more effective solution would be giving each item multiple in-game purposes.
The game that handles getting mundane loot better than any other I've played is Dungeons & Dragons.
If a player finds an old wooden pipe with strange runes engraved on the side in almost any video game, they'll probably sell it instantly.
But in D&D, players hold onto items like this because they can interact with them in meaningful ways.
For instance, the player could use the pipe to fit in with a group of snooty nobles who could prove to be valuable allies later on.
Or they could develop a smoking habit that might give them temporary relief but have consequences in the long run.
Or they could hold onto it as a keepsake to show how far they've come since the start of their adventure.
Due to it being a tabletop game, the only real limitation in D&D is imagination, so it's way easier to implement this sort of thing than it would be in a video game.
However, I think a lot of video games would benefit from incorporating a simplified version of it.
There doesn't need to be infinite possibilities, but having even just two or three uses for any given item a player can find would give a greater importance to every little thing in the world.
So if they find a rabbit's foot, there could be a function where they can rub it and every once in a while it will give them some sort of luck bonus.
Also, maybe if a superstitious person sees them with it, they may be more inclined to like the player character.
This may be the sort of thing that doesn't interest a lot of people, but it would get me to actually pay attention to the more mundane items I pick up.
As for more substantial items like weapons or armor, more often than not, players are just looking at the numbers to see if they are higher than whatever they have equipped.
It definitely feels good seeing those stats go up, but oftentimes they don't really change up gameplay that much.
So players are really just met with a barrage of weapons with slightly higher chances to crit or

## The Legend of Korra: A Beautiful Mess
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fVUb8Ta7vZ8

When it comes to any kind of creative work, there are few things harder to do than follow up a project that is widely considered to be a masterpiece. No matter how good the new project is, it will always be scrutinized against something that people cherish and often view as infallible. And this is the nearly insurmountable task that Brian Konietzko and Michael DiMartino were faced with when creating The Legend of Korra.
I love Avatar The Last Airbender, and since releasing my video on it, I've wanted to talk about The Legend of Korra. Because when it comes to Korra, I feel conflicted. On one hand, it delivers some truly powerful moments, giving viewers the chance to peer into the lives of raw and flawed characters who deal with hardships in ways that I still find myself connecting with today. On the other hand, it moves too quickly and clumsily to earn all of its powerful moments, and it expects viewers to care about things that they were never really set up to care about. When watching, I find myself being moved by the show's narrative while also feeling frustrated by it. And this stems from how it is structured. Each season more or less operates as its own story that leads into the next, instead of focusing on a single clear overarching plot the way its predecessor did. The Last Airbender centers around one primary goal, defeating the Fire Lore to end the war before the Fire Nation wipes out the rest of the world. To do this, Aang needs to master the four elements, which he does under the tutelage of his companions Katara, Toph, and Zuko.
Hey, what about me?
Sokka helps too. There's a goal for the series and goals for each season, and as these are met, all of the major characters have substantial arcs where they grow into the heroes they need to become. The development of the main cast affects the main plot, which winds up making the rest of Team Avatar feel just as important as Aang. On top of that, almost every episode ties into the main plot, giving a sense that any moment is important to the story. The Legend of Korra centers around Korra. Each season has its own arc, but the closest thing to an overarching storyline is Korra's struggle to find her identity, something she inches closer to by defeating each villain she confronts. The most important relationship in any given season is between Korra and her foe, which is something The Last Airbender explored with the relationship between Zuko and, well, pretty much everyone, but here it's the focal point of Korra's development. Where Aang learns from the people who have become his friends, Korra learns from her enemies. This is a cool inversion, and I like that Korra doesn't follow the exact same path as Aang. In fact, in terms of self-discovery and battling adversity, Korra's arc is much closer to Zuko's, which is a good thing because Zuko's arc is the best one in The Last Airbender and honestly maybe in anything ever. While Korra's personal journey never reaches the same heights as Zuko's, watching her struggle over and over to figure out how she fits into the world is something I found both familiar and compelling. While there is nothing wrong with stories that focus more on the development of a single character and less on any sort of overarching plot, the issue is there isn't enough time in each season to properly explore any character's growth other than Korra's, but the writers still tried to. Given the greater focus on contained seasonal arcs, each one requires the introduction of a new villain and conflict, and this ends up taking a substantial amount of time in each season, which are only around 13 episodes long. On top of this, it has a pretty large recurring cast. The Last Airbender has 13 characters who appear in 10 or more episodes and have some sort of line or animal sound, and each of those characters, with the exception of Momo, I guess, have pretty satisfying arcs. The Legend of Korra has 26 characters who appear in 10 episodes or more in this same way. While not every character in a show needs to have an amazing story, when so much screen time is spread across this many characters, it ends up making each of them feel less important. A lot of them have interesting concepts, but most of their potential goes untapped throughout the series. I wanted to see so much more from Lin, Jinora, Tenzin, and the new team Avatar, but there just wasn't enough time. Focusing so much of the show's limited time on other characters also hurt Korra's arc, especially in the first two seasons where too much time is spent on stuff that has little impact on the main plot. I think the writers wanted to tell a story that focused on Korra and her friends, but the constraints of the show's structure made it hard to do this. The Last Airbender had time for the characters to interact without the threat of an incoming plot point, but The Legend of Korra's plot is always driving forward. This often leads to Korra going off and doing her own thing while the other members of team Avatar have somewhat inconsequential subplots. Bolin ends up having the most to do of all the side characters, but while entertaining, it often feels like filler. Mako is just kind of boring. After he isn't being used as part of the contrived love triangle stuff, he's just kind of there and only serves to look cool during fights. In fairness, he does. And Asami. I feel like Asami should be my favorite character in this show, as some of the most interesting stuff happens to her, but most of her moments that could have been great are rushed. This can be seen in her relationship with her father, which had great potential, but because the show didn't have enough time to develop that thread over each of the four seasons, most viewers don't care about that relationship. So when it resolves in Hiroshi's death, Asami is given less than 10 seconds to react to it, and pretty much no one, fans or even the other characters, care. Where I bought that team Avatar and The Last Airbender were a group of best friends, I never felt the same way about the group in The Legend of Korra, and that's because they don't do a good job establishing the group's friendship, and the four of them spend so much time apart. However, they're still presented as best friends, which seems off. In some ways, the new team Avatar feels like a holdover from The Last Airbender meant to appeal to fans of the original series. Best friends saving the world together. I think this approach led to the expectation that these characters would get the same treatment Toph, Katara, Sokka, Zuko, and even Iroh got in The Last Airbender. But between the plot of each season and all of the other characters in the show, there just wasn't enough time to give them the justice they deserved. Zuko's Agni Kai against Azula, Katara's face-off against the man who killed her mother, and Iroh's return to Ba Sing Se as a liberator instead of a conqueror are all moments that feel built up to and earned. However, Mako's attempted sacrifice, Asami's loss of her father, and Bolin's... Honestly, Bolin doesn't even really have anything like this, but I guess him deciding to leave Kuvira's army? These moments don't land in the same way because the build-up isn't there.
Another area where I feel conflicted is how they shifted the established rules and limitations of the world. The Last Airbender does an incredible job creating an understandable and unique setting with a consistent set of rules that almost never get broken. And when they do, the break usually has a solid explanation. The Legend of Korra breaks the rules without providing the same type of context, often leading to a string of questions. My least favorite of these moments comes right after Korra is separated from the Avatar spirit. She sits in the Tree of Time, turns into a giant blue projection of herself, and is transported halfway across the world to fight Unovatu. Aang did a similar thing in The Last Airbender, but that involved fusing with a powerful spirit and using the Avatar state, neither of which are present here. It made me wonder why Korra was able to do this. Was it just because she was in the Tree of Time? Korra was technically no longer the Avatar, so does that mean anyone could sit in the Tree of Time and turn giant and blue? If so, why didn't anyone else do that? Why did they just leave it on her? And I know all of this might sound like nitpicking, but it's notable because The Last Airbender almost never fell victim to this sort of line of questioning. Almost. Not only are there good reasons as to why stuff works the way it does, but also most things are explained outright. The flow of chi, lightning bending, metal bending, blood bending, unlocking the Avatar state, all of these things are described in interesting ways, but The Legend of Korra doesn't do this as thoroughly. Things like Korra airbending after Amon takes her powers away, or even just Amon's use of bloodbending to take people's powers away, are never really explained, making it so viewers have to work out and justify how these things fit into the rules and limitations of the world, which comes off as careless writing. With all that said, some of my favorite aspects of the show came from these big departures. One example of this is lava bending. I don't fully grasp why it works, and it adds another point to a long list of why earthbenders are overpowered. However, it gave Bolin an interesting arc as he failed to learn metalbending, but then observed the style of an enemy to develop a new

## An Open Letter to Indiana
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k0-XTZD31hE

There's a sign posted on some God-fearing farmer's land along I-65 that I saw every time I drove back to Indiana. It read, hell is real. And I always thought, I know. I live here too. My time in Indiana was filled with the thought, I don't belong here. After five years of living in the Hoosier State, I feel as disconnected from it now as I did when my girlfriend and I first moved. Something about it always felt temporary. Like, even the state's slogan is the crossroads of America, which is just a nice way of saying no one wants to stay here longer than they need to. And I relate to that because I didn't spend one second longer there than I needed to. It's hard to properly describe why I hate Indiana. Everything I say will seem petty and exaggerated, which in fairness it is. And most of it has more to do with who I am than anything else. But here are my grievances. First off, the state is flatter than it has any business being. Wherever you are, it feels like you can see miles and miles of cornfields or soybean fields, depending on the crop rotation. Meaning from an aesthetic standpoint, it's pretty much saying, hello, I'm boring. Also, people everywhere like to focus on how messed up the weather is. And despite having relatively normal weather, the people of Indiana are no exception. It will snow two inches and everyone in the state will lose their collective minds. The best thing is that a week later it will be mildly warm and you will hear at least 4,000 people make the same comment that the weather really just needs to make up its mind. The real issue isn't the weather, it's that the state never learned how to deal with the various types of weather it gets. So when it rains, everything floods. And when it snows more than a dusty and approximately 90% of drivers just forget how to drive. Despite getting it every year, Indiana does not know how to deal with snow. And I think it's because the state views itself as the South, but it forgets it's north of the Mason-Dixon line. People think Indiana's part of the Midwest, but culturally it's not. It's really its own thing. Indiana is like a little brother who wants to be just like his older brother, in this case, the South. So in an effort to emulate his brother, he put sweet tea and confederate flags all around his room. However, the South never really gave him the acceptance he so desperately needed, leading Indiana to fall back on his very kind older sister, the Midwest, who accepted him for who he was. But she was too bashful to point out that all the confederate flags were in poor taste and that the sweet tea would likely give him diabetes. So he ended up keeping those things around. Indiana takes a lot of pride in this ruralness, which is not inherently a bad thing. However, the country lifestyle is really not for me. Now, maybe the worst thing about Indiana is that the majority of it is in eastern time. It's pressed up against the western side of that time zone, which means during the winter, if you work a day job, you will probably never see the sun. And in summer, it stays light out pretty much all night. Look, eastern time sucks. If you're watching any live event, it goes way too late. If you have friends living on the west coast, just learn to never speak with them again because your schedules won't line up. All of these things together make Indiana's identity an amalgamation of the regions surrounding it, creating a Frankenstein's monster of culture that I still do not understand. And although I never felt like I truly fit in, for the past five years, Indiana has been my home. It's where my girlfriend and I first started living together, and we went from being two people who loved each other to being partners in every sense of the word. It's where I eventually proposed to her and she made a massive mistake by saying yes. It's where I worked my first real adult-type job, taking on more responsibilities than I ever had before and feeling like an imposter the entire time. It's where I put down new roots, even if they never went that deep, finding people I liked, restaurants I deemed tolerable, and various places to go to distract from the fact that I lived in a cornfield. I got comfortable there, and there's something to be said for that. I learned about the city I lived in and the ones around it. I explored places enough for them to become familiar. I met a lot of new people, and while the values, interests, and hobbies of most of them ended up being far different than mine, their mixture of Midwestern niceness and Southern politeness made me feel welcome. And as a long-time Midwesterner, their ability to make meaningful conversations about anything, even the fucking weather, is something I can appreciate. Indiana was the world I spent every day navigating. If you wanted to get to Walmart, I could annoyingly give you directions to it, even though we both know it would be much easier for you to just look it up on your phone. Walking out of the places that I frequented over the past five years, knowing that I will most likely never set foot in them again, gave me the strange sensation that I was forgetting something inside of them, that I left something behind, that I would need to go back. But I don't. And in all honesty, I probably won't. Home is a weird thing, and I think it has more to do with the people you're around than the place you are in. Indiana is where my fiancée and I started our first home together, and a part of me is always going to be in those places I left behind. Despite being beyond excited to be moving somewhere that is more me, I will always owe Indiana for that. So, thank you, Indiana. I still hate you, though. Sincerely, Rez. P.S. Indianapolis, I know you're watching this. This is not about you. You're cool. Have a good one. Peace.

## God of War And Growing Up
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0zjmVH9wacs

I've been drawn to coming-of-age stories since, well, since I started coming-of-age. As a kid, they offered varied looks at the struggles I found myself going through, namely the awkwardness and unsureness that comes from stepping out of the warm comforts of childhood and into the unknown. I saw my life and the lives of my friends reflected in these kinds of stories, giving me a greater understanding that the decisions we made would influence the types of people we might become, and pressuring me to decide if I should lean into that or run as far away from some potential future as possible. Growing up is beautiful and tragic, and it leaves a mark on everyone who experiences it, which is why I think these stories are relevant to people even well after they have come of age. We all share in the joys and dissatisfactions that come from shedding your layer of innocence and becoming a more permanent version of yourself. A version of yourself that is different from who everyone else thought you would become, from who you thought you would become. A version that, for this reason, is in some way a disappointment. And now that I've gotten a little dark here, you're probably wondering when is he going to talk about a goddamn video game? The answer is now. With improvements in technology and increased standards in what players look for in a narrative, coming-of-age stories have become more and more prominent in the video game scene. The different tools at game developers' disposal allow them to bring these stories to life in ways that books and films really can't. From giving players choices that influence the story to simply controlling the movements of a character, games have the ability to blur the line between a player and protagonist, allowing them to simulate the tumultuous experience of growing up in a way that its counterparts can't really replicate. There have been loads of great titles, especially indie ones, that center on these journeys of self-discovery and growing up. But I want to focus on one game in particular that has stuck with me because of how powerfully it deals with the fear of becoming someone no one wants you to be. 2018's God of War. At the heart of God of War are two intertwined character arcs, a tale of redemption for Kratos and a coming-of-age story for Atreus. This kind of setup has gotten a lot of play recently, and I think it's because of how well these two narrative threads link together. On one hand, there's the character with a bright and open future, taking those first steps into growing up. And on the other, there's the character with a dark past, who has the nearly impossible task of leaving the pain and the guilt from it behind. From the onset, it's clear that the last thing Kratos wants is for Atreus to become like him, to be fueled purely by revenge and destructive rage. Atreus is an extremely likable character. He's clever, kind, funny, and genuinely helpful from a gameplay perspective, all of which led me to want the best for him. Sharing in the same fears Kratos has about his future, I found myself feeling protective over the boy. When playing, I wanted to keep his sense of wonder intact, the same wonder he showed when seeing the marvels of Midgard. I appreciated the kindness he displayed to every stranger we came across, and I hoped he would never lose that. So, when Atreus finds out he's a god and starts acting flippantly about the world around him, and maliciously to those who considered him a friend, I was disappointed in him, and I started to worry where it might lead. And when he eventually did learn the error of his ways and repented for what he did, I felt a sense of relief, being able to believe in his pureness again. By the way, this is where I spoil the entire game. To me, what makes God of War such a powerful, true-to-life, coming-of-age story, is that at the end, after a climactic scene where Kratos assures Atreus and the player that the boy will turn out okay, Who I was is not who you be. We must be better. A single line calls all of that into question, playing on the fears that Kratos and the player both hold about Atreus' future. I guess there's just one thing I don't understand. My name on the wall. The Giants called me... Loki? Loki? This reveal comes with a lot of baggage because anyone even mildly familiar with any of Loki's representations know that he is an asshole. For a lot of people, especially those from places outside of Europe where Norse mythology is less likely to be taught in school, their perception of Loki probably comes from Marvel. Me being in that camp, the reveal worried me because it went directly against what I wanted for Atreus' future. Loki is an incredibly interesting and deep character in the Marvel films and comics, but I didn't want Atreus, a certified good lad, to become anything other than a good lad. With that said, while Marvel does draw from the original Norse mythology, all in all, that version of Loki is an entirely different and separate character. So, I read Neil Gaiman's Norse Mythology to gain more context on what Atreus' transformation into Loki might actually mean. Which, by the way, if you have any interest in the Norse pantheon, I would highly recommend this book because the stories are fascinating and Neil Gaiman's writing is impeccable. And amazingly, it made me feel even worse about Atreus' future. In the myth, Loki constantly tested his tenuous relationship with the other gods and eventually pushed things too far. So, they tracked Loki down, captured him, and turned one of his sons into a feral wolf who then ripped his other son to shreds. The gods then proceeded to tie Loki to a stone with his son's entrails, which became unbreakable bonds. If that weren't enough, they hung a venomous snake that dripped acid on his face all but forcing his wife to stand over him with a bull so that the only time he'd get acid on him was when she needed to empty it. This is said to go on until Ragnarok happens, which foretells Loki escaping his bonds and leading an army of the dead, giants, and his other children, the giant wolf Fenrir, the world serpent, and Hel, the ruler of the dead, in an invasion against Asgard, causing the death of almost all the gods and bringing about the destruction of the world by a great flood. Imagine if you played the other God of War games, this is starting to sound familiar. From the gods being responsible for the death of his family to seeking revenge for that, to storming their holy realm with giants in tow, to the world ending with a great flood. Loki's story parallels Kratos' from the original trilogy. Now, obviously, God of War takes a ton of liberties with its source material, and based on things that have already happened in the game, as well as the ways the creative team has changed events and characters from the Norse myths, Atreus' path will be drastically different from the Loki of legend. And what I've laid out here could have nothing to do with God of War's future. With that said, the fact that the developers chose the god in the Norse pantheon who reflects the tale of Kratos' to be his son seems to be too big of a connection to just be a coincidence. I don't know the intentions of the developers, but I would have to imagine that when they decided for Atreus to be Loki, they considered the reaction people would have to the name itself. They considered how players would look at Atreus in an entirely new way despite him not really doing anything to warrant it. They considered how people would associate him with other versions of Loki, and because of that, many players would assume that the kind-hearted kid was destined to fall from grace. So when Kratos says, Who I was is not who you will be, I find it hard to believe, because in the Norse myth, Loki is Kratos. And while Atreus might not have kids to avenge, he does have a father, one who we can only assume will die starting the whole cycle anew. The more I think about God of War's ending and delve into the implications and possibilities, the more I feel like Atreus' story is an incredible reflection of growing up. No matter how much promise you show, no matter how much a parent may try to protect you from making the mistakes they made, no matter how hard you try to stick to your childhood dreams, you will have failures. You will struggle in ways your parents hoped you wouldn't, and you will not become the exact reflection of your 10-year-old self's ideal adult. And that's usually a good thing. Inner struggle is part of growing up, it's part of being a human. There is a very real possibility that Atreus will be nothing like the Loki from Norse mythology. Kratos may succeed in stopping his son from repeating his own mistakes. But regardless, adding the revelation at the end of this game so doubt into my mind about who Atreus would become. Throughout the story I found myself thinking about the thousands of possibilities his future may hold. After it I could really only see one path. A path I imagine most would not want for him. My point in all this is that growing up will always be met with some level of disappointment. It's bittersweet. And a large part of that is because the path we end up taking in life is just one of seemingly infinite possibilities that are in front of us when we're 10 years old. When I went off to college I was terrified of growing up. I felt like even deciding on my major would cut away hundreds of other potential futures that I once dreamed about. I feared that I would let someone down because of my choices. That I would let myself down because of them. And

## Creating a Likable Video Game Companion
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0iPyq6a3jsY

I've been thinking a lot about my favorite video game characters, and I've realized that the vast majority of them are either villains or companions. I found this a little strange at first, but after thinking about it for a while, it kind of made sense. The gaming landscape is filled with titles starring main playable characters that are either silent or fairly generic, following the idea that the less distance someone has to travel in order to relate to a character they're controlling, the better. This leaves a lot of room for villains and companions to stand out. They often have more eccentric and distinctive personalities because they're meant to be people players see as friends or enemies and not as themselves. Players are supposed to develop bonds with them, creating memorable interactions and providing further motivation to finish a game. Honestly, in games, companions and villains are typically the ones who push stories forward, with villains forcing the protagonist to overcome conflicts and companions convincing them to overcome said conflicts. The main character's relationship with companions and villains gives the player insight on how a world works, what's important, and what needs to be done. The best examples of this are carefully crafted to elicit certain reactions from players, and while it is ultimately impossible to hit home with everyone, some games get pretty close. Games with villains who you despise but have an odd respect for, and companions who you're willing to go to the ends of the earth to help. And while I'm certainly interested in how games get players to hate a character, I've always wanted to explore how they get them to love one, and beyond that how these characters pull a player into a story and keep them there for its duration. To do this, I'm going to look at the two companions I've found myself most connected to in a game, Ellie from The Last of Us and Elizabeth from Bioshock Infinite. Both turn out to be the heart and soul of their respective games, and neither title would really work without players being made to care about them. So the big question is, how are we made to care about them? And the best place to find an answer is in what draws us to people we care about in real life. For instance, it's been pretty well established that we're drawn to people who are similar to us, often in the form of personality traits, opinions, backgrounds, or really anything of that nature. A common way writers create this connection is through two things, desires and flaws, both of which give characters depth and meaning to their actions. Like in Bioshock Infinite, more than anything else, Elizabeth wants to escape her tower and go to Paris, a place she has read, painted, and dreamed about her entire life. Until the final act, everything she does is in service of this goal. And while I relate to her desire for freedom and exploration, more than that, I relate to the mere fact that she has a desire at all. Seeing a character like Elizabeth, who literally travels through time and space in an attempt to achieve her goal, is really easy to latch onto, because on some level, the struggle to get what one wants is a universal experience, and seeing her struggle so much is relatable. This is why in most stories, characters with the strongest desires are the driving force of the plot, and they're often the most interesting as well. Seeing Elizabeth's desire and motivation from the start of the adventure puts her in the driver's seat, and makes it much easier to align with her goals. While Booker does have his own aspirations, the ones shown to the player early on don't define his character as much as they define his situation. Based on the initial context, his greatest desire isn't to bring them the girl and wipe away the debt, it's just a task he needs to complete to survive, and that's not really as compelling as the kind of desire Elizabeth has. The kind that comes from dreams instead of bad decisions. So whether it be Elizabeth's need to get to Paris, or say, Ellie's desire for companionship, players relate to the act of having a desire as much, if not more, than the desire itself. And while desires are important, flaws play just as crucial a role in defining a character. In fiction, flaws work best when they are fairly common and mostly forgivable. For instance, Ellie cusses a lot, which is understood to be generally frowned upon, but given most people do it anyway, players included, it's more endearing than anything else. Also, her swearing is aggressive instead of downright offensive, making it comical instead of hurtful. Another example is how impulsive and brash she is. Ellie often will act without thinking, putting herself at risk, and while this behavior could be seen as annoying, it works here because almost every time she does act irresponsibly, it ends up helping Joel and the player instead of getting them in trouble. With Bioshock Infinite, Elizabeth is undeniably naive, but based on how well-read she is, assumes she has a grasp on how the world works, which causes nearly every plan she comes up with to be met with a misstep. However, the innocence that comes with her naivety is easy to appreciate. The way she marvels at the world around her is still one of my favorite aspects of her character. All in all, flaws allow players to relate to and even appreciate these blemishes without having to fully experience the potentially annoying consequences. Being able to take solace in the fact that a character has messed up in the same ways you have creates a bond. Honestly, that's the basis of most of my real-life friendships. Along with desires and flaws, both Bioshock Infinite and The Last of Us emphasize just how crucial a role cooperation plays in endearing companions to a player. As each game goes on, the amount players rely on both companions grows, with Ellie providing cover fire and well-timed backstabs, and Elizabeth opening tears to turn the tide in combat and throwing Booker everything from spare change to a rocket launcher. There are multiple moments in each game where the companion ends up saving the playable character's life, not only making them mechanically valuable, but more importantly building trust. Furthermore, the fact that neither of them really face much danger in combat avoids player frustration. How the hell are you breathing in this stuff? Having to constantly worry about a companion, like Ashley in Resident Evil 4, leads to players being stressed out any time she's around. Making companions nearly invulnerable in combat situations is definitely a cop-out, but at least it means their presence doesn't hinder the player, which led me to actually want both Ellie and Elizabeth around all the time. And the comfort of their presence is something games use in order to condition players. Arguably the scariest moments of these two games happen when the player is separated from their companion. In The Last of Us, Joel loses Ellie after he falls down an elevator shaft, leaving him alone with only the sounds of swift footsteps in the darkness. Creeping through the dank, partially submerged rooms with the imminent threat of an ambush left me feeling beyond uneasy, and the relief that came after reuniting with Ellie was palpable. Bioshock Infinite does this during the asylum section after Songbird takes Elizabeth away. While most battles in Infinite end up being about direct confrontation with enemies, this is one of the few times where players are given the option to be stealthy, and I imagined most approached it this way because the consequence for not is terrifying. Everything from the atmosphere to the inhabitants of the asylum placed me on edge, and I was afraid to fight without having Elizabeth there to support me. Moments like these condition players to feel uneasy when their companion is not around, heightening the importance of sticking with them. And even though players still encounter a ton of stress and conflict while with their respective companions, it isn't the same kind of skin-crawling uneasiness. In fact, the kind of stress that players normally go through, like action set pieces and large-scale battles, actually add to feeling a connection to a character. Some research indicates that shared pain can lead to individuals feeling closer with each other. Like if you were sitting next to a stranger on a plane that almost crashed, you would most likely feel closer to them than if the flight just went by with no troubles. The fact that players go on these intense adventures, where practically the only person they can rely on is the companion, strengthens this bond. The player and companion have been through some shit, and that ends up meaning a lot. From an external standpoint, it's worth noting that performances can alter how an audience views a character. And for these two games, the executions by Courtney Draper as Elizabeth and Ashley Johnson as Ellie are near perfect. The amount of emotion both actresses exude from just their voices is staggering. Draper and Johnson helped shape the direction of their respective characters, and I think this greatly benefited their performances. Along with the vocal performances, the motion capture and general programming of the characters both matter as well. Ellie and Elizabeth move and interact with objects and things in the world like actual humans would, creating a sense that they can act independently of the player. A lot of companions before this point just moved when the player told them to move, and any other development was saved for cutscenes. But the more a character can seem like they exist regardless of a player's input, the more likely they'll feel like an actual person. On a similar note, physical attractiveness also plays a role. And while this seems shallow, it isn't really surprising. People gravitate towards beauty, which is why so much of our culture is based around the celebration of it. There's even research that suggests being good-looking can lead to others assuming one is more talented, intelligent, and honest. Bioshock Infinite leans on this pretty heavily, with Elizabeth being a combination of the girl next door and a Disney princess. And while it is impossible to measure the exact effects her looks have on players, it doesn't feel like a huge stretch to say that her attractiveness was another reason people were interested in her. Ken Levine has stated many times that Bioshock Infinite was trying to pull in

## Kendrick's Control
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CAVTOo4Dk04

It's pretty safe to say that Kendrick Lamar has established himself as one of the most notable rappers of this generation. His rise as an artist has been ripe with thought-provoking tracks and powerful live performances, both of which have uncanny ways of gripping the public's attention. One of the most interesting instances of him falling into the spotlight and stirring up controversy happened in August of 2013 when Big Sean released Control, a track where over the course of 10 seconds, Kendrick calls out 11 other rappers, two of which appear on it with him, and sends a pretty strong message. The reaction to this was massive, garnering responses from some of the rappers mentioned, and far more from the ones who weren't. Of course, the majority of the noise surrounding this came from fans and critics, mostly giving it high praises and in a handful of cases, deeming it as one of the most important verses of the decade. A lot of prominent voices shared the sentiment that Kendrick had just changed the course of modern hip-hop. Obviously, Kendrick is not the first person to ever name-drop, and he's also far from being the first person to make this claim. I'm the king of New York, king of the coast, one hand, I juggle them both. In fact, that line itself is a reference to a Krupp lyric from a collaboration they did called Get Busy. I'm important like the pope, I'm the king of New York. And when I said it, nobody said shit. Then when Kendrick said it, everybody wanted to go against the boy. The potency of Control had very little to do with what was said, or even how it was said, but rather that Kendrick was the one to say it. There's this mythos that has developed around him, painting him as a sort of heroic link between modern and old-school hip-hop. The story that Kendrick has been sold on is compelling. This kid from Compton who kept getting pushed around by his city used music as a way out, and with some support and mentoring from West Coast legends like Snoop Dogg, The Game, and Dr. Dre, he pulled together his experiences and expressed them with a fresh yet familiar feeling record. And although that simplified account of his early career certainly contains exaggerations and inaccuracies, it is the narrative that people latch onto, and it's given him credibility. Once Good Kid, Mad City dropped, a lot of people saw Kendrick as the future of hip-hop. So when he seemingly criticized the state of it, they listened. The verse isn't as much of an insult as it is a challenge. Although a lot of headlines spun it as a diss track, Kendrick's statements of wanting to raise the bar and be better than the rest weren't meant to put anyone down, but rather to question their motives. There are so many concessions that artists are pushed into making by labels, and a lot of times it comes at the cost of the music's integrity. But Kendrick's proven that hits can still have substance, so him saying this sort of thing comes from a place of knowledge. This entire verse is about Kendrick not only leaving his mark on hip-hop, but leaving a mark that is uniquely his, and not one compromised by needing to appeal to the mass market. It's a message to his fellow artists to do the same. The names he mentioned are the names of people he expects a lot out of. In fact, most people theorize that the bigger diss was not to be one of the people mentioned, which explains why a lot of those artists responded. For instance, B.o.B. shot back with a track called How to Rap, which, among other things, mocked Kendrick's flow in songs like Swimming Pools. Also, Lupe Fiasco, who made fun of Kendrick, claiming to juggle both of the coasts. The significance of Control comes from the reaction people had to it. It created a discussion about hip-hop, and even if it was just for a few weeks, proved that rap could still be competitive. Looking at it now, a few years out, it's clear that the verse had a much bigger impact on fans of hip-hop than it did on hip-hop itself. A lot of the artists who Kendrick mentioned have released some of their best work since the song dropped, but to say that was all Kendrick's doing would be more than a stretch. However, it certainly did put them under a microscope, which gave them exposure and raised expectations. To the public, it became important what those artists put out next, and a lot of them lived up to the call. Of course, the artist under the most scrutiny after the song dropped was Kendrick himself, so it was paramount for him to create something that lived up to his claims. To pimp a butterfly while not the album people expected did this. It received nearly universal respect, further elevating him as an icon who talks about real issues through mainstream music in a way that doesn't feel preachy or overdone. It seems pretty clear that Kendrick wants to make a difference for people the way artists he listened to made a difference for him, and beyond all the name-dropping and joking threats, that's what Control's about. Building a legacy. It's not about actually being the king of whatever culture. It's about leaving a mark as great as Biggie, as great as Pac. But for the most part, it's about how great I want to be at the end of the day. Nobody's going to stop me.

## Hamilton: A Musical For Anyone
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gGuBj_RFXac

During Thanksgiving dinner in 2014, my brother kept bringing up this play he planned to see in previews, a hip-hop musical about the rise and fall of America's first Treasury Secretary, Alexander Hamilton. Due to the strangeness of the idea, I assumed I would never hear about it again. Of course, I was wrong. The hit Broadway musical Hamilton. Hamilton. Biggest hit, Hamilton. Hamilton. Hamilton. Hamilton. Go see! Alexander Hamilton. Hamilton has found a prominent place in popular culture that only a handful of Broadway shows have been able to do in modern times. It has been the center of praise and controversy, and it's been labeled as everything from being the reinvention of theater to being highly overrated. But regardless of what's been said about the show, it has stayed in the public's consciousness since its debut. As the production has grown in notability, the quick pitch my brother gave me, which I've since heard from dozens of news outlets, countless celebrities, and the show's creator and star, Lin-Manuel Miranda, no longer seems so weird. And the question I keep coming back to is, why? Why has this play that seems too specific and too niche to succeed become so widely accepted? A classification as particular as historical hip-hop musical runs the risk of only appealing to people who are interested in the intersection of the three. However, Hamilton's audience goes far beyond that. And what it kind of comes down to is that it seems to be constructed in a way where it can be appreciated for any of its bases, making it accessible to anyone interested in hip-hop or musicals or historical fiction. It isn't dependent on people being fans of all three. In fact, it seems like it almost expects people not to be. Instead of constricting the potential audience, its blending of genres has created more entry points, expanding its reach. And most importantly, the general consensus has been that the show does justice to each of its bases, which has given it staying power. Like most other music that sees a lot of success, Hamilton is catchy. From a lyrical standpoint, it manages to do so by using and combining popular conventions of both musicals and hip-hop. And honestly, it all kind of boils down to repetition. A common feature of musicals are lyrical motifs, which are repeated ideas and phrases often tied to a certain character or situation. And Hamilton takes this to another level. Just about every major character has at least one lyrical motif associated with them that develops and changes in meaning throughout the play. They're pivotal to a lot of character arcs, making them impossible to forget. The central conflict revolving around Alexander Hamilton's and Aaron Burr's lifelong rivalry is highlighted by their lyrical motifs, with Hamilton's being, I am not throwing away my shot, signifying his refusal to pass up opportunities, and Aaron Burr's being variations of the phrase, wait for it, showing his reluctance to dedicate himself to a particular stance before knowing if it's the absolute best course of action. The two live by these opposite tenets throughout the entire show, until their eventual duo where Hamilton literally throws away a shot by raising his gun straight in the air, and Burr, in a rare impulsive act, fires first. This is the most prominent crossing of contrasting motifs in the show, but it is far from being the only one. And it's these moments when the motifs contrast with each other and transfer between characters that are some of the most powerful. These lines become catchy because it's the easiest way to understand what's going on at the heart of the show. In regard to the lyrical structure of individual songs, Hamilton uses a lot of staples of hip-hop, most notably with its use of internal rhyme. Words and phrases constantly play off of each other through the repetition of similar consonant and vowel sounds, also known as consonants and assonants, which leaves very few spaces that don't have some type of rhyme, whether it be partial or perfect. The action in the street is exciting, but Jesus, between all the bleeding and fighting, I've been reading and writing, we need to handle our financial situation. We're a nation of states, what's the state of our nation? I'm past patiently waiting, I'm passionately smashing every expectation, every action's an act of creation. I'm laughing in the face of casualties and sorrow, for the first time I'm thinking past tomorrow. The rhymes are infectious and memorable, and the level of care and skill that Lin-Manuel Miranda put into these lyrics is something that other hip-hop artists have taken note of. Sometimes in hip-hop we say, real recognize real. So I could recognize immediately that Lin was a real one and that this was a real story. In the eyes of the public, getting this type of acceptance from other musicians legitimized Hamilton as a work of hip-hop. Questlove and Black Thought ended up producing the cast album, artists including Common, Busta Rhymes, and Chance the Rapper did features on the Hamilton mixtape, and rappers ranging from Talib Kweli to Jay-Z to Eminem attended the production, all showing some level of support and recognition for it. And it makes sense because Hamilton is entrenched in the history and culture of hip-hop, and acts as a celebration of the medium, which is a feat that seems nearly impossible for a musical to pull off. Regardless, it manages to be a love letter to hip-hop while also being one to traditional Broadway shows. There are a ton of allusions throughout the play, ranging from Mobb Deep to Pirates of Penzance. Hip-hop has always been a genre that wears its influences on its sleeve, and this is no different. The references largely manage to not feel forced or hokey, and they help tie modern struggles to those of a man who died over 200 years ago. In all the shows that Steve and I have written together, including Assassins, you reach a point, I think, where the research is over and you then invent the character who actually existed in history. But they live in a kind of a penumbral area where they are who they were, but they are also who you want them to be. And ultimately, this is the job of historical fiction, bringing life and emotional depth into a person that is normally learned about in ways that lack those elements. Miranda does this by tying it to hip-hop culture. As he has stressed regularly, Alexander Hamilton's life mirrors the classic rap story. A poor kid with no status writes his way out of poverty and into prominence. It's familiar, and seeing this through line from 1776 to today shows that although so much has changed over that time, the base idea of the American Dream hasn't. And the show's casting, which has gotten a lot of press, both positive and negative, further reflects that idea. The roles of the Founding Fathers are cast primarily with Black and Latino actors, which is another way of connecting the past to the present. There are a lot of reasons that people have celebrated this choice, but in terms of making it feel like a credible hip-hop show, the importance is simply that they cast actors who would be most successful at performing the parts. Talib Kweli put it best when he was talking about the actor playing Thomas Jefferson, Davi Diggs, saying, That's an MC. That's not a traditional Broadway dude. That's a guy who raps and was put in the play because he raps. There are still plenty of traditional Broadway actors in the show, but the inclusion of an artist like

## Avatar: The Last Airbender - Realistic Fantasy
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C54c5n9uefo

Every year, I find myself rewatching Avatar: The Last Airbender. It's a treasure trove of good storytelling, beautiful animation, stunning choreography, and satisfying character arcs. The amount of thematic depth that its 61 episodes cover is beyond impressive, and every time I go back, I can't help but fall in love with it all over again. What appeals to me most is that something about it feels real. Amidst ancient spirits, people with the power to control the elements, and flying bison, Avatar's world and the lives of the characters in it are easy to understand and connect with. This is a quality that many of the best fantasy stories have, being able to take something that out of context seems wholly unbelievable and then finding a way to make it believable. Avatar's creators, Brian Konietzko and Michael DiMartino, achieved this in the way they created and presented their world. Crafting a new world, especially one that's drastically different from reality, comes with a cavalcade of challenges, chief among which is convincing viewers to suspend their disbelief and start feeling engaged in the inner workings of the world. For this to happen, the world needs to be consistent in regard to how it follows its own internal rules and logic. A story's ability to pull this off is one of the major factors that plays into if it's just okay or great, and Avatar manages this successfully in a few different ways. First off, Konietzko and DiMartino put a strong focus on creating and defining limitations early on in the show's development as a way to never let things get out of hand. To me, limitations are good. They allow things to happen without you going, wait a minute. They didn't want to run the risk of introducing something that undermined the narrative they planned out, so they made rules that couldn't be broken. Like bending had to come from the body and only could affect nearby areas. Only the Avatar could bend more than one element. Bending is something one must be born with. I'm an Earthbender! I'm not! And there are no magical items that give people unlimited power. These limitations made the show easy to understand while also lessening the risk of power creep, which is something that occurs when new aspects are introduced that overpower existing elements of the world, making everything feel a bit bloated and over the top. And this is something that plagues a lot of shows that center around fighting. There are certainly a few holes in the limitations the creators set for themselves, most notably with the inner workings of the spirits and Aang's abilities, but they did a solid job of not using those holes too often, which is something that the follow-up series, The Legend of Korra, kind of struggled with. At most, Avatar only ever slightly stretches its limitations, but it never breaks through them. The additions to bending and Aang's powers don't feel random or cheap, but rather a natural extension of the rules of the world. What's more is that everything in Avatar's world, whether it be clothing, culture, or infrastructure, is influenced by bending. For instance, the city of Amashu uses a combination of gravity and earthbending to transport supplies. Ba Sing Se is surrounded by a giant wall that only earthbenders could create and maintain with relative ease. The Northern Water Tribe's buildings are made of ice, and the locals use waterbending as a way to open and close the gate to their city. The Air Nomads built temples on high mountains that could only be easily reached by airbending, and they have a hermetic set of ideals to reflect this isolation. And the Fire Nation were the first to enter an industrial revolution of sorts because of their ability to generate power and presumably manipulate metals with their bending of fire and lightning. These details may seem small, but they establish a consistency in the world, which is what gives it that quality of feeling real. Another struggle that comes with creating a new world is making something original, yet not too out there that it becomes hard for audiences to follow. Konezko and DiMartino solved this issue by using and combining popular and easy-to-understand ideas instead of building everything from the ground up. Like, while there are plenty of shows that center around martial arts and many others that have characters who can manipulate various elements, none have done it with as much cohesion between the two concepts. Also, instead of populating the world with entirely made-up creatures, they simply combined real animals together, which creates interesting and humorous animals that viewers understand by just hearing the name. It might take some time to figure out what a plimpy is in Harry Potter, but it is immediately clear what to expect from a saber-toothed moose lion. Even the show itself, which is clearly inspired by anime, is offset with jokes and ideas that are unique to being a show on Nickelodeon. Avatar is a mashup, and when looking at each of its core aspects independently, it treads a lot of familiar ground, but the fusion of all these ideas together makes it one of a kind. Now, if worldbuilding were to be split into two steps, development and presentation, all of this would fall into development. The second and maybe more difficult step is presenting the world. A writer can create the most in-depth and detailed histories, but if these things aren't presented to the audience in the right way, they won't be effective in the slightest. In fiction, the purpose of a world is to support the story being told, and Avatar achieves this by using its world to create high stakes for the main characters. A pretty common and effective approach to introducing a fictional world is having the protagonists in the audience learn about the world at the same time. For example, walking through a wardrobe and discovering a magical land, or learning about some secret innate power, or the often frowned upon case of amnesia. These approaches allow audiences to view the world through the same lens as the main character, which opens up the potential for explaining how the world works without it feeling out of place. Avatar slightly twists these tropes by having Aang not know anything about the current state of the world due to him being frozen for 100 years, but being extremely knowledgeable about the past. Because of this, and how the group travels to so many unfamiliar places, from a narrative standpoint, it makes sense for other characters to explain the inner workings of the modern world to Aang, as in turn, he describes to them what the past was like. Ultimately showing viewers not only how the world works, but also making the world feel lived in by showing how much has changed. And in a lot of cases, how much has changed for the worse. Which is important because arguably, Aang's disappearance costs it all. Almost every place that Aang and company visit throughout the series is affected in some way by the same issue. War. Seeing the different ways that the war between the Fire Nation and the rest of the world has affected not only each of the four nations, but individual cities and towns, serves to flesh out the world and introduce backstories and histories that viewers become connected to because they see characters directly affected by events from the past. It is far easier to care about the history of a place when the effects of said history are clear and personal. And that is how Avatar presents its world, through the various people that Aang meets on his journey to master the four elements. During this adventure, it becomes clear how diverse yet relatable the people and places of this world are. For instance, the Earth Nation is not one uniformed country. Each city's views are dependent on their experiences, which differ across the board. Some cities are under Fire Nation control, and others have barely been touched by the war. Even views from inside the same city like Ba Sing Se are entirely different depending on which economic level one lives in. As each city across the world is explored, a great sense of the struggle and turmoil that has been caused by the war develops. And this is so powerful because Aang blames himself for everything becoming this way. The history of Avatar's world is intertwined so tightly with the struggle of the protagonist, which makes each location's backstory tied to Aang. In turn, this makes it so, for viewers, the world is actually worth saving. A lot of films and shows center around the protagonist needing to save the world, but in most cases, the only reason a viewer would care if the world is saved is because that's just how you're supposed to feel. Which is boring and too easy. In Avatar, the majority of the show is spent exploring the world, giving hundreds of reasons why it is important to save. Every episode strengthens this resolve, playing into the series-long arc of defeating the Fire Lord. And because of this, no episode really feels like a filler, despite there being a handful of them that deviate far from the main plot. The show is the perfect length to tell the story that the creators intended to tell. While a part of me will always wish for more Avatar The Last Airbender, I'm glad this installment of the story stopped where it did. Avatar's world is interesting and engaging. Kanetsuko and DiMartino did an excellent job of utilizing every aspect of what bending could do in a world, and it followed a consistent logic, never really stretching its rules too thin. This created a perfect backdrop to tell a fantastical yet very human story about a war-torn world filled with everything from sacrifice, suffering, and loss, to betrayal, self-examination, and redemption, to independence, wisdom, and kindness. I think I speak for most fans of the show when I say that Avatar has one of those special worlds that you dream of living in. When watching, I can escape into a different world while still being able to examine it next to my life and my struggles. And that's why I come back to it every year.

## The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild - The Power of Questions
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h8J6Crxj7YE

So, I love Breath of the Wild. I don't know that I can say it's the best Zelda game ever made, or even my favorite, but it is definitely the Zelda game that I and presumably most fans of the series needed to play right now in order to remember how special this franchise can be. Skyward Sword agitated a lot of people, myself included, with its hand-holding design choices, and Breath of the Wild is the perfect response to those frustrations. The amount of player freedom it offers is staggering, and unlike many modern games, it trusts that players aren't total idiots, allowing them to answer questions like where to go, what to do, and how to do things without constant instruction or reminders, which is immensely refreshing. Having a game answer these kinds of questions for the players before they even get the chance to answer them takes away agency and leads to a feeling of being on autopilot. Instead of providing answers, Breath of the Wild starts almost every quest, diversion, and plot point with the question. They are often quick and easy to answer, but Breath of the Wild's ability to link together tiny activities through these questions plays a huge role in building the sense of freedom and adventure that makes this title so special. Journeys are intrinsically focused on finding answers, whether they be about the world, oneself, or anything in between. And giving players the opportunity to constantly answer questions leads directly into the theme of adventure. To be honest, I really expected not to like Breath of the Wild. After hearing that this entry would feature an open world, I assumed it wasn't really for me. If you've been around my channel for a while, you know that a lot of staples of the genre bother me. So many titles don't do the heavy lifting when it comes to world design, which makes things like minimaps and fast travel become crutches that are leaned on far too often. These functions often strip away mystery and organic discovery. Surprisingly though, the way Breath of the Wild approaches travel and navigation pretty much lines up with what I've been hoping to see from open world games for a while now. The world is densely peppered with tons of little things to do while heading to a destination that don't take up much time and give useful rewards. In general, Nintendo did a superb job with placing and creating notable stuff in every nook and cranny of the map. When playing, it seemed like no matter where I went, I found something worthwhile. Although Breath of the Wild feels like one massive adventure, it is really just a well-connected string of tiny ones. And a large part of that derives from that idea of the game presenting almost everything as a question instead of as an answer. This can be best seen with one of the game's main collectibles, the Korok Seeds. Instead of just being an actual item scattered across the map that players can run to and quickly pick up, the developers opted to hide the Korok Seeds behind small inconsistencies in the world. So instead of saying, oh, there's a little thing I should pick up, an actual question is formed. Why is there a circle of rocks in this lake? Or what are these blocks doing here? They are simple questions with simple answers, but they act as quick hooks that lead to small challenges and rewards. There's mystery to each Korok Seed, which is far more compelling than just seeing a blue orb and grabbing it. Even when the connection between these inconsistencies and Korok Seeds is made, there's always the question of what do I do to get it? So that sense of uncertainty never fully goes away. This same idea is also exhibited by the way quests, especially side quests, are approached. During side quests in most open world games I've played, an NPC will give the quest and then a waypoint will appear on the map showing where to go. However, in Breath of the Wild, more often than not, NPCs will either give a riddle or point in the direction of a landmark for reference. From there, it is the player's job to figure out what it means. Instead of having the game do all the work, the player actually has to figure something out, which unfortunately in this day and age is not a given. Turning these things into questions may seem simple, but it ends up being the difference between following a trail of breadcrumbs and actually engaging in a world. It gives a hook that players want to follow, and frankly, it makes players feel smart for knowing to follow it.
