This makes navigation center around following mysteries and solving them, opposed to following a waypoint or a line on the minimap. In general, the way Breath of the Wild approaches assisting the player is incredibly effective. For instance, despite having a busy HUD that at first glance seems overbearing, all the information on it can be picked up from audio and visual cues, whether it be from Link's body language or the terrain itself. The first thing I did when I started playing was turn off the minimap, and at no point did I struggle with navigation. There are so many memorable landmarks, all but forcing players to become familiar with the layout of Hyrule despite its enormous size. Also, the game's massive draw distance makes it really easy to examine the landscape, identify familiar places, pick a path, and move accordingly. While I usually get tired of traveling across a map due to boring movement mechanics and there not being enough to do between quest markers, I didn't really feel those issues with Breath of the Wild because of how bombarded I was with all those tiny questions. What's over this hill? Is there anything near this monster camp that could help me take them out? What else do I need to do to solve this riddle? And the fact that there are multiple ways to answer any given question also adds to feeling powerful as a player, and Link's mobility is actually one of the main sources of that player freedom. Being able to climb on anything and glide from place to place opens up a lot of possibilities for traversal and exploration, which pairs well with the fact that there's so much to discover. At the same time, there are enough limitations with his mobility that players are incentivized to either increase Link's abilities or find creative ways to navigate areas. With the proper vantage point or enough stamina, players can go anywhere in Breath of the Wild. And being able to travel anywhere in order to answer a question, whether it be in regards to a collectible or location, satisfies the basic premise of what an open world can be. The biggest question presented in Breath of the Wild is how are you going to defeat Ganon? And the fact that the answer is not exclusively complete the main quest is kind of amazing. See, I've noticed a lot of open world games have stories that don't really need an open world to be told. Because of this, in many titles, I often get railroaded by the main quest and end up missing out on things that don't affect the primary objective. For example, in The Witcher 3, the main quest is extremely compelling. Geralt needs to find his adoptive daughter Ciri before the people pursuing her do. This raises the stakes and gives Geralt and the player a strong motivation, which makes for an interesting story. But, at least for how I approach games, it doesn't really support the elements of open worlds that make them captivating. The fun of an open world comes from discovery, but The Witcher 3's story constantly calls for urgency. So I rode right past the interesting things sprinkled throughout the world, foregoing exploration in favor of completing the story. Which is a shame, because The Witcher 3's world and main story are both incredible, but they don't really work in tandem. And I'm sure that plenty of players have the ability to not focus too much on the main quest and be able to enjoy the diversions. And that's awesome for them, but it doesn't really work for me. In general, it seems a little backwards to not create a story that supports the world it takes place in. Which has led me to want an open world game that doesn't have such a strong story. One where the world and exploration of it directly supports the main quest. And Breath of the Wild does this better than any open world game I've played. The main objective is simple, defeat Ganon. The best way to do this is by getting more powerful, and there are a handful of main quests that help players do that. But the completion of those quests is not necessary. This opens the door for players to choose how they want to take on Ganon. Like primarily searching for the choicest bugs and food ingredients in order to make a ridiculous amount of elixirs and recipes is actually a viable, albeit impractical, approach to beating the game. And that's incredible. Almost every diversion and side activity supports the main goal of getting stronger. Whether it's completing trials in order to get more health and stamina. Doing side quests to earn money and get better gear. Raiding monster camps to get useful weapons and materials. Or finding Korok seeds in order to increase inventory size. And more importantly, to stop getting the notification saying there is no more room for weapons. Which, by the way, is a really obnoxious way to push the player toward wanting to keep searching for Koroks, but also an effective one. There is this powerful sense that everything is building toward a single effect. And that no matter what you are doing, it is the right thing to be doing. To me, that is how an open world game should feel. And that is why this one has struck such a chord with me. It asks the question, how do you want to do this? And you actually get to answer that however you want. The fact that this is the game we got is pretty amazing. Considering that Skyward Sword received nearly universal acclaim from review outlets, which most developers would take as a sign to keep doing what they're doing. Instead, Breath of the Wild is pretty much the exact opposite of Skyward Sword, at least in terms of how it handles progression and direction. And this seems to indicate that Nintendo prioritized the

## Shhh...I've Never Played Pikmin
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hhGo8FMIhuk

One of the biggest reasons I continue to buy Nintendo products despite the company's many shortcomings is that the games they make are filled with charm.
Over the past 30 years, Nintendo has created some of the most beloved experiences in gaming.
They've crafted more memorable characters and worlds than any other video game company, and they've done it with a consistent level of polish in regard to gameplay and presentation.
However, the most impressive thing about Nintendo's charm is their ability to come up with ideas that people don't really want and then turn them into compelling games that fans can't help but fall in love with.
Things that look awful on paper don't scare Nintendo, they inspire them.
In my opinion, the best examples of Nintendo pulling this sort of thing off can primarily be found on the GameCube, which instead of following the trends of its competitors, doubled down on titles that were uniquely Nintendo.
Its catalog is filled with games that fans never asked for but grew to love anyway.
They made strange but fun spin-offs like Kirby Air Ride.
They reworked Zelda and Mario, redefining what both of those series could be.
They even launched the console with a new franchise starring Luigi as a ghost hunter instead of one of their tried and trusted series.
And they made an RTS action game, which by all means should be a nightmare for a console title, but by most accounts, it's not.
Look, most of you know how the show works by now, so let me just say, shh, I've never played Pikmin.
Pikmin is a series that I kind of actively avoided.
When the first two titles released, I was in the keep-me-away-from-kids-games phase, and even though it may not have deserved to be, Pikmin fell into that category.
But now, some of my favorite pieces of media are ones that have the ability to appeal to both kids and adults in meaningful ways.
And Pikmin certainly does that.
It strikes a solid balance between silliness and seriousness.
The world is lush and colorful and filled with Pikmin who are cute and expressive.
But a threatening tension hangs over it all due to the main character, Captain Olimar, being stranded and only having 30 days to repair his ship before running out of life support.
It had me on edge in the best way possible.
Funny moments like watching the Pikmin trip or get distracted are offset by terrifying ones like having a Bulborb swallow ten Pikmin at once.
It's adorably disturbing, and this mood is highlighted through the musings of Captain Olimar.
One of the biggest reasons I find Olimar interesting stems from how fundamentally different he is compared to Nintendo's other major icons.
Nintendo is kind of famous for building characters who really only convey information about their personality through their appearance and actions.
More often than not, these characters never talk, but Olimar's most charming and intriguing feature is his voice.
The observations and quips he makes when finding a ship component or writing a voyage log range from being funny to helpful to strangely poignant.
And I think that might be part of why he never caught on the way that characters like Link or Kirby or Mario did.
He's too deep to understand in a glance.
Without his internal dialogue describing his hardships and the life he's trying to get back to, he doesn't appear to be all that interested of a character, which means he can't be quickly sold to an audience.
Although it's only a small part of the game, seeing his thoughts about the Pikmin, his family, and life on a new planet created a greater sense of importance to completing the mission.
And it made Olimar go from being a character I didn't care about at all to one of my favorites.
The Pikmin themselves are also very endearing.
It's hard not to feel guilty or panicked when leading them into dangerous places.
Overall, I felt a strong connection to the primary cast, which practically forced me to become invested.
Pikmin's gameplay centers around growth and retrieval.
Captain Olimar leads the Pikmin around the planet and throws them at things to get them to do one of their two major functions, carry stuff or beat the shit out of stuff.
There's a pretty wide range of things they can beat the shit out of, whether it be walls that open pathways to new areas or giant bugs whose corpses can be brought back to base to create more Pikmin.
On a whole, the Pikmin are pretty limited in what they can do, and this works in the game's favor.
If they had too many functions, there would most likely need to be some sort of bulky menu, which would take away from how smoothly the game plays.
Instead of giving a single type of Pikmin a lot of different things to do, Nintendo opted to create various types of Pikmin with different passive abilities.
This works great because it allows for streamlined gameplay while still providing a multitude of options for how to approach a task.
Selecting the optimal composition of Pikmin for any given excursion can be the difference between retrieving more than one ship part in a day or dying in a fiery mess.
As more ship parts are found, more of the world opens up to be explored, and overall, the pacing of this is pretty solid.
I never felt like I was stuck in one spot for too long, but opening new areas still felt deserved.
There are five different zones, but only three have any real bulk to them, which is a little light on the level variety side of things.
It would have been nice to have one or two more places with substance to explore.
The three main areas are different enough from each other, but this kind of comes at the cost of underutilizing a couple features.
For example, a few enemies are only encountered once, which is a shame because some of them have really interesting abilities that would have been cool to see in other situations.
For me, the crux of Pikmin's experience comes from the limited amount of time given to accomplish the various tasks the game sets out.
There are 30 days to collect as many ship parts as possible, and each day lasts about 15 minutes.
Achieving this goal isn't that difficult, but having the countdowns in place adds a ton of weight to each day.
If Olimar runs out of health or Pikmin, he must return to his ship and miss out on the rest of the day, which adds that much more pressure to collect more parts the next day.
What I like about this is that it punishes failure in a way that isn't entirely defeating, but still puts players in a bad spot, making every accomplishment that much sweeter.
Getting multiple groups of Pikmin to do as many different tasks as possible at the same time is paramount to completing the mission quickly.
With that said, there is a lot of buffer room for players who never quite figure out how to manage their time well, which opens up the title to either be a casual experience or a speedrunning challenge.
No matter how it's approached, Pikmin manages to be very chill and calming to play while still having high stakes, which I'm not really sure how it pulls off, but it does.
In the grand scheme of things, Pikmin does a pretty good job of dealing with the limitations of being an RTS-like game on console, but throughout my time with it, I couldn't help but think that it would play better on a keyboard.
When away from the base, there isn't a reliable way to pick out a specific number of Pikmin to form a group.
They can be selected in a large number with Olimar's whistle or in a smaller one by running into them when they're deselected, but neither are precise.
This made it so I accidentally grabbed Pikmin that I didn't need, forcing me to deselect and try again.
This is a pretty small annoyance, but when it happens over and over, it gets tiring.
Also, while the developers made a smart decision by primarily giving the Pikmin passive abilities, there are still a few active ones that can be frustrating to control.
I had a really hard time getting a yellow Pikmin to pick up and throw bombs without blowing up my entire colony.
Precision is almost non-existent here, which makes for a lot of wasted time in a game where time is a key factor.
What frustrated me more than anything else was the camera.
Olimar's movement is tied to the thumbstick and the Pikmin's movement is tied to the c-stick, leaving button controls for the camera, which is unsurprisingly awful.
The views are restricted, making it difficult to ever really feel comfortable while playing.
None of these things ruined my experience, but there was definitely a lot of room for improvement.
I imagine a lot of these issues were addressed in later titles, but some problems are just the cost of playing on console.
Maybe one of the most endearing things about Pikmin is that even if the player doesn't fix the ship within the 30 days, there is still a sense of finishing the game.
In a lot of titles, failure typically leads to a loss of progress that needs to be redone, but in Pikmin, that isn't really the case.
Nothing important on the level resets due to a fail state, and the only thing that's lost is time.
In the end, players either collect every piece before the time limit is up, or they don't.
And whether they fail or succeed, the story of Captain Olimar is wrapped up.
If Olimar hasn't collected enough ship parts, the launch will fail and he ends up being transformed into a sort of half-Pikmin, half-human thing.
If enough parts are collected, though, the launch is a success and Captain Olimar heads back home.
On my first playthrough, I just barely collected every piece, getting the last part on the final day.
Regardless, what I admire so much about the multiple endings, especially the bad ending, is that the player isn't forced to succeed.
So many games have fail states that never impact the story and can typically be ignored once the game is beaten, but in Pikmin, that doesn't happen.
Failure leads to a failed ending, and that's okay.
This approach doesn't work in

## I Hate Fast Travel
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ySLXfC7XAdU

I hate fast travel. It certainly serves a useful function, but it's a feature that's power is easy to overlook and abuse. Fast travel has practically become a given in most open-world games, which seems a little backwards because companies market their titles on massive worlds that they then let players move across in an instant with little to no cost or consequence. At its worst, it disconnects players from everything between point A and point B, shrinking worlds down to menu interactions and distracting players from the vision that developers most likely intended. It takes an expansive, non-linear experience and squeezes it into a tiny hallway where players are no longer on a journey, but rather a quick path to being done with a game. Now, the obvious counter to everything I just said is to not use it. But that actually leads me to what I hate most about fast travel. In too many titles, it feels unavoidable. And that's mostly because the act of manually traveling to a specific location is pretty boring. The way I see it, there are two major factors that play into this. The first is that a lot of open-world games have dumb movement mechanics, and the second is that there isn't enough to do when traveling to a specific location. Starting with movement, it's often very basic, and while some games try to throw in free running or vehicles, heading to a destination often just feels like pressing forward and sometimes watching a stamina bar deplete and then replenish. It's mindless. Hell, The Witcher 3 even went as far as making movement partially automated. There should be more to it than that. In my experience, third-person titles typically handle movement in more interesting ways than first-person ones. This is mostly because they tend to be less focused on realism, allowing for more possibilities. For example, Prototype, while lacking in many other areas, excelled in having free and fluid movement when traveling around the city. Stringing together different powers to avoid touching the ground was satisfying, and it took a hell of a lot more effort than just pressing forward. Movement in this and other games like Infamous, Arkham City, and Sunset Overdrive become challenges in seeing how long one can go without touching the ground, which adds an entire new layer to traversal. Giving players more things around a map to interact with and more ways to interact with them is important in making movement less tedious. It's also important to give players a reason to manually travel. A great example of this can be found in Oblivion, where running and jumping are both tied to skills that level up the more they are used. This makes travel feel like it progresses a character by acting as a reward for not just skipping over everything. In general, it seems pointless to have giant worlds if moving across them is both joyless and unrewarding. And this leads me into my second point. There isn't enough to do when moving toward a specific destination. I want to be clear, I'm not saying that there aren't a lot of things to do in most open world games, because there certainly are. However, I have two very different mindsets for when I'm exploring versus when I'm traveling. When I'm exploring, things like checking out caves, chilling with locals, and battling fords of enemies are all great times. But when I'm traveling to complete a quest, I have very little interest in doing things that aren't directly going to help me complete that quest. So for a player like me, all of those cool things become non-factors. In open world games, the conventional wisdom in making heading to an objective more interesting is to have quick interactions that keep players entertained without slowing them down too much, which plenty of games try to do, but often struggle to pull off. Mad Max does a decent job with this by having different outposts that players can take out from their car, along with random events like dust storms that they need to avoid. The same idea can be seen in pretty much every JRPG ever in the form of random encounters. What winds up being the issue with these examples is, like anything else, they start to feel very samey over time. Having a mercenary say, pay a toll or die, might be interesting when it first happens, but experiencing it for a second and third time lessens its effectiveness. To avoid players burning out, these events need to be frequent and diverse. This is extremely important to do with games that consistently have players travel back and forth to the same locations. Some quests intentionally have players go to out of the way and difficult to reach places that are then revisited multiple times. Like in Skyrim, the main quest has players travel to High Hrothgar on more than one occasion, which stops being fun after the first trip. Places that need to be returned to frequently should be centralized and easy to get to. In theory, Fallout 4 does a pretty good job with this by having Diamond City located in the center of the map. With that said, when playing, I found myself returning to my home base far more often, which was in the starting location at the top left. All of this really comes down to improving how games approach world and quest design. With open world games being so huge, players spend a lot of time traveling from quest marker to quest marker. I would like to see quests put a bigger focus on how to get somewhere rather than just getting there. The Witcher 3 does some interesting things in this regard with its implementation of the Witcher Sense, which is used for tracking in various quests. In the end, it is just another thing that pops up on the screen to follow, but it makes sense contextually and it focuses on a smaller scale, making the moment to moment travel more interesting than chasing a dot in the distance. But this issue as a whole isn't something that can be solved solely by character abilities. Worlds need to change as well. Although it would slightly impede on players' freedom, a good way to do this would be by making certain areas only accessible by various travel-based quests. Instead of being told to talk to this person in this place, I'd find it more interesting if quest descriptions were closer to, figure out how to get to this place, here are some reliable options. Maybe there's a ferry that leads to a town and the player would be given a free ride if they helped protect it. Or maybe there's a cave that's the most direct path to the same town, but it's the home to a big old monster. For this to work and still give players agency, there would need to be multiple paths like this to every location, and ideally, new options would open up to replace old ones. This would break up travel so it isn't just one long, boring trek, and it would make worlds feel more than just cities surrounded by big, open, empty spaces that reuse the same assets over and over. In the end, there isn't just one solution for making travel less boring in open world titles. It depends heavily on the type of game, so certain ideas I've suggested might work great in one, but make little to no sense in another. I don't think that fast travel should be completely eliminated from games, because it gives players the option to play how they want to. With that said, I do think it needs to have stricter limitations. First and foremost, there should really be an in-game reason that explains why fast travel is possible. It could be magic, it could be a train, just anything other than it being a spot that has already been visited. Secondly, there needs to be a consequence. A lot of games will have time pass, but players don't actually lose anything. It needs to either cost money, or have the player miss out on an opportunity, or put the player in a potentially dangerous situation. Lastly, there need to be set spots that players can travel to and from. Being able to travel from anywhere to anywhere is a bit ridiculous, and it also renders other systems, like encumbrance, nearly useless. Fast travel is not inherently bad, and in theory, it lets players approach a game at their own pace and in their own way. It makes games more accessible to more types of players, which is a good thing. I just wish it didn't come at the cost of making other parts of the game so damn tedious.

## Inside and Character Motivation
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IGhlABrNhDg

I just finished playing Inside by Playdead, and it has me thinking a lot about character motivation. More specifically, how my assumption of what motivated the main character was drastically different from what actually did. Over the span of just a few minutes, my perception of him shifted immensely, and it wasn't because he grew as a character, but rather that I began to understand him and his intentions better. Throughout the majority of the game, I assumed that the boy simply wanted to survive, and he'd do this by escaping from the terrifying dystopian society where almost everything wants him dead. But near the end, as the boy moves through the research facility and comes face to face with the giant blob of flesh and limbs connected to plugs that bear a strong resemblance to the mind control helmets used earlier, part of his actual purpose became clear to me. He's been trying to get to the blob the whole time. Traveling all the way to what feels like this society's center of operations, finding a way inside of the blob's tank, and taking off the cords attached to it aren't accidents. They're what the character intended to do from the start. Now, I'm not going to claim to be completely certain of the boy's motivations, because I'm not. But based on what's presented, the blob seems to have control over a large portion of the population, and either the boy is trying to disconnect it to take away its hold over the world, or the blob is controlling the boy the entire time in order to free itself. Due to the secret ending that shows the boy unplugging what looks like a computer terminal wired to a mind control device, and then folding into the same position that the human husks do when they aren't being controlled, it's most likely the latter. And this threw me for a loop, because I was so convinced that the boy wanted to get away, but in reality, he didn't. Now, this kind of twist isn't revolutionary, and it's been explored in all types of media. One of the most notable examples of it in a video game, and the one I keep coming back to when thinking about Inside, is Bioshock, with the reveal that Atlas, who acts as a guide to the main character throughout the majority of the game, is actually controlling him with the trigger phrase, would you kindly. This acts as a sort of meta-commentary about player control, and following a game's instructions blindly, and Inside treads a lot of the same ground. But what sets it apart from Bioshock and other similar examples is how it establishes its twist. See, Bioshock explicitly lies to the player. Atlas manipulates the main character, and sets objectives for him to complete, which in turn manipulates the player into thinking that this is the right thing to do. But Inside doesn't really lie to the player. It doesn't even set an actual objective. It only implies one. Inside's absence of dialogue makes it a story told entirely through movement. So, the action that takes place in the first ten minutes established my expectations for the rest of the game. This starts with the boy clambering down a small cliff in the middle of a forest, and sneaking up to a truck loaded with people. On my first playthrough, I assumed that the boy somehow managed to avoid being rounded up, and now wanted to get as far away from the threat as possible. The rest of the section being filled with strange figures wearing masks, relentlessly chasing the kid, only served to reinforce this idea. In order to motivate players, it exploits one of the most primal and powerful emotions. Fear. Every close call, every moment spent hidden behind something, and even every gruesome way that the boy can die, pushed me to solely focus on surviving. And because of this, I assumed the boy shared the same focus. After he becomes a part of the blob, I realize that I misread the introduction entirely. In this section, and the game as a whole, the kid moves with purpose and confidence that goes beyond how a person simply trying to survive would act. When I looked back at the first scene, I realized that he isn't trying to hide from the truck, he's trying to follow it. I held onto this feeling that the kid wanted to get away from the weird authoritarian government that's controlling everything. But the game starts in an extremely remote location, and the character only moves closer and closer to civilization and the center of it all. Despite all these warning signs, I never wondered what I was doing when playing, because I thought I knew. I certainly had questions about the world, but I didn't have all that many about the character himself, because he clearly had purpose. I just didn't actually know what that purpose was. I admire the subtlety of this kind of storytelling. It plays with and understands the assumptions that players will make, but it doesn't do it explicitly, and it allows players to have different interpretations of the main character's motivation. Instead of feeling like a passive audience member, I felt involved in the story being crafted, and I think that's something a lot of people want to feel when playing games. This isn't the first time something like this has been done before, but regardless, I'm impressed by how well Playdead manipulated the way I viewed the main character and the game as a whole with... movement.

## Shhh...I've Never Played Sonic The Hedgehog
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ve0XW1Ao22g

Maintaining a long-running video game franchise is a pretty difficult task to pull off. As a series ages, a lot of things start to get in the way. Development teams lose members who have been critical to the franchise's success, gaming trends change, forcing devs to adapt or run the risk of becoming stale and irrelevant, and nostalgia makes fans sensitive to any changes made to what they originally fell in love with, leading to public outcry over just about anything. There are so many difficult questions with unclear answers that developers are faced with, and unfortunately there are a lot of cases where these questions end up being approached in the wrong way. Cue Sonic the Hedgehog. The past decade for Sonic has been shaky at best. Every step forward seems to be followed with a much more memorable step back, and it's left a lot of the fanbase divided on what's good, what's bad, and what's wanted for the future. Sonic is in a place where the past is really the only thing that a lot of people think is worth talking about, so that's what fans focus on. The glory days. The time when the most compelling thing about the franchise wasn't its Twitter account. Namely, back when Sonic was 2D. And this is an era that I completely missed. Not jumping in until the Adventure games, I didn't experience the rise of this series. And while I enjoyed Sonic Adventure 2, I don't know that I can say I've actually ever played a good Sonic game. For me, Adventure 2 was like The Phantom Menace or Fun Dip. Pretty great when I was 11, but now it just leaves me with a stomachache and a severe sense of self-doubt. In general, it's become really popular to hate on Sonic, so I want to figure out for myself what the deal with this series is, and just as much how this whole thing got started. So it's time to admit that I'm Sonic the Hedgehog. After 25 years, the Sonic canon has become so confusing and convoluted that at times it seems like it's ripped straight from fanfiction.net. So seeing it in its simplest form was actually really refreshing. Pretty much Sonic is just trying to save animals from Dr. Eggman, who's turning them into robots. It is certainly still stupid, but it's the kind of stupid that I like. Opposed to... I'm Sonic! Sonic the Hedgehog! Anyway, I found the first stage, Green Hill Zone, to be surprisingly familiar. I think it's because whenever I hear people talk about Sonic's level design, this stage is almost always mentioned. It's highly celebrated, and for pretty good reason, as it solidly sets up the main elements promised by Sega in their original marketing. A spirited protagonist, a detailed and colorful environment, and of course, a lot of speed. I was immediately intrigued by each stage having multiple paths to the finish. There are a lot of layers, and new players will most likely wind up at the bottom, which is almost always the slowest way to the end. Just seeing the different paths incentivizes replaying the levels to find faster routes. All in all, these stages are relatively easy, which lets players move through them quickly, satisfying the promise of the title. For all of these reasons, Green Hill Zone is a pretty great first set of stages. However, this actually ends up being one of the biggest issues with Sonic 1. Green Hill Zone is really as good as it gets. For the most part, the theming of each zone is pretty top-notch. For instance, Labyrinth Zone, while one of my least favorite to play, was definitely my favorite to look at, which was a nice little consolation. But although the zones are drastically different from each other, there isn't a whole lot of variation between the stages in each zone. Most of them get very samey very quickly, as certain elements seem to just be copied and pasted onto different parts of each level. I ended up feeling like I was running through the same loop over and over, which got tiring pretty quickly. However, the biggest issue is that with the exception of maybe Starlight Zone, none of the other zones are all that well built around Sonic's speed. Marble Zone is especially frustrating because it comes just after learning the basics of how to move quickly, and instead of being allowed to really start running fast, I had to wait. A lot. Really, every zone, even the ones that I thought were pretty solid, seemed to be at odds in some way with Sonic's movement, which is where a lot of my problems with the game stem from. While playing Sonic 1, I noticed that there's an important difference between a character feeling fast and a player feeling fast. Other than obviously the speed at which they move, a character feeling fast is mostly about appearances. So in this case, things like Sonic's running animation, the speed at which the screen scrolls, and the empty areas where players only need to hold right without worrying about hitting any obstacles all add to Sonic seeming fast. But feeling fast as a player is almost entirely about fluidity. The actual speed of the character, while still a factor, becomes secondary, and instead what matters is being able to think quickly in order to move without interruption. I never felt fast as a player while playing Sonic 1. I found the time between seeing an obstacle and running into that obstacle to be far too short to react to. Other than me being bad at video games, this is mainly because the camera that follows Sonic is too close to him, and he's in the center of the screen when he should be on the far left of it. A setup like this might cut it for a slower character, but Sonic needs more space to work with to account for his speed. I think this was done to make it seem like Sonic covers more ground than he actually does, but it really only ends up slowing down his movement. This makes enemies and obstacles operate on a, hey, remember this is here next time basis, which is a bummer because what makes speed interesting is maintaining momentum, not losing it. It's possible to feel fast as a player in Sonic 1, but achieving this comes from memorization instead of true responsiveness. With that said, due to the game's difficulty, players will most likely get a fair amount of game overs and need to restart, causing them to eventually get pretty familiar with the stages. But I find this approach to be much more frustrating and boring than just being given the chance to react. In general, the level design in Sonic 1 isn't all that intuitive for a first timer. There are spots where it's difficult to tell if the direction changed or if you're just moving backwards on an alternate path, and there are too many points where levels transition from fast sections to instant death pit sections. I started to realize that the only way I stood a chance at beating this game was by moving slowly, which Sonic isn't all that good at doing and more importantly, isn't all that fun. At low speeds, Sonic just feels sluggish. His acceleration is painfully slow, and he's far too floaty and slippery for precise platforming, which there ends up being a lot of. All of this makes it become a game about patience and caution instead of one about speed and carefreeness. On subsequent playthroughs, it was easier and much more enjoyable, but its relatively high skill floor makes getting to the end for the first time incredibly frustrating. Surprisingly, one of my favorite things about Sonic 1 actually ended up being Dr. Eggman. The boss fights with him are okay. To be fair, most 2D platformers that focus more on movement than combat have subpar bosses. Regardless, I like that each battle incorporates some element of its own. So like how the fight in Marble Zone has a lava pit in the middle, and the one in Starlight Zone uses the seesaws and spiky balls. It was a nice way to vary up the fights. But what I really like about Eggman is that he's such a fucking goon. His character design is hilarious, and seeing him in a context where he's not just spitting out generic bad guy lines is actually really refreshing. Here, his comedy derives solely from visual gags, which isn't something I've seen the 3D games pull off very well. I really love that everything I needed to know about him I learned in the first fight. He's a mechanical genius who is also a bumbling idiot. Where some villains are great because they're so despicable you can't help but appreciate them, Eggman is great because he's just straight up likable. At least in this game. While looking at any game, considering when it released is extremely important in understanding why certain design choices were made. Sonic 1 is very much a reflection of what the gaming industry was like in the early 90s, which was a time where there weren't thousands of cheap and worthwhile games to play. We don't really consume titles in the same way that we used to. Having replay value now is dependent on things like diverse character builds, worthwhile side quests, and procedurally or randomly generated levels. But back then it had less to do with the contents of a title and more to do with there being nothing else to play. So while playing a game like Sonic 1 that calls for you to practically memorize the level's layout in order to move fluidly is frustrating in today's landscape, it makes a lot of sense for a game made in 1991 marketed towards kids. It's meant to be played over and over again. It's meant to be perfected. I think that a lot of people who look back fondly on Sonic 1 didn't just beat it once, but beat it so many times that they've lost track. Because of this, they most certainly would have played Green Hill Zone more than any other, leaving that as their impression of the game. I'm pretty sure I get why people liked and still like Sonic 1, but with that said, it really wasn't for me. I don't have the patience or time to actually get good at Sonic, and

## Until Dawn: Fear and the Unknown
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tim1iZ82jyI

I play a lot of what's best classified as choice-based games. Focused more on the navigation of a story than conventional gameplay, these titles let players control certain aspects of a narrative in order to weave fairly personalized and unique experiences. As the primary mechanic is making story-based decisions, they rely on providing morally ambiguous choices with heavy emotional weight tied to them. When playing, we're supposed to second-guess ourselves and submit to the natural fear of having to make a choice. More specifically, the fear of making the wrong choice, leading to all sorts of unwanted and unexpected consequences. What makes games and choices like these memorable is rarely the outcome, but rather how the deciding moment makes you feel, and this is something that Until Dawn captures effectively. Placed in charge of the actions of a group of teenagers who could only really exist in a horror story, you either become their savior or angel of death. However, especially on the first playthrough, the natural instinct is to keep them alive for two simple reasons. The first is that this is a game and typically players want to win games. Letting characters die is usually not a good way to do this. The other is that, for the most part, the characters are likable enough to want to see them survive to the end. They're all flawed and in certain combinations almost insufferable, but as each get their spotlight, likable traits come to the surface. Caring about these characters, or at the very least their survival, is what creates suspense when each choice comes along. There's no game over screen, so every decision is permanent, and given the genre, the majority of them feel like they could get any character killed. Even in low pressure situations, the existence of meters that track the changes in character traits and relationship statuses based off certain actions creates a fear of causing strife between the cast that could potentially lead to their demise. Of course, the majority of suspense derives from the high intensity moments, where the lives of characters seemingly hang in the balance, eliciting a feeling of paralysis as you stare at the screen, not being able to form full sentences, watching the short amount of time you have to make a decision quickly fade away. What fuels these moments is the uncertainty of what will come next. The unknown has always been closely associated with horror, and Until Dawn runs with this concept from the very beginning. The intro cinematic promises that every choice will have a consequence that drastically changes the game's outcome, but like many games that promise this sort of thing, that's not actually the case. The majority of choices don't have much bearing on the arc of the primary story. They'll change up locations of scenes, how conversations play out, the amount of clothing a character has on, but very few, especially ones in the first half, actually affect what happens. That isn't to say that your input is entirely unimportant, because in the end, your choices do dictate who lives and who doesn't, which is certainly significant. But the only effect that a character's death actually has on the story is that he or she will be absent from it. So if Matt dies early on, it doesn't affect the other characters' abilities to complete future tasks or events, it just means Matt won't be there anymore. The plot pushes forward pretty much in the same way regardless. No matter what, the last scene will be in this house. No matter what, Mike and Sam will be there. And no matter what, it'll end up on fire. Admittedly, once you come to the realization that the story doesn't branch out as far as it promises, a lot of what the game has going for it is lost. But unless you're overly cynical about Until Dawn delivering on his butterfly effect promise, this won't be noticeable until later playthroughs. Which raises the question, is it important to actually have control, or is it enough to just have the illusion of control? If you're the type who will go through it multiple times to see every outcome, then you will more than likely be disappointed when your persistence goes relatively unrewarded. But if you're the type who only plans to do one playthrough, the illusion of control should be enough to give you the sense of agency that you're looking for in a game of this nature. For this to work, the illusion must be carefully created and cleverly maintained. In Until Dawn, the illusion of control is first established by the aforementioned introduction to the butterfly effect, and is further supported by character's dialogue and also this screen in the options menu that shows an overwhelming amount of choices and possibilities. These things set the tone that you are seemingly in charge of how the game will play out. What's more complex is how the illusion is maintained. Some of the characters who play a more minor role in the overall story can die fairly early if you mess up inputs or make clearly unadvisable choices. This is meant to show players who are either intentionally making poor decisions or just being too slow on the draw that they can and will be punished. Granted, most players won't experience these deaths on the first playthrough as they're likely compelled to keep everyone alive. For these players, the devs added a few moments early on where, after a difficult choice, certain characters will seemingly die. As it turns out, these are scripted events where the character will later be revealed to be alright. All of these are meant to throw you off balance and make you assume that you messed up, so regardless of how you play, the effect is the same. You feel responsible for what seems like the biggest way a person could affect a story. The death of a character. If you can get someone killed, it's easy to make the jump that you can influence the narrative in any way. And that is a powerful feeling. In reality, Until Dawn ends up being a train ride where you do control when certain characters get off, but where it starts and ends is out of your hands. It might seem like a character dying is a huge deal, but when the emotional fallout is explored for at maximum 10 seconds, it starts to feel like an afterthought. Despite this, for the first playthrough, the developers successfully created the feeling that any moment could make or break the story. So I felt fear, joy, and a lot in between as what seemed like my own decisions manifested into a personalized narrative. The promise of the butterfly effect is a lie, but I don't think it was a malicious one made to trick consumers. Rather, it's a playful one meant to set the expectations of players. Although I'm interested in seeing a game that actually has drastic deviations based off your input, the way you'd feel while playing something like that wouldn't be far different from how you'd feel with just thinking that it's like that. Similar to many other stories in this genre, once the mystery of what's lurking around the corner is revealed, Until Dawn loses a lot of the fear and dread that goes along with playing it. Only here, instead of a monster or serial killer, what's actually around the corner is the fact that your choices don't count for much. But that'll never stop that they felt like they did, even if it was just for a moment.

## Psychonauts: Maturity From Immaturity
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vnJrjZSMTCE

When thinking about mature storytelling, stories made for adults are usually what come to mind. However, to assume that media directed towards children can't also contain mature themes hugely undersells it. The most universal pieces of children's media are as applicable if not more so to adults than kids. For instance, more adults cry during this scene than kids did. This is due to them being able to view the story through the lens of their personal experiences growing up. A moment that a kid finds funny or heartwarming, an adult can as well, but for completely different reasons and with an entirely different perspective. Ultimately, the maturity of these stories is deeply rooted in immaturity, and Psychonauts is a prime example of this idea. Its child-led cast and summer camp setting are aimed to appeal primarily to kids, but the theming and writing make it approachable to anyone. This is most apparent by the great amount of thought that was put into creating such a deep and diverse set of levels. Most platformers share a handful of similar settings for stages that appear frequently, creating fatigue and staleness in the genre. Psychonauts largely avoids this issue by having levels with immense amounts of complexity that are rarely found in video games of this nature. The basic premise of having each stage take place inside of a character's mind really allowed Double Fine to push the boundaries of variety. Its stages range from a haunted theater that puts on low-rate performances, to a city run by fish creatures under attack by a giant human. These ideas aren't unheard of, but in the context of a video game, they are relatively foreign. Diverse level design, however impressive, doesn't necessarily play into creating an accessible and wide palette for the audience. It comes down to how Double Fine intrinsically ties these complex ideas into not only environments, but to the experiences of its wider player base. From real-world imagery, both innocent and complex, the stage The Milkman Conspiracy encapsulates a broad set of concepts very much understanding of the wide range of its audience. This stage is centered around Boyd, a former security guard who falls into some bad times and instead of looking for a new job, decides to torch his old one. Wrecked with guilt, he's admitted into an insane asylum, and in his fragile state, Boyd is manipulated into guarding the asylum gates, where he rambles incoherently about the Milkman. Upon entering Boyd's mind, a Cold War-inspired 1950s-esque town is introduced, that has the ever-present fear of being constantly monitored and punished for the slightest misstep looming over it. There are government agents aptly named the G-Men posing as ordinary people, seemingly inanimate objects with cameras in them, and members of the Girl Scout equivalent, the Rainbow Squirts, who are clearly hiding something. As someone who took U.S. history, the connection to McCarthyism and the Red Scare is pretty clear. No one can be trusted, and even the smallest perceived association with communism, or in this case, the Milkman, will lead to loads of trouble. These real-world inspirations would probably fly right over a kid's head. However, young players can still comprehend the ideas at play here. Paranoia, unjust persecution in the name of protection, invasion of privacy, all of these can be boiled down to unfairness, which kids feel they are constantly the victim of. And honestly, without meaning to, parents often become the ultimate G-Men. Many are overly fearful of what their kids are up to, reluctant to let them do certain activities because they could get hurt, and unabashedly snoopy. Kids might not understand how it ties into governmental control, but they sure as hell get how it relates to parental control. More importantly, they see how ridiculous this process can be. Although the target audience won't fully understand what is being parodied, based off the established tone, they can infer a few things. The G-Men want control, they aren't as sneaky as they think they are, and their process for finding questionable figures is flawed. The G-Men display their uselessness with uninspired cover stories, and a complete lack of understanding on how to do the jobs they're pretending to do. To someone with knowledge of past and present government surveillance, they can laugh at how this level shows the hypocrisy of people in power trying to protect the masses by putting them under a microscope. And someone without that knowledge can laugh at a guy in a fancy suit humping a plunger, which really is getting the same point across. People with unchecked power can become really stupid. Even more depth can be found when taking into consideration that this is all a delusion inside of Boyd's head. The Milkman represents the part of him that snapped and lit up his old place of business. Despite trying to disassociate from the Milkman, Boyd never is fully separated from him and begins to lose his own identity in the process. He can't escape the pressures that originally led to his dark and destructive side taking over. These pressures, now manifested as G-Men, always creep up on him, making him teeter on the brink of becoming a destructive force that can only be quelled by delivering his hot milk. I need to rewrite that, probably. While this is relatable to most, it is more meaningful to an older audience because on some level, they probably felt a similar way. And by that I mean being under a lot of pressure, not delivering hot milk. But that too. Psychonauts respects its audience, no matter what age they are. The story and themes don't belittle them or penalize them for not having previous knowledge. Instead, it offers levels of understanding that provides different types of enjoyment to different players. There are themes that take a bit of digging to understand, and this subtle type of storytelling feels far more mature than ones that throw these ideas in an audience's face. Hidden beneath goofy animations and names like Rainbow Squirts, there is a lot of depth in great storytelling in Psychonauts. It further proves that mature stories don't need to be overtly mature. In fact, when complex ideas are hidden in stories based around simplicity, it gives them an opportunity to shine brighter. It breaks down our expectations and leaves us in a vulnerable place where understanding is a bit clearer.

## Shhh...I've Never Played Mega Man X
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2oopnYvGOk0

Pretty much since video games became powerful enough to show somewhat detailed characters, people have felt connected to them. Just about everybody has a character they feel linked to, creating an affinity that transcends the game itself and reminds the person of the time in his or her life that is most associated with that character. For most people it is probably Mario, but for many others it might be Sonic, Pikachu, Crash Bandicoot, or if your parents didn't love you enough to buy good games it's probably Bubsy. These characters were drawn on the backs of hundreds of thousands of school notebooks, etched into bathroom stalls, and tattooed onto actual human skin to act as a constant reminder of the meaning that these characters have. And over the past couple years I've noticed that Mega Man elicits these reactions from fans as much if not more than any other character I've seen. Which makes me assume that something must be pretty special about this series. So it's probably about time that I actually play a Mega Man game, huh? Shh, I've never played Mega Man X. People really love Mega Man. Like, a lot. Most of the games are touted for incredible level design, precise controls, and sweet looking character models. Also for being really hard. The main thing that held me back from getting into the series was simply not knowing where to start. I wanted to begin with the original Mega Man, but I was assured that I should only do that if I wanted to be miserable, so I decided to jump into the series with the well-loved Mega Man X. Will it be any good? I mean, probably. Everyone says it is, so, you know. Going into a series without any background information can be a bit confusing, but I realized pretty quickly that all I needed to know about this series was that it's about good robots who fight bad robots. And that's pretty much where this game picks up. The intro screen has a message about how a robot named X was trained extensively to be able to distinguish right from wrong. But he shouldn't be activated because despite possessing great potential to help the world, the risk of him harming a human would be too high. Then you start the game and there's X. Without showing any actual depictions of how serious the situation is, it is immediately clear that things must be bad simply based off X being there. He's established as a last resort, so his presence must be the response to something truly terrible. That's really all the motivation I needed to get invested. With that said, there is a fair amount of vital story information that is presented only in the game manual. This creates a slight disconnect between what the player thinks the story is about based on gameplay and what the story is actually about. To be fair, this was made in the era where developers were really just starting to add more story elements into actual games. But it still seemed like an odd choice to have part of the story be told from an external source. However, I didn't really want all that many story elements. Anytime there was even a short cutscene, I got a little annoyed that I wasn't just playing. This isn't because I don't like narrative-based games, because I really do. But there's something about Mega Man that made me not care about anything but the gameplay. It's been pretty well established that Mega Man X is one of those games that teaches you how to play simply by playing it. Enemy placement, various set pieces, and power-up demonstrations inform players of the various ways they can tackle a level. And having finally played it, I can say that, yeah, it does this. Granted, most games, especially 2D platformers, that are worth a damn do as well. But because of the solid design, Mega Man X has a ton of what I'll call My Bad moments. Oh, these light things are flying through the stage. I bet one will fly through right as I'm trying to make... Oh, my bad. Oh, Storm Eagle flies in the same pattern. If I make sure... My bad. They throw pickaxes. My bad. Falling platforms. My bad. Helmet. My bad. My bad. My bad. My bad. It's hard, and most of the time it's your fault, which makes you feel even worse. Mega Man X seems like a simple side-scroller, but like many other platformers, if you blindly push through a level without stopping to think, you're gonna get killed. You need to take in the surroundings of a level and apply what you know about enemies in the game to be able to beat it. And when you finally do figure it all out, it feels really good and makes exploring the levels a joy. In Mega Man X, you get to choose the order in which you complete the levels. Theoretically, you could beat them in any order, but some paths make more sense than others. Not knowing these paths, I bashed my head against a few levels before making any progress. Eventually, I came across Chill Penguin Stage, which is most likely the intended first level because Chill Penguin is a relatively easy boss, and unlike any other stage, there's a mandatory upgrade on the intended path. As is customary in Mega Man games, defeating a boss awards you with a new weapon, which can unlock secrets and make certain areas and bosses much easier to beat, creating a somewhat natural path of progression. With that said, it wasn't all that obvious what this path was. It still took a lot of trial and error, and for a less skilled player like myself, it was really frustrating to get to a boss and not be able to beat him because I didn't have the right weapon. This made me want to look up a strategy guide to find the best path, which really shouldn't have to happen. It would have been nice if there had been hints spread throughout the game that made the preferred path clear. One of the most interesting features of Mega Man X is as you beat some levels, other levels change. Like after beating Chill Penguin, the hot goo, or lava, I guess, in Flame Mammoth Stage is frozen. After beating Launch Octopus, Sting Chameleon Stage is flooded, and after beating Storm Eagle, Spark Mandrill Stage has blackouts. Some of these changes make it possible to reach secrets, and they also generally make portions of the level easier. This element is cool, but I do have a few issues with it. First being, there is no real explanation as to why the levels change. Like, why would Chill Penguin die and freeze just this specific area? I guess maybe he was able to control the cold, and without him alive, the area freezes because no one could stop it from spreading anymore, but that's stupid. It would have been way cooler if these changes were triggered by using the weapons received from beating the boss instead of them just happening automatically. Like on Flame Mammoth Stage, they could have had you shoot the hot goo to freeze it. Oh, that was a sentence. On Sting Chameleon Stage, they could have added a dam that the homing missile could destroy. This would have made the changes feel more like a result of things you've accomplished instead of just something that happens. I also felt that there weren't enough of the level changes. Honestly, I wanted beating every stage to bring about change in another. Furthermore, I would have liked if some of the changes made levels more challenging. This way, the player could create so many viable and varied paths to the end. Games are often about the journey, and while Mega Man X gives more variation on its journey than most games, I would have loved to see even more. After clearing the first eight levels, a new set of stages open up. Before I jumped into them, though, I went back to get all the collectibles and upgrades that I missed the first time through. This consisted of getting permanent health upgrades, sub-tanks that restore life when used, and a few more suit upgrades, the most important of which increased the power of X's blaster and the strength of his armor. What I love about the upgrades in Mega Man X is that most of them are rewards for exploration and skilled play, opposed to something that you just get. The majority are tucked away in each level and guarded by some challenge. It might be timing a difficult jump or defeating a strong foe, but it almost always feels deserved. Once I was equipped with everything I could get, I was on to the final stages. At this point, I was under the impression that Vile would be the final boss based off how bad he kicked my ass in the beginning. In fact, I thought Vile was actually named Sigma because Zero says the name right after beating him. Due to all this, I was a little confused when the new level had this guy's face on it, who clearly isn't Vile. This, as most of you probably know, is actually Sigma. There's a fair amount of information about his villainy in the manual, but as far as someone just playing the game is concerned, Vile is set up to be the primary antagonist when he isn't. This would have been a fine bait and switch had it been intended, but it's pretty clear that it was not. Anyway, the first new stage ramps up the difficulty a bit, primarily because of this section. Even after I realized I could use the charged rolling shield to kill all the enemies that came my way, I still struggled. Aside from this part, the rest of the Sigma levels aren't all that memorable or difficult. Pretty much these stages consist of fighting all the bosses you took on earlier in the game for a second time, along with a few new ones added in. I found this fairly easy because I knew all the bosses' weaknesses and had all the upgrades, but it was a lot of fun to quickly dominate all the enemies that gave me a lot of trouble earlier. While this section is a little underwhelming, it does a good job of making it clear that everything is ramping up to something bigger. And that is where Sigma comes in, who, as a final boss should be, is the

## What Mass Effect Could Learn From Darkest Dungeon
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QkD3mowG45M

Mass Effect offers a fairly deep and unique experience. The series as a whole has solid gameplay, intriguing character interactions, and an immense universe. With that said, those aspects don't build off of each other as well as they could. See, there's a clear distinction between combat sections and role-playing sections. The typical flow of the game is Commander Shepard talks about doing a thing, then does said thing, and follows that with talking about what happened while doing the thing. Role-playing might be placed in the middle of a combat section, or vice versa, but they still feel like two different phases of the game. This isn't inherently bad. It'd be pretty unwieldy to focus on picking dialogue options while charging at enemies head-on. The issue stems from the two sections having very little to do with each other in terms of rewards and consequences. A choice made through role-playing might affect combat by determining the enemies you face or if an NPC helps you in a battle, but these consequences really don't have much weight to them. The actual consequences of a choice is almost always addressed in later role-playing sections. On the other side of things, a choice made in combat pretty much never have an impact on role-playing. In a series that is supposed to be based around choice and consequence, it stands to reason that the things that happen in and out of battle should have a direct relationship to one another. This is where I think the next Mass Effect entry could learn something from the indie roguelike game Darkest Dungeon. Darkest Dungeon is centered around the affliction system. Essentially, every time you bring a party into a dungeon, characters can take two different types of damage, physical and mental. If characters take too much physical damage, they die permanently, and if they take too much mental damage, they typically become afflicted with a negative trait. Characters gain stress from various things like not eating enough food, having low torchlight, falling into a trap, or being hit by certain enemy attacks. When a character has an affliction, he or she might decide to not attack for a round or refuse to use any healing items. The afflicted character will also cause the stress levels of the rest of the party to go up because of his or her bad attitude. All in all, having an afflicted party member is no good. Adversely, a character can have a heroic response to the stress bar being filled up, which provides a bonus that buffs the character and helps reduce the party's stress levels. Along with afflictions and heroics, party members can also develop positive and negative quirks. Quirks raise and lower stats and also dictate what characters can and can't do. While exploring, quirks are developed from interacting with objects, battling enemies, or retreating from a dungeon. For example, if a rabid dog bites one of your characters, he might contract rabies, which raises attack but lowers accuracy. This entire system makes you constantly make decisions about the well-being of your party. Do you open a treasure and risk it being trapped? Do you continue into an unexplored room when your party is teetering on the brink of insanity? It makes every decision have weight to it, and it doesn't stop there. These decisions carry over to other parts of the game. Like Mass Effect, Darkest Dungeon also has two distinct phases. Once your party returns from questing, you spend time recuperating in town. Here, characters' health gets regenerated automatically, but their stress levels do not. To lower a character's stress, you have to send him or her to get treated at various establishments in town. Treatments lower stress significantly, but when characters are being treated, they have to sit out the next quest. Doing this also costs gold and runs the risk of giving your characters more quirks. Like if you send a character to the brothel, she might contract syphilis and take a stat penalty. Or if you send a character to gamble, he could get caught cheating and not be allowed to gamble in town in the future. This is where the combat phase and role-playing phase really start to overlap. It gets even deeper when you take into consideration how the game handles resource management. Along with paying for stress-reducing treatments, gold can also be used to have quirks removed, buy items to use in dungeons, and upgrade armor, weapons, and attacks. However, gold is not an overly abundant resource, so spending it on one thing usually means that you won't have enough to spend it on another. You also collect heirlooms while adventuring, which can be used to permanently upgrade the various buildings in town. Again, like gold, when you use them to upgrade one thing, you probably won't have enough to upgrade another. All of this creates a huge set of difficult questions to consider when in and out of a dungeon. And that's because the two phases work in tandem. Quirks that you get in combat affect actions when in town and vice versa. They're clearly different phases, but they need each other to exist. While in Mass Effect, combat and role-playing can almost be two different games. But if they implemented a system like Darkest Dungeon, the relationship between the two phases would work together instead of as two separate entities. The characters in your squad could each have a stress bar and also develop quirks as various things happen during missions and conversations. For instance, if one of your squadmates gets tackled and punched in the face by a Krogan on a mission, then maybe she would become afraid of Krogan and do less damage when fighting against them. In turn, this would cause her to become distrustful of the Krogan member in your squad, which might lead to problems in the future. Or maybe something you say while role-playing would distress a character in the party and make him feel hopeless, like it isn't worthwhile to fight. This might make him move slower and lag behind while on missions and be erratic during conversations. When these issues arise, you'd have to figure out different ways for characters to reduce stress and eliminate negative quirks. Maybe you'd be able to talk a squad member down if you had high enough charisma. Or maybe they just need to get a solid kill on the battlefield to work their confidence back up. But in some cases, the easiest solution might be throwing money at the problem. Working to keep your team members from becoming afflicted would be vital. Leaving a squadmate's affliction untreated for long enough could lead to the character abandoning or betraying the team, getting killed, or overusing valuable resources. All of this would also give a solid incentive to use more characters on your team. While playing the Mass Effect trilogy, I pretty much always chose the characters I thought were the coolest to join me on missions. The only time I really used other characters was in Mass Effect 2 to do all the loyalty missions. In general, Shepard does most of the work in a fight, so I didn't have much of a reason to change it up. However, with stress meters, quirks, and afflictions, it would become a necessity. Figuring out how to best utilize your squads would be a huge factor in your success. It would also lead to more interesting character interactions and make the squad feel more like a cohesive unit. Furthermore, dealing with stress and afflictions would lead to having to decide when it is best to abandon a mission. At almost any time in Darkest Dungeon, you can quit a quest, but it comes at the cost of stressing out your party and adding another quirk to their list. In the next Mass Effect game, assuming you are taking the role of a leader, this would have you make decisions that a leader would actually have to make. Do you withdraw from a mission or push forward and risk your party getting injured or even killed? In general, I don't like how most games typically handle failure that affects the narrative. In a lot of games, this type of failure occurs in a cutscene after you've done something successfully. Like in Mass Effect 3 when you beat Kai Leng, the cutscene comes and even though you are able to fight him off, you lose. This sort of thing places distance between gameplay and story. But if Mass Effect let you fail in the narrative because of a choice made in combat, it would make each phase of the game feel truly connected. A Mass Effect entry like this would be an ambitious and difficult game to make and play, but it would be a rare cohesive experience that really only games can provide. I like the end of Mass Effect 2 because it provides this cohesion to a degree. You have to decide which characters to send on certain tasks depending on their skills and their loyalty. If you make poor decisions, it could lead to squadmates and even Shepard dying. It was a neat concept that brought the two phases closer together and I'd like to see more of it. Taking some of these ideas from Darkest Dungeon would really breathe new life into the series. There are a few things that I'm not entirely sure how to implement into Mass Effect's formula. Primarily permadeath. Not that it couldn't be done, but it would have to be much harder to kill a character because a Mass Effect game can't generate random characters and still have them make a strong impact on the narrative the way Darkest Dungeon can. Also, in Darkest Dungeon there isn't really a main playable character like Shepard. Assuming the next Mass Effect game has one central character that you play as, it might be weird having missions that potentially don't include that character because he or she is recovering. In general, I'm not sure how quirks and afflictions might need to affect your character differently. A balance would need to be struck so you don't feel too much at odds with the person you are playing as. Overall, implementing concepts from Darkest Dungeon would lead to a much more cohesive and robust Mass Effect game which I would love to see. But what do you think? Would these changes make Mass Effect too hard? Would there be too much micromanaging? Would you prefer it to be more of a shooter than

## Mini-Maps Are Stupid
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4FfG-4HKoWQ

Minimaps are stupid. Okay, that isn't fair. Minimaps aren't stupid, but the way a lot of games utilize them is. Effective minimaps help show you where you are so that you can use the knowledge of your surroundings to get somewhere new. Like Legend of Zelda. The minimap shows that you're in an area and there are other areas next to it. It's simple and it works. Minimaps like this don't really tell you where to go or what's at a certain place, just that there are places you can go and where you are in relation to them. It acts as a guide without making things feel linear and it doesn't take away from your satisfaction when you stumble upon a secret. With more modern games, though, that's not the case. Like Final Fantasy XIII. The minimap shows where every enemy is and also provides the layout of an area without even letting you explore it first. It takes away the element of surprise that comes from an enemy attack and also the main drive of exploration, which is discovery. Honestly, you could just look at the minimap to play the game. You don't even need all the graphics and pretty stuff. And there lies the problem with most minimaps. You spend too much time looking at the corner of a screen and not enough time looking at the pretty stuff. It happens in Grand Theft Auto V, too. For instance, when you want to go somewhere, you set a waypoint and are provided with the most direct path to the destination on your minimap. And that is where you look. At the minimap. In a huge open world game like this, it is alright to give a player direction, but it shouldn't come at the cost of ignoring the world. This doesn't just affect traveling. It also affects gameplay. Like when you're in a car chase with the cops. Instead of looking at the action to see where they are, it is much more valuable to be consulted in the minimap, which shows their line of sight so you can best avoid them. It pretty much becomes a glorified game of asteroids. It happens in Assassin's Creed, also. There are enemy movements shown on the minimap and it provides you with which direction they're facing. You end up spending these stealthy missions looking at the corner of your screen instead of taking in the surroundings of an area, which is what you would actually do when on a stealth mission. It pulls the focus away from what is important and puts it on an uninteresting circle. Which is sometimes a square. Minimap's now provides so much information that is integral to successful gameplay, thus forcing players to become over-reliant on them. They are overwhelmingly cluttered, which is often more stressful than helpful. It makes things seem more like completing a checklist than exploring, which isn't fun. Ultimately, minimaps often make exploration feel trivial, which is far from ideal and in most cases not what the developer was aiming to do. Immersion is something that so many games say they are trying to accomplish, but I don't think that this is a way to do it. So the question becomes, what can be done to fix the issue? Honestly, I'm not sure. The best modern minimaps that I can think of are from games like Borderlands 1, Skyrim, and Fallout. They act more as compasses and give you an idea of where to go without making you rely on them too heavily. This allows for more strain from the path and in turn more surprises on your journey. I also like when games place a beacon on the screen that shows a waypoint or an objective. This can lead to screen clutter, but generally it provides direction while still letting you focus on the world. Exploration in video games should be intuitive. Honestly, minimaps kind of seem like a cop-out, a way to avoid putting detailed visual clues of where to go in a game. Clues like memorable landmarks or purposeful lighting that helps guide a player in a specific direction. A game is most effective when it gets you to do something that it wants you to do without you realizing that it wants you to do it. I understand that in a massive open world game, these sort of cues don't really translate, but I still think there is a better solution than putting it all on a minimap. But that's just what I think. Let me know what you think. Do you like how these games use minimaps? Is there a better alternative? Is it a necessary evil? Is it even an evil? Put your ideas in the comments if you want, or I don't know, do what you do. Also, I know you might be thinking, if you hate minimaps so much, then why don't you just turn them off because most games let you. And yeah, that's a good idea. I think I'll do that from now on. Thank you for watching. It has been a while since I last posted a video, and that's not because I haven't wanted to, but because of life and busyness and other obstacles that get in the way of making free stuff on YouTube. I hope to make some more videos soon and would love if you all watched them. So, see you soon. I'm Rasputin. Have a good day. Thank you.

## Final Fantasy 9: The Introduction
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oukFE68fki4

Alright, I want to talk about a Final Fantasy game that I don't think gets enough love. Everyone is so busy drooling over 6, 7, 8, and 10 that Final Fantasy 9 gets left out in the cold. There are a lot of important things about it, but I want to talk about my favorite part, the opening segment. First I'm going to go over everything that happens in it and then I'm going to go into why it's awesome. Ready? Good. The opening shot is of a ship in troubled waters. On the ship there are two women, one of which appears to be a child. Things look bad, but then it's revealed it's all a dream. The girl having the dream is the princess of Alexandria, Garnet. She walks to her window and looks out longingly. Coming into the kingdom is a giant airship that pretty much puts all other airships to shame. Badass. On the ship is a boy with a tail. This is Zidane. He enters a dark room looking for his boss and finds three of his comrades, Marcus, Cinna, and Blank, but there is no sign of their leader. Then a man with a dragon head bursts through the door and they promptly kick his ass. The mask breaks and the man wearing it is none other than their boss Baku. Their meeting begins and it is revealed that they plan to capture the princess. Original.
