Under the guise of the Tantalus Theater Company, they will give a performance of I Want to Be Your Canary, Gaia's version of Romeo and Juliet. When everyone is distracted by the performance, Zidane and Blank will sneak into her chambers, give her a sleeping potion, and take her from the castle. The plan seems solid, but the one thing I know about heists is they never go as intended. Inside the city, everyone is bustling in the streets excited for the performance by the Tantalus Theater Company. Among them is a boy in a pointed hat, Vivi. He's a klutz. Vivi has a ticket for the show and starts heading toward the booth. On his way, he gets the opportunity to meet a variety of people in the city. There's this rat kid that no matter how much you try to avoid him, he'll run into you. This walking and talking hippo named Hapal, which begs the question if every humanoid hippo has a pun in their name or if his parents are just real assholes. And these girls jumping rope that ask Vivi to join them. But it turns out that jumping rope is pretty hard. When Vivi finally does get to the booth, it is revealed that his ticket was a fake. Dejected, he walks into a back alley where he runs into the rat kid again. The kid tells him he knows a way to get Vivi into the show, but in return, Vivi must become his slave. Despite being opposed to entering such a bleak contract, it's the only way to progress, so Vivi agrees. That show better be good. The rat kid, whose name turns out to be Puck, steals the ladder and they make their way to the performance by way of the rooftops. The airship, which doubles as a stage, pulls into port and the show begins. Here we are introduced to the Queen, Brawn. It's pretty clear now that Princess Garnett is either adopted or that she's going to have a pretty rough time of it when she hits her 30s. Standing behind them is the leader of the Knights of Pluto, Steiner. He has weird eyelashes. The first act gets underway and in it there's a battle between the romantic lead Marcus, played by Marcus and his lover's father King Leo, played by Baku. An onstage battle ensues with drama, stunning combat, and even special effects. Nice touch. The battle ends and King Leo runs away. In character, Zidane tries to go after him, but Blank stops him saying that peace will come across the land if the King's daughter marries someone else. They have a sword fight and depending on the performance, the crowd will either be underwhelmed or demand an encore. Don't mind if I do. After their sword fight, Zidane and Blank rush offstage and liberate a few uniforms from some unsuspecting Knights of Pluto. They arrive at the princess's chambers when a woman in a white hood comes rushing out. Zidane questions her for a moment, but then she runs away. Knowing the woman in the white hood is actually Princess Garnett, Zidane and Blank make chase after her. Sensing something is awry, the court jesters Zorn and Thorn go to warn the queen that the princess is in danger. Their gag is they repeat what the other one says, but one says it like Yoda would, which isn't annoying at all. They report to the queen's guard Beatrix, who orders Steiner to retrieve the princess. He frantically searches the castle for her, assembling various Knights of Pluto to aid him in his search. They range from cowardly to lazy to womanizery. A great bunch. After climbing a ridiculously long set of spiral stairs, Steiner sees the princess being chased around a tower by Zidane. She jumps from the tower and grabs a streamer to swing over to the airship. Zidane follows her and so does Steiner, but with a little less luck. Once in the airship with Zidane, Garnett reveals her true identity and asks him to kidnap her. Well, that's convenient. Steiner continues to pursue the pair, and after some hijinks, they all end up on stage. Now wanting to blow their cover, they play along with the show. Garnett picks up the role of the king's daughter and Marcus's love, Cornelia. The pair embrace and ask the king to allow them to marry. He refuses, and in a fit of rage, Marcus draws a sword and makes to murder the king, but at the last second, the princess steps in front of the blade because despite everything, she still loves her father. This whole time, Steiner is too petrified by stage fright to move and doesn't seem to grasp that everything happening is part of the play. Meanwhile, Vivi and Puck move closer to the performance for a better view. However, a few Knights of Pluto see them and make chase. They run onto the stage and in a panic, Vivi shoots a fireball at the knights. In typical klutz fashion, he misses and ignites the princess's hood on fire, forcing her to throw it off and reveal to everyone now her true identity. A battle ensues between Steiner and the kidnappers, which ends with him being wounded. Knowing that they've overstayed their welcome, Baku heads to the pilot's cabin to make their escape. Not wanting them to get away, the queen orders to shoot the airship with a bunch of grappling hooks. It does a lot of damage, but somehow the ship stays afloat. In a last-ditch effort, the queen opens a cannon from behind her that shoots a giant fireball. It seems like the ship is lost, but then it pulls away from the explosion and no one is harmed. After escaping Alexandria, the ship loses steam and crashes into a forest. This is where I consider the opening segment to end and the real journey to begin. So what makes it so special? First off, it provides a safe environment to learn combat. Most of the battles are for show, which lowers the stakes, but the battles serve a greater purpose in completing the heist, which raises them again. It's a good balance between not being afraid to experiment with combat while still having each battle feel important. The intro also does a great job of setting up the world that the game takes place in. Based off the weapons, the city, and the giant airship, it is clear that this game is closer to the high fantasy roots of Final Fantasy than the previous few titles in the series. Everyone has their own preference, but I lean toward the old-timey fantasy vibe opposed to the futuristic with spaceships, sort of... The most important thing the intro does is set the tone for an interesting story with multiple compelling characters. Wazidant seems to be the main protagonist by being able to also control Vivian Steiner, it shows that their stories are equally as important. Most RPGs with a big cast of characters stick you in just one of them, and if you ever move around to someone else, it feels foreign. Here, right off the bat, we are shown that the story will be told from multiple points of view and that each character's perspective will put an interesting spin on the story. It adds a dynamic that a lot of RPGs don't have, which is characters in your party with different, and more importantly, opposing goals. By experiencing the intro from different characters' perspectives, it blurs the line between right and wrong. While playing as Zidane, it is clear that Steiner is an antagonist, but when playing as Steiner, the opposite is true. Both are the hero of their own story, which makes them interesting. Perspective is important, and maybe it's just because I'm a sucker for A Song of Ice and Fire, but using multiple points of view to tell a story, especially a fantasy story of this magnitude, seems to be the best approach. This intro sets the tone and plot for the entire story in an interesting and unique way. Experiencing the chaos of the day from multiple perspectives increases the scope of the story in a very efficient way. My one complaint is you don't play as Garnet in this introduction, which is weird because she becomes a party member and is a very important part of the story. Anyway, the introduction to Final Fantasy IX is one of my favorite in the series, and really in all of video games. It was memorable, unique, and executed almost to perfection. If you've never played Final Fantasy IX, I definitely recommend playing the entire game, but at the very least, check out the first hour because it's an awesome ride. I'm Raz Buten, and thanks for

## Shhh...I've Never Played: Super Metroid
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FyVs9t2nKY4

I've heard a lot of people say that there aren't enough video games that feature a female as the main playable character, but that can't be true. I mean, I can think of a bunch of games that I've played recently with a woman as the main playable character. Like, Lara Croft in Tomb Raider, Lightning in Final Fantasy XIII, um, you're a girl in Portal, right? Did I say Lara Croft already? Obviously there are more examples of females as main playable characters in video games, but it really is few and far between for AAA titles. I've seen many awesome female characters with prominent roles, but rarely starring ones. Sometimes these characters will get their chance to be the star in DLC or sequels, but there just aren't a ton of franchises where a woman gets to be the lead right off the bat. However, there is a series that has had an awesome female protagonist for the past 25 years, and for the most part portrays her very well. Above all, I haven't played a single game in the series. So this is when I say to you, shh, I've never played Super Metroid. For the longest time, Samus Aran was just another Smash Bros. character to me. I knew that she must come from a different series because that's kind of the point of Smash Bros., but I didn't really think about it that much. As I got older and learned about the Metroid series, it never really appealed to me. I heard that you fight space pirates, and I expected this when it really turned out to be this, which was deeply disappointing to me. In my head, it was a Nintendo franchise that was lesser than what I considered to be the premiere franchises, i.e. Zelda and Mario. But recently I've noticed that a fair amount of Metroid games are considered to be as good if not better than games from those series. The two that get the most praise are Metroid Prime for the GameCube and Super Metroid for the SNES. I figured that it's about time for me to see what all the fuss is about and play the game that really launched Metroid into the mainstream. So, let's see what Super Metroid has to offer.
After a quick recap of the past two games, Super Metroid begins with the space pirate Ridley stealing the Metroid embryo that Samus recovered in her previous adventure. She pursues Ridley to the planet Zebes in hopes of recovering the stolen Metroid. This is where the adventure begins. The core aspect and driving feature of Super Metroid is exploration. There are six main areas, and while each segment is unique, the planet as a whole manages to have a very cohesive feel. The higher levels have a lot of vegetation and life, but as you move deeper into the planet's core, the green starts to fade away and is replaced with molten rocks and lava. These subtle yet substantial changes in environment sets a tone for each individual area along with the planet as a whole. The music helps add to this tone even more. Its purpose isn't to stand out, but rather to blend in. It's the type of soundtrack that you sometimes forget is playing, but at the same time would notice its absence if it actually stopped. Between the music, the art design, and the sheer amount of secrets to be found, it's very easy to get pulled into the experience that Super Metroid offers. When you first come into a new area, you unlock parts of the map by moving from screen to screen. However, pretty early on in each section, there is a machine that fills in the map data for that area. While it fills in the key places that you will want to explore, some rooms are still left off the map, which makes you question if there is something hidden in every room you enter. It's a good balance between leading you in the right direction while not giving away every secret. The best part of exploring in Super Metroid is pretty much everything you find actually helps you. Whether it's missiles or energy tanks, it all improves Samus permanently. I've played a lot of games where exploring rewards you with something inconsequential, but in Super Metroid, every secret you collect feels important. Which is awesome. A common complaint that I've heard about the Metroid series is how much backtracking there is. I can understand how it would bother some people, but it didn't bother me. As you move through Zebes, you start to notice doors and other obstacles that you can't get past. Over time, you obtain the necessary power-ups and weaponry that allow you through these roadblocks. To me, there is something cool about seeing areas that I couldn't access until later. With that said, if you play the game in multiple sit-ins, it's easy to forget where these doors were or that they even existed, which can waste some time. But the biggest reason that I had to go through areas more than once was because I would forget to save often enough and then die, making me lose a lot of progress. There are only a handful of save points, and in my desire to explore new areas, along with being used to living in the era of autosave where you can barely take three steps before seeing the save icon on the bottom corner of your screen letting you know that it's okay to die, I kept on forgetting to save. Super Metroid is pretty generous with letting you experiment on new terrain and enemies, but there are a few long stretches without save points, and unless you backtrack to an earlier one, there is a risk of losing a lot of progress. The easiest solution to this problem is just to not die, but that was not an option for me. The only part of the game where I was a little annoyed with backtracking was right after beating Ridley for the second time. You had to make your way from his lair all the way to the first area, which is a long, long way. However, once I actually started heading back, I saw the beauty in being forced to backtravel. By this point in the game, Samus has powered up quite a bit, making the way back a breeze. Going through rooms that everyone struggled to get through were easy due to Samus' awesome power. There was something really neat about seeing this growth. Backtracking is a good way of showing the player how far they've come. I'm glad this level of it isn't in all games, but I think it works well here. You aren't really told how to do anything in Super Metroid. You have to figure it out on your own. Things like jumping, sprinting, and switching weapons are all pretty straightforward. It did take me a little while to figure out how to use the Morph Ball. It's as simple as hitting down on the D-pad twice, which I guess is pretty intuitive, but I would prefer it to be assigned to a button. The Y button has no function other than deselecting weapons, which I rarely used. There were moments where I was trying to switch into my Morph Ball quickly, but couldn't really do it in time. Also, I switched out of my Morph Ball all too frequently by pressing up on accident. Having it just be Y would have made certain maneuvers a little less frustrating. But, whatever. Anyway, instead of giving you written prompts, Super Metroid teaches you how to play with its level design. For instance, when it wants to teach you that Samus has different types of jumps, it places you in a room with enemies above and below you, forcing you to do a short hop. By using Samus' abilities in practical ways, it helps you better figure out how to control her. With that said, I really had trouble grasping the movement of Samus' jump. I always seemed to over or undershoot where I was trying to land. But, I guess I'll put that on me. Spread throughout the planet are animals that teach you certain maneuvers. There are these koala deer things that show you how to do a wall jump, and this emu that shows you how to do a super jump. Seeing these animals in action gave me all the explanation I needed to accomplish these tasks. It gave enough information to assist me, but not too much so I still felt rewarded when I figured it out. It's refreshing to see a show-don't-tell approach, opposed to what modern games do and give you a tell-and-then-tell-again approach. And then tell a third time. Combat seems to almost be an afterthought in Super Metroid. It's not because it isn't fun or done well, but because it takes a backseat to exploring. It was satisfying to take out enemies, but I never entered a room thinking the fun would come from fighting. It was always the need to find secrets. There is a lot of enemy variety, and each interaction feels unique. The enemies that I found to be most interesting were the ones that assisted you. There are certain areas where you can only progress by figuring out the best way to utilize a foe. The initial response to seeing just about anything is to shoot it, but there are some times where this will only hurt you. It's a really cool element that makes you rethink the way you approach a battle. As far as bosses go, I didn't really find those to be very memorable. There were a handful of them where my main strategy was to hide in a corner and shoot every once in a while until they went down. The only battles that really stood out to me were Kraid because of how massive and disgusting he was, Crocomire because I thought the mechanic of gaining and losing ground was really interesting, and Ridley because he can go fuck himself. As I already said, combat was not my main focus while playing Super Metroid, so I'm not really surprised that a handful of the bosses didn't stick out to me. But that's really just a result of how I approached the game, and I imagine it's different for everyone. Aside from the summary at the beginning of the game, Super Metroid is very light on plot. ## Shhh...I've Never Played: Castlevania
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XsjzPepEnnY

Remember when mainstream video games used to be... hard? Back then it wasn't a question of when you would be able to beat a game, but if you would be able to beat a game. Nothing was guaranteed. As quick as you got to the end, you could be shot right back to the beginning. There just aren't major games like that anymore. Games where you have to suffer and endure to make progress. Games where you die over and over and it's only until you learn lessons from past mistakes that you can clear a level. Mainstream games now give so many options to ease up the experience. When you fail, games insist that you lower the difficulty or offer you a power-up that allows you to breeze through a level, or give you the option to skip an entire level altogether. I want to be clear that I'm not saying these things are bad. Not all gamers possess the same skill sets, and having these extra options widens the accessibility of video games to a greater audience, which is okay. I just feel that there is something to be said about those hard games that made it so you actually became good at playing them. I've been in the mood to play a game that actually challenges me, and it just so happens that there's a pretty huge classic NES title that I'm a little embarrassed to say that I've missed out on. Shh, I've never played Castlevania. Castlevania is a very storied franchise. There have been about... a fuckton of Castlevania games since the original's release in 1986. Now the series seems to have fallen into a bit of a 3D pitfall, but Castlevania is known to have some of the best 2D action platforming of any series out there. There's no real reason as to why I never played it. I just didn't. But I'm ready now, and I thought what better place to start than the original. I'm going into knowing pretty much nothing about the series other than you have a whip and you're supposed to kill Dracula. So, let's see how this goes. From the start, it is clear that Castlevania is a very aesthetically pleasing game. Of course, me saying this is like saying that donuts are tasty or having money is nice. People already know. The colors pop and little details give the levels a lot of texture. The game just looks good. Sure, there are things that could have looked better, but as a whole, it has aged fairly well. For the most part, the artistic choices were strong enough that the primitive graphics don't really matter. It manages to have a dark mood while still using a lot of colors. What pulled me even further into the experience was the music. This might be because when I started up the game for the first time, there wasn't any. When it showed Simon Belmont, the game's protagonist, walk up to Dracula's castle, a little fanfare played, but then the level started and there was nothing. This apparently was caused by a glitch that turns off the music if you let the three demos play on the intro screen. When you die, the music will start playing like normal, but until then, you have to deal with the eerie silence. I don't know why, but seeing what the game was like without its music made me appreciate it that much more when it kicked in. It's pretty typical 8-bit dungeon crawling music, but it's a fucking 8-bit dungeon crawler, so it makes sense. Castlevania's gameplay is really fun. It's platformy, but you can't just jump over enemies like Mario. You actually have to deal with them, and dealing with them can be a bitch, but also rewarding. As everyone probably knows, Castlevania has very restrictive controls. When you jump, you can't change the trajectory of your jump, when you move, you move slowly, and when you attack, you stop moving altogether. These aren't bad things. In fact, they make the action more intense, and you actually have to think about the buttons you press so you don't fuck yourself over. But the restricted field does take some getting used to. Figuring out how to control myself and take out enemies proved to be the most important part of the game. I was able to do most of it with my whip, but various items helped me overcome the challenges that I otherwise would have struggled to get past. There's the axe, which hits enemies that are above you, the dagger, which can be thrown, the cross, which can also be thrown, but it comes back to you, making the dagger kind of look like a piece of shit, the watch, which stops time for a few brief seconds, and water. Holy water. It seems lame, but it's actually the best item in the game. Collecting hearts allows you to use items more, because that's a fucking normal game convention, and while it isn't necessary to use items, they can really help ease your troubles. The game is comprised of six levels, which features everything from a banquet hall to a torture chamber to a bunch of balconies to a swamp to some steampunky shit. Yeah, I didn't really think the last one fit in either. All in all, the game is pretty short. If you know what you're doing and you don't die, you could probably beat it in under 30 minutes. But if it's your first time and you suck at video games, then it will take a little longer. Yeah. Each level presents new challenges, and for the most part, it scales in difficulty pretty well. What's cool is Simon doesn't really get lasting power-ups. Yeah, there are the whip upgrades, but there are only a few of them, and you lose them each time you die. The only way to get good enough to conquer the increasing difficulty is by powering up your own fucking mind. Enemies always appear in the same spots and typically move in a certain pattern. There are certainly exceptions, but you have the opportunity to kill just about every enemy you encounter before they can hit you. It's discovering these patterns where the fun comes in. At first, enemy interactions often turn out to be lethal, but after a while, you figure it out. Fleeman? Easy. Bone towers? Ha! Give me a real challenge. Bats? No problem. God damn it! Once you practice enough, you can get to the boss with little to no troubles. In my opinion, the way bosses work is a little weird. If you primarily use your whip, each battle will be extremely difficult and harrowing. However, if you have the right item, then a lot of the bosses are pretty easy. For example, if you have the cross, you can take out the mummies in one hit. And if you have the holy water, you can make it so death doesn't even get the chance to move. I didn't really experiment much with holy water in other bosses, but I'm sure a bunch would have also been susceptible to it. I felt like bosses should be the hardest part of each level. But if you explore enough and get the right item, a lot of them end up being pushovers. It's good that the game rewards you for exploring, but being able to take them out so easily is a little ridiculous. And yeah, I know I could have just not used the items that make the bosses super easy, but maybe you could just stop being such a judgmental fucking bitch. Once you kill enough ghouls and other monsters, you reach Dracula's tower. Visually, this was my favorite part of the game. The moon looks good, and fucking just look at that moss. That is some good-looking moss. Anyway, Dracula is tough. In a very original final boss fashion, he teleports around the room and shoots fireballs at you. What's worse is he doesn't have a set pattern to how he moves. He teleports depending on your movements. But I began to realize that I could manipulate him into teleporting to certain spots if I moved the right way. Once I figured that out, I discovered the perfect timing to jump and attack so I could avoid getting hit. Much like the rest of the game, it was a process. I died a lot trying to beat him, but each time I got a little closer. Luckily, once you reach his tower, if you get a game over, you start right before him instead of at the beginning of the level. Once I got good enough, I was able to beat his first form without taking any damage. But then, of course, he transforms in the way only a final boss could. To a form so terrifying, so strong, that oh, holy water works. Uh, well, this is easy. Huh. Castlevania has had a pretty big impact on gaming. I can't really talk for how it's impacted the rest of the series, but there's a lot of them, so fucking, it probably has in some way. Castlevania was one of the first action platformers of its kind. Now that I've played it, it's pretty obvious that a lot of games have used its formula. For instance, I always wondered why Zelda II was the way it was, and now I realize it was probably an effort to make another game like Castlevania. Castlevania has fun, challenging gameplay. There's no real story in sight, or really even motivation as to why Simon wants to kill all these monsters other than they're probably evil, but I didn't really care. I just enjoyed the ride. Castlevania has aged very well, and is a classic that everyone kinda owes it to themselves to check out. It's not perfect, but what is? I'm just glad that I'm no longer the loser that has never played Castlevania. Now I'm just another loser who has played Castlevania. Which, when I say that out loud, it kinda seems worse, but... Thanks for watching! If you like the video, then press the like button and subscribe, because I'm making more videos like this, and you wouldn't wanna miss it. If you have missed my videos, you can click one of these

## Shhh...I've Never Played: A Link To The Past
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1PKq5K8GyH0

The Legend of Zelda series is awesome. I know it, you know it, fucking John Travolta knows it, everyone knows it. There have been 17 entries to the series, and each one is special in its own right. The original Legend of Zelda for the NES showed us how much fun exploration could be in video games. Ocarina of Time led Zelda into the 3D realm, changing the series forever. Majora's Mask and Wind Waker showed us that straying from typical Zelda conventions could still lead to amazing results. And A Link to the Past showed us, um, it showed us that, um, I mean, it showed us a lot of stuff that I totally know about because I've definitely played the game. Shh, I've never played A Link to the Past. A Link to the Past is not just seen as one of the greatest Zelda games of all time, but as one of the greatest games of all time. I've noticed that people born after 1990 typically view Ocarina of Time as a gift from the heavens that not only defines Zelda, but what all games should strive to be. While people born before 1990 think that that is a crock of shit because A Link to the Past is the crowning accomplishment in the series. Falling into the first category, I didn't have a ton of interest in playing A Link to the Past. It is one of my greater gaming sins. The weirdest part is I've beaten every other Zelda game. That includes Zelda II, which, fuck, just fuck. Hell, I've even beaten A Link Between Worlds, which is based off of A Link to the Past. I've been meaning to get around to it for a while, and now I have no more excuses, so let's do it. After starting up the game, a cutscene plays that explains the basic premise of the plot. Already there is way more information and detail than in the first two games. Which pretty much just said, get the Triforce and save Zelda. A Link to the Past tells you some backstory of Hyrule, it shows you actual visuals of the backstory, and then tells you to save Zelda, because some things never change. You wake up, go to the castle, find your dead uncle, save Zelda, and start your quest to get the Master Sword. I could go in depth about the story, but the game's fucking 20 years old, and I imagine everyone already knows it. After playing it for five minutes, it feels pretty Zelda-ish. It's clear that every 2D Zelda that came out after A Link to the Past is heavily influenced by it. Movement, swordplay, and enemy actions felt really familiar to me, even though I had never played this game before. Aside from the gameplay, I quickly realized a lot of things that are staples in the Zelda franchise originated from A Link to the Past. The first thing I noticed was the music. Kakariko Village's theme and Zelda's lullaby appear, along with the Master Sword theme. Being the Ocarina of Time scrub that I am, I always assumed that those songs originated from Ocarina, because I'm dumb. There are many other things that got started here too. For instance, this is the first appearance of the Master Sword, which is one of the most recognizable things in the series. It also introduces the kakus that will ruin your shit, capturing fairies in bottles, the hookshot, the ocarina, the sages, Link having pink hair. Scratch that last one, that last one is not right. It also introduced a theme that I'll call the Dual Worlds theme. In A Link to the Past, you gain access to the Dark World, a parallel dimension to Hyrule created by Ganon. Switching between the worlds allows you to access different parts of the map, which makes it possible to progress through the game and unlock various secrets. This premise is rampant in the series. It can be seen in the Oracle games, with transporting between past and present in ages, and through different seasons and seasons. It can also be seen in Twilight Princess, when switching between the Twilight Realm and the Normal Realm. It can be seen in the Minish Cap, when you change sizes. Skyward Sword has different puzzles where you have to manipulate time in certain areas to solve them. And even Ocarina of Time has you switch between Young Link and Adult Link to access different parts of Hyrule and explore it in new ways. It allows the developers to utilize various assets and keep the world a manageable size while still having a ton to explore. Another convention that started in A Link to the Past is that Zelda actually does stuff. I mean, some stuff. She's no Sheik or Tetra, but at least she isn't Sleeping Beauty anymore, most of the time. She talks and gives advice, but still feels very much like a damsel in distress. While some might argue that Zelda is a damsel in distress in every game, I feel like Nintendo has empowered her and given her more depth in each passing title. The difference between how Zelda is portrayed now and how she was portrayed in A Link to the Past is pretty huge. But with that said, A Link to the Past at least makes her feel less like a goal that has to be reached, more like a person that Link actually cares about. Along with Zelda being more prevalent, so are other characters. As in, there are actually other characters. Sure, Zelda 1 had Old Man and Zelda 2 had Bagu and townsfolk who look exactly the same but are different colors, but A Link to the Past has a ton of new characters that you actually have somewhat meaningful interactions with. It's important because the whole point of the game is to save people, and if you don't care about the people you're saving, then why bother? Having more characters that Link is connected to makes you feel like this is your world and your people that you need to save. It takes away a lot of the emptiness that existed in the earlier titles. This trend of appealing to players' sense of emotion by having Link interact and care about people has grown in every release since A Link to the Past. It is one of the many reasons that so many people are immersed in the Zelda franchise. It gives direction and motivation, which this game has a lot of. As a whole, the game made a lot more sense than the previous two titles. Figuring out certain paths and how to progress challenged me, but rarely infuriated me like the original Legend of Zelda. The only part I got remotely frustrated with was figuring out how to find the Aether Medallion to open the Swamp Dungeon and the Quake Medallion to open up Turtle Rock. There isn't a lot of direction on where to find them and you kind of just have to stumble upon where they are by exploring the world. At the time, figuring out where to find these medallions pissed me off, but looking back now, I kind of realized that's the point. These medallions are needed to open two of the later dungeons in the game, and it seems like the developer's way of saying, explore the fucking world before the game is over. Exploration is a huge part of the series, so while I would have liked to have a little more direction on how to find the medallions, I can appreciate why they didn't put it in. For me, the most difficult part of the game was combat. Fighting in A Link to the Past is straightforward, but fucking hard. Especially in the Dark World, enemies rinse through your health, so you have to be really careful when battling. Getting all four bottles becomes extremely important if you don't want to restart all the time. Obtaining the blue and red armor, which lessens the amount of damage you take, helps, but it didn't stop me from dying a shit ton. While enemies and bosses were hard, everything did feel fair. When I died, it was usually my fault, and that's okay. Trial and error are big parts of A Link to the Past. Figuring out the best way to dispose of an enemy or a boss takes experimentation, which is why figuring these things out is so satisfying. Well, now that I've beaten all the dungeons, it's time to face Ganon. Over the years, I have fought Ganon many times, but none of those fights made me half as furious as this one did. It really isn't that hard, especially if you have fairies and the red tunic, but there is a point where he creates holes around the outer edge of the chamber, which you can fall down. If that happens, then you have to start the whole entire fight over. I imagine players that are better than myself didn't have a lot of trouble with not falling down the holes, but I did. I had a lot of trouble with not falling down the holes. I will say, though, that having all this built-up frustration made beating him feel that much better. A Link to the Past is a really good game, but if I'm being honest, there are a lot of Zelda games that I enjoyed playing more. It fell somewhere in the middle for me. With that said, I appreciate it for what it did for the franchise. It set up a lot of the mythos and themes that are prevalent in the series. As far as what makes Zelda games Zelda games, the things introduced in A Link to the Past have as much, if not more, to do with it than any other game in the series. The only other games that come close are the original because it's the fucking original and Ocarina of Time because of the transition into a 3D world. A Link to the Past is a classic. It should be honored, cherished, and remembered as the game that led the Zelda series into greatness. Yeah, it's not my favorite, but I'm still happy to say that I have beaten A Link to the Past. ## Top 10 Books In Video Games

There are many people who think that video games have no educational value, but how can that be true when so many video games have books in them, huh? Bioshock Infinite, books. Red Dead Redemption, books. Metal Gear Solid 4, books. God damn it, Snake. Books appear in video games fairly often, so I decided to make a list highlighting my top 10 favorite books in all of video games. Let go. Skyrim has a lot of books in it. Like, a lot of books. If I'm being honest, I didn't really read most of them. In fact, whenever I found a book, I was more likely to do something like this with it. Colby. Colby. Shit. Colby. God damn it. But there were a few books I did read. Well, there was one I read. Okay, I didn't actually read it, but I heard it was good. That book is Colvin the Dragon, an adventure tale for young Nord boys. What I like about this book is how much it reminds me of the Choose Your Own Adventure books I read as a kid. By that, I mean most of your choices lead to a gruesome and terrible death. There are six endings, and only one of them ends with you surviving. You can be eaten by the dragon, possessed by a ghost, and even poisoned by high elves that run a nearby tavern. The book is a nice little break from the actual game where you pretty much do the same kind of stuff. Yoshi's Story starts with the Yoshis living happily until Baby Bowser steals a super happy tree and puts a spell on their island turning it into a pop-up storybook. The remaining Yoshis must work through each page to get the super happy tree back. While the plot should definitely be called into question, the presentation of this game is actually pretty great. Each page of the storybook is detailed and varied in theme. It's the pop-up book that every kid would want to have. A big part of this is there's something on each page for everyone to enjoy. Maybe it's the group of shy guy pirates sailing across the ocean. Maybe it's the magma monster that's screaming or yawning. I don't know. I can never really tell. Or maybe it's Poochie, the dog. I mean, I know he's supposed to be a dog, but really? While there are a lot of things in Yoshi's Story that don't hold up as well as they used to, the storybook presentation is still extremely entertaining. When people think of LittleBigPlanet, happiness is generally the first thing that comes to mind. I think this is why Clive Hampforth is so funny. Everything from his voice to his mannerisms are downright depressing. If I'm being honest, the only reason Clive is on this list is because I'm pretty sure he would have offed himself if he wasn't. Clive is the owner of the Factory of a Better Tomorrow, which created the world's most accurate calendars and spaceships until it was taken over by the Negativitron. Clive wasn't really that happy before any of this happened, so you can only imagine how much worse it's gotten since. Helping Clive get back his factory was one of my favorite parts of LittleBigPlanet 2. Something about his misery had a direct line to my funny bone. I don't know if this means it was really good writing or that I'm a bad person that feels better about myself when others are miserable. I mean, I'm guessing a bit of both. During The Last of Us, there are certain moments in the game where Ellie will take a break and read some jokes from a book she found called No Pun Intended. There are two volumes of the book, but I prefer volume one because the cover says, you gotta be kidding me on it, which is hilarious. Hearing Ellie tell jokes is a nice break from strangling dudes and running from infected. The jokes are bad. Why did the scarecrow get a promotion? I don't know. Because he was outstanding in his field. Really bad. But something about Ellie's charm made the jokes worthwhile and something I look forward to hearing. I walked into my sister's room and tripped on a bra. It was a booby trap. I don't get it. After being transformed into the Deku Shrub in Majora's Mask, you come in contact with a small-time gang clock town named the Bombers. To join their ranks, you have to play a game of hide-and-seek. After finding all five of them, they give you a secret code to their hideout. However, they don't let you become a full member because you're not human. Racist son of a bitch. Once you're turned back into a human, you can play hide-and-seek again, and after it, they'll make you a full member. Upon becoming a member, you are presented with the Bomber's Notebook, which keeps track of townfolks' schedules, their problems, and if you help them. The book also proves that despite acting like little punks, at the end of the day, the Bombers just want to make the world a better place. A place without Deku shrubs. Minecraft lets you do just about anything, which is good because I like doing things, but bad because I spend too much time doing these things. Things like building a giant fort in a tree, filling my friend's house with chickens, and relaxing in my underground grotto. But in regards to the list, one of the other great things you can do in Minecraft is grab a book and read. The best thing about the books in Minecraft is they can be any book you want them to be. Want to read Game of Thrones? Done. Hunger Games? Easy. Fifty Shades of Grey? No. Don't. The only problem with this is you have to write each book word for word, which is pretty time consuming. Whatever, it's Minecraft. You're gonna spend a thousand hours in it anyway, so why not? Right? In Sid Meier's Pirates, you get to sail around the Caribbean, pillaging, burning, and dancing. Actually, dancing might be the most important part. As you gain notoriety across the Caribbean, you'll get the opportunity to dance with many governor's daughters who, if they take a fancy to you, will give you cool stuff. There are a lot of items that help throughout the game, but my favorite is the Dutch Rudder. The Dutch Rudder is a navigational journal that improves your map by showing more settlements. More importantly though, Dutch Rudder sounds exactly like Dutch Rudder, which is also a slang term for when a man grabs his... You know, you should just look it up on Urban Dictionary. That in itself is actually only okay. Also, the Spanish Rudder is technically better, but its name doesn't make me giggle as much. The Dutch Rudder really only made the list because I'm immature. Yeah. There are many characters that keep a personal journal with them, but my favorite belongs to Nathan Drake. He details the places he's been, things he finds interesting, clues to puzzles, and Sully's facial hair. The journal adds a whole new element of immersion into the game. Opening your journal near the beginning of Uncharted 2 and seeing an entire page dedicated to Lana makes you understand Drake in a whole new way. It's the little details that really make his journal so special. I found myself constantly checking it, hoping that there would be a new entry. In a game centered around storytelling, it's no wonder that Drake has one of the finest journals in all of gaming. Banjo-Kazooie. This game is filled with amazing characters, but only one of them is a book. Hidden across Gruntilda's lair is Cheeto, Grunty's spellbook that, if I bet you couldn't have guessed it, helps you cheat. Cheeto is hidden in three different locations throughout the lair. Each time you find him, he gives you a code. One that increases the amount of eggs you can have, one that increases the amount of red feathers you can have, and one that increases the amount of gold feathers you can have. Cheeto earns his spot on the list not only because he gives you upgrades, but also because he gives more meaning to exploring the overworld. Is that enough? Oh, you wanted a joke of some type. Huh. Well, I don't have one. One of my favorite books to read as a kid was Winnie the Pooh, so it only seems right to put Hundred Acre Woods from Kingdom Hearts at the top of the list. Spread throughout the various worlds in Kingdom Hearts are five torn pages that belong to the book. If you visit Merlin's house, you can put the pages back in the book and explore Hundred Acre Woods in a way that you never have before. There's a lot of stuff to do, and it's actually all pretty fun. You keep bees away from Pooh as he flies up the honey tree, bounce around with Tigger and Roo, and ruin Rabbit's garden. Fuck you! My favorite part about this level is that there are no Heartless. There are a lot of reasons why this is nice, but the biggest is it keeps Winnie the Pooh feeling like Winnie the Pooh. The rest of the worlds try very hard to shove the Heartless storyline into the original Disney features, which usually feels forced. In Hundred Acre Woods, your only focus is exploring and meeting the inhabitants of the forest. Maybe it's due to nostalgia, but Hundred Acre Woods is my favorite book in any video game. A big part of what you do in Animal Crossing is getting villagers to like you. In my attempts to do this, I realized I did things for them that I would probably never do for my real friends. Run errands, do their yard work, write them letters, ask them how they're doing. You know, the type of stuff that if you did for your real friends, you wouldn't be given a cool t-shirt for doing, so what's the point? It's the only game that made me feel guilty for not playing extended periods of time. The townsfolk know exactly how long I've been gone, which makes it seem like they really care. I mean, it's pretty clear that they're obsessed with me. In the end, I wanted to impress the townsfolk in Animal Crossing because there wasn't much of a game without it. I mean, there's not really much of a game with it, either. But, whatever. While some players certainly preferred Aeris, throughout my many playthroughs of Final Fantasy VII, I always tried to impress Tifa. For some reason, I made Cloud chronically lie about Tifa being his girlfriend. Maybe it's because of the sweetness of their childhood friendship, maybe it's because she's a badass who fights with a fist, or maybe it's because she could change clothes just by spinning. While the timing is never right, their relationship feels destined. Making Cloud seem cool in front of her becomes a must throughout the game. Also, on a personal level, I played this game way before I ever started talking to girls, so it gave me some much-needed practice in flirting. Oh, yeah, I know how to do this one. Yeah, give me something hard. Uh, wait. I mean, I'll give you something hard? This one is a little different than the others. I liked Sam the whole way through Dishonored, but I didn't want to impress him until the very end. On the way to the final mission, he laid this one on me. There's an ending where Sam is even more upset with you, but for me, hearing that he was disappointed felt worse. Traveling with Sam, I had grown to respect him, but I never thought about how he viewed me. When I realized this was it, I felt so terrible that I went back to play the game with as little chaos as possible in the hopes that he might respect me. But then I remembered I suck at stealth because I have no patience. Sorry, Sam. I wish you loved me. Tetra is my personal favorite version of Princess Zelda, and there are two big reasons for this. A, she's the captain of a pirate ship, and B, she's the captain of a pirate ship. B doesn't have to be different than A. A is good enough to also be B. Tetra is anything but a proper lady, and this is what makes her so compelling. Other versions of Zelda are solely interested in protecting the kingdom, while Tetra's main interest is whatever she damn well pleases. To me, this makes the good things she does have more of an impact. While one of my main motivations was to save my sister, I also wanted to show Tetra how much Link was worth. At the start of the game, she views him the way I viewed the Booger Kid. I wanted to prove that Link was less like this and more like this. I mean this. Ellie is one of the most well-written and interesting characters in all of storytelling. The first time you meet, Joel doesn't seem to care for her much. However, it was already obvious that they would end up growing close. I started the game viewing Ellie as a peer, but as I progressed, I felt more and more like her caretaker. Whenever we walked past a mountain of bodies, I hoped she would look away. Whenever she asked for a gun, I felt conflicted about what would keep her safer. And whenever I strangled some gangbang motherfuckers, I tried to make sure she thought I was just putting them down for a nap. I did these things because I cared about how she viewed Joel and the world around her. I wanted to make sure she viewed Joel as a friend and not a monster. Falco might be the most popular character in the Star Fox franchise. Why? I mean, look at him. He's a BAMF. In fact, when you look up BAMF in the dictionary, there's nothing there because BAMF isn't actually a word, but if it were, there'd be a picture of Falco about to shake hands with Bruce Lee while Gregorio Rasputin stands by idly watching. Falco spends a lot of his time shitting on Fox. Even when he's being nice, he comes off as a dick. Despite this, it's hard not to respect him. He has a lot of confidence and holds himself well, and all of his insults really made me want to prove that Fox had just as much skill as him. I felt proud when I beat Andross and finally heard, Okay, I'll admit it. You did good, Fox. Yeah, you better admit it, you blue feathered fuck. I mean, who else could it have been? While everyone has their own opinions about Bioshock Infinite, it is undisputed that there is something special about Elizabeth. I think I speak for everyone who finished the game when I say I wish we could have just stayed here. When you're with Elizabeth, you feel a range of emotions. Watching her interact with the world and see things for the first time is exciting, while the moment she looks at Booker like he's a monster feels terrible. Along with Ellie, Elizabeth is the closest a video game character has come to being a real person. Her feelings seem legitimate, so it's hard not to take her seriously. She's caring and smart, which makes her so likable. Pretty early on, I wanted to do whatever I could to get her to Paris, and I got mad at Booker until he felt the same way. Elizabeth is the number one character I tried to impress because she is the character that impressed me the most. Thanks for watching!
